News.title: Major search off Welsh coast for missing man
News.content:
Major search off Welsh coast for missing man

Dyfed-Powys Police said Ben had intended to go rock climbing outside St Davids but he has not been heard from since around midday on Wednesday

View Image Rock climber Ben, 47, went missing after heading out to Carreg y Barcud or Caer Bwdy Bay (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Rescuers are searching an area off the Welsh coast for a man who vanished after heading on a rock climbing trip.

‌



A boat and helicopter from the coastguard have been scrambled to search for the missing man, named only as Ben, who is said to be from St. Davids.

‌



The emergency crews are searching for Ben in an area on the coast of Pembrokeshire after the 47-year-old was last spoken to by his family at around midday on Wednesday, according to police.

‌



It is believed he intended to go rock climbing, either in the Carreg y Barcud area, near Trelerw, or Caer Bwdy Bay, outside St Davids, Wales Online reports.

Dyfed-Powys Police said Ben is described as around 5ft 11in tall, of athletic build, with short brown/greying hair and brown eyes.

Article continues below

He was carrying an orange bag and wearing black climbing shoes with an orange strap at the time he went missing.

The force said anyone who has seen or spoken to Ben since midday on Wednesday is urgently asked to get in touch.

The force can be contacted online, by calling 101 or emailing 101@dyfed-powys.police.uk. Quote reference 429 of August 5.

News.title: US fast food chain to open in UK as fans say 'finally' - 10 more sites may follow
News.content:
US fast food chain to open in UK as fans say 'finally' - 10 more sites may follow

It is preparing to open its first UK restaurant but many more could follow in its footsteps as food fans hail the news

View 2 Images The US chain could open several chains in the UK (Image: Jam Press/@masonslobster.uk)

A popular American fast food chain that serves lobster rolls for roughly the same price as a burger has plans to open multiple stores in the UK. Mason's Famous Lobster Rolls is gearing up to open its first British restaurant, with the potential to launch further locations over the next three years.

‌



The first site will be located on Lamb Street in London's Spitalfields Market and is expected to open shortly. Between five and ten additional restaurants could follow during the next 15 to 18 months.

‌



The brand specialises in lobster served in toasted rolls, but says it keeps the traditionally expensive ingredient affordable thanks to what it calls its centralised purchasing system. Pietro Funaro, the businessman behind bringing the chain to Europe, told hospitality publication Propel that the brand buys lobster collectively from the same fishermen and negotiates discounts based on volume.

‌



The full menu and pricing for the first UK restaurant are yet to be announced. Mr Funaro said the chain anticipates its average customer spend to be comparable to that at Five Guys.

Mason's Famous Lobster Rolls was founded in the US in 2014 by former restaurant seafood buyer Dan Beck. Mr Beck had spent time with lobster fishermen in Maine and built the business around the importance of sourcing top-quality seafood. The chain has since grown to around 45 locations across the US.

‌



Italian investment banker and businessman Mr Funaro stumbled upon the brand during a trip to America in 2023. He felt that Europe already had no shortage of burger, fried chicken and poke restaurants, but was lacking an affordable lobster-roll chain.

Mr Funaro brought Mason's to Europe last year and currently runs two restaurants in Milan, as well as sites in Florence and Venice. He hopes the company can reach 40 European restaurants over the next five years, with its forthcoming London launch playing a key role in that expansion.

View 2 Images Some fans say they cannot wait for the chain to open in the UK (Image: Jam Press/@masonslobster.uk)

‌



Explaining why he chose the capital for the chain's UK debut, Mr Funaro said in an Instagram video: "London is a city that never sleeps and never stops surprising you with new ideas and a vibrant energy." Eager diners have already been reacting to photographs and videos posted by the brand on social media.

"Finally! A lobster roll place in London! Can't wait," one person said. Another social media user familiar with the American version added: "Looks SOOOOOO authentic!!! Feels like I'm back in Maine!!"

"Can't waitttt," someone else wrote, while another urged the restaurant to: "Come SOONER."

Article continues below

Mason's Famous Lobster Rolls is yet to announce an official opening date or UK prices for its Spitalfields restaurant.

News.title: 'Food banks are scrambling' - drought pushes families to the brink
News.content:
'Food banks are scrambling' - drought pushes families to the brink

As concerns grow over food cost inflation warnings before the year is out, those behind the scenes of Britain's food banks fear what's next for those on the breadline

View 10 Images Britain's foodbanks are already facing the impact of climate change (stock photo) (Image: Getty Images)

After a fresh wave of food price inflation threatens to push vulnerable families over the brink, anti-poverty campaigners are calling on the government to expand its NHS Healthy Start scheme to prevent widespread child hunger.

‌



After a fourth heatwave and a prolonged drought devastating harvests across the country, experts warn that low-income households - already struggling during the long summer holidays - face further spikes in the cost of basic fruits and vegetables.

‌



Now Andrew Forsey, OBE, National Director of Feeding Britain, says the government must draw upon its "all-too-secret weapon" Healthy Start, to fend off the worst of what's to come.

‌



Administered by the NHS, the scheme provides eligible low-income families with at least £4.65 per week towards the cost of fruit, vegetables, milk, and pulses, with this allowance doubled for children under one.

View 10 Images Extreme weather has severely affected this year's crops (Image: Getty Images)

‌



However, Andrew warns that this safety net is underused and failing to keep pace with soaring costs. "The sad truth is, even on a good day, you have between a quarter and a third of all eligible families not signed up for the Healthy Start allowance, so they're missing out on that vital help," he said.

"Given that families find it hard enough to access and afford a good range of vegetables for a healthy diet, any increase in the cost or restrictions in availability will make it even harder for poorer families. That's clearly a concern.

‌



"And then if we look at the actual real-terms value of that weekly allowance, it is worth less today than it was 20 years ago. Depending on what, whether it's general inflation or food inflation, you use as your yardstick, it's worth around a fifth less today than it was five years ago."

View 10 Images The price of fruit and veg could rise steeply in the years to come (Image: Getty Images)

The call to expand Healthy Start comes alongside new research from the Education Policy Institute (EPI), which found that almost a quarter (24 per cent) of UK families with children under five are now experiencing food poverty - skipping meals, eating less, or losing weight because they can't afford food.

‌



While progress has been made for school-age children, including the upcoming extension of free school meals for Universal Credit recipients, support for toddlers and infants remains inconsistent.

Recent data from The Food Foundation shows that 65% of food-insecure households had bought less fruit over the past month, while 55% bought less vegetables.

View 10 Images The National Farmers' Union (NFU) has warned that food shortages could be on the way (Image: Getty Images)

‌



It's at this time of year that many parents caring for children over the long summer holidays are left struggling to cover gaps usually filled by free school meals.

Nationally, 6.5 million adults and 2.2 million children currently live in food-insecure households, with nine per cent needing support in the past six months, the most common being food banks.

Campaigners warn that the crisis will deepen as the ongoing drought, coupled with the scorching heatwaves, wreaks havoc on British agriculture.

‌



View 10 Images Supermarket shoppers are expected to feel the pinch of further inflation later this year (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

It's had a severe impact with woeful salad crops, early cereal harvests and broccoli yield, while there's also been drops in milk production from cows struggling with heat stress.

As a country currently largely reliant on imports, the UK has also felt the economic aftershock of fierce wildfires in the continent, which have affected the production of everything from olives to wheat.

‌



According to recent industry reports, wholesale prices have spiked dramatically, with the tomatoes up 60 per cent, while iceberg lettuce has climbed by 90 per cent and potatoes by over 40 per cent.

View 10 Images Ordinary fruit and veg items could soon become a luxury (Image: Getty Images)

Unfortunately, there could be even greater challenges ahead. The Bank of England forecasts that food price inflation will rise to 3.5% before the end of the year.

‌



While the impoverishing effects of climate change are well underway and can already be felt at the checkouts, think tank The Autonomy Institute warns that climate disruption could push the price of fruit and veg, turning produce into an unaffordable luxury.

It predicts that heatwaves could add 11% to the current prices of the top 20 fruit and veg items in the UK by the year 2035, rising again by a staggering 68% by 2050 "under a high emissions scenario", when taking into account normal inflation rates.

View 10 Images This year has seen the driest July on record (Image: Getty Images)

‌



On the grounds of climate change alone, the price of tropical favourites such as melons, oranges, bananas, easy peelers and grapes could rise by 12 per cent to 14 per cent by 2035 and 80 per cent to 93 per cent by 2050. When taking all these figures into account, it's estimated that, by 2050, a basket of fruit and veg could be 170 per cent more expensive than current costs.

As checkout prices rise, charities are now calling upon the government to protect those most vulnerable before the pangs of further inflation set in.

Rising living costs mean that households that previously donated to food banks are now cutting back, leaving charities struggling with depleted stocks just as demand surges. Andrew and his team have noted a notable decrease in donations to food banks during the recent heatwaves, a trend he partly attributes to working-class households that were previously able to donate, now struggling to cover their own food needs on top of other everyday bills.

‌



View 10 Images It's at this time of year that many parents caring for children over the long summer holidays are left struggling to cover gaps usually filled by free school meals (Image: PA)

According to Andrew: "It's that one part of their weekly routine they've had to sacrifice, namely that giving of either food or money to their local food bank." He continued: "On the whole, we're seeing reductions in the amounts of donated goods from the public to food banks, while the need for food banks remains still unacceptably high. So food banks are struggling to square that circle of reduced donations on the one hand, but stubbornly high demand on the other."

Matt Stallard, chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, told the Mirror: "We currently support about 16,000 people a year. When we were coming out of the pandemic, we were supporting about 8,000 people a year.

‌



"So, we've seen that double since the pandemic, with the cost-of-living challenges that have happened, layer upon layer across these last few years. Any additional pressures on the food supply or fuel are going to push the cost of living up further. That is undoubtedly a concern for us.

View 10 Images Nationally, 6.5 million adults and 2.2 million children currently live in food-insecure households (Image: PA)

"If everyone is having to ration, they aren't going to donate as much. If we're scrambling with everyone else to get food, obviously, it's the most in-need people who will suffer the most."

‌



Sabine Goodwin, Director of the Independent Food Aid Network (IFAN), agreed that emergency food aid can't be a permanent solution.

She said: "A charitable food aid response to poverty has proved itself to be ineffective at reducing food insecurity while climate change has been the elephant in the room for far too long."

"What's needed are sustainable solutions to both problems, ensuring everyone in our society has enough money to not only afford the bare essentials but to live well."

‌



View 10 Images Sabine Goodwin, Director of the Independent Food Aid Network (IFAN), has warned that emergency food aid can't be a permanent solution (Image: PA)

Andrew continued: "My overriding concern is for the ability of poorer households to access and afford the food they need for a decent life. And clearly, some of the global trends we're seeing at the moment pose a threat to those households' ability to access and afford the food they need.

"So that's why we need to look at initiatives such as the national endeavour to end avoidable food waste in the UK, which should see the trebling of the amount of surplus goods that flow from the farm gate into communities as an important policy."

‌



Meanwhile, going forward, Matt hopes to see a "properly joined-up, funded and long-term vision for anti-poverty strategies". Over in Manchester, which, despite its glossy image of growth, has a child poverty rate of 43.6 per cent, Matt and other anti-poverty campaigners are working to pursue community-led initiatives to put an end to food banks for good.

This, for example, includes replacing food banks with more "dignified" social supermarkets, led by the "local community that can also hook into other kinds of support". Going forward, Matt is calling upon the government to ensure anti-poverty charities and food provision charities have access to food.

"But also the supermarkets. We buy wholesale from supermarkets and wholesale suppliers, as well as using donated cash, and having food donated. For us to keep maintaining some kind of service, even if it were kind of limited or reduced, we'd need to still get access to the wholesalers and retailers to actually buy the food. So if there are limits or if it's harder for us to actually order the food because they're prioritising their own shops, for example, we all will suffer."

Article continues below

He added: "If there was some way to ensure that anti-poverty charities, food distribution charities could secure the food that they need, I think that would obviously help us do our job better.

Do you have a story to share? Email me at julia.banim@reachplc.com

News.title: Bruce Willis' wife's guilt at celebrating 50th birthday after his dementia diagnosis
News.content:
Bruce Willis' wife's guilt at celebrating 50th birthday after his dementia diagnosis

Bruce Willis stepped away from the spotlight over his health in 2022, with wife Emma and ex-wife, Demi Moore issuing a public statement announcing his dementia diagnosis

View 3 Images Bruce Willis is being supported by wife Emma (Image: EMMAHEMINGWILLIS/INSTAGRAM)

Emma Heming Willis has revealed that she felt guilty about celebrating her 50th birthday amid husband Bruce Wiilis’ devastating health battles.

‌



The Die Hard star, 71, was previously diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) - a form of the condition that affects behaviour and language - in 2023. His loved ones have rallied around him ever since, and raised awareness for the illness.

‌



During an appearance on the Making Space podcast, Emma said she'd struggled to think how she would celebrate her milestone birthday in June, and explained that her friends convinced she had to do something.

‌



“The celebration was lovely,” she told host Hoda Kotb. “I have not really been in the celebratory feelings of late. I was unsure if I really wanted to do anything. But I had a friend of mine who kept sort of pushing and saying, 'You don’t wanna miss out on your 50th. You have to celebrate in some form or fashion.'

“I really sat with that, and I thought about it. And I thought, 'You know what? I don’t wanna look back and think, why didn’t I celebrate 50?' It is something to celebrate. My mum and some friends put together this really lovely party at the house.”

Instead of a huge affair, Emma - who shares two children with the Hollywood icon - enjoyed a lowkey night surrounded by friends and family, as they enjoyed tacos and margaritas.

‌



However, she explained that she “wrestled” with guilt throughout the celebration, amid Bruce’s ongoing struggles with his health.

View 3 Images Emma turned 50 this year but said she struggled with the celebrations (Image: emmahemmingwillis / Instagram)

View 3 Images Bruce is dad to five daughters; three with ex-wife Demi Moore and two with wife Emma (Image: emmahemingwillis/Instagram)

‌



"I always wrestle with it. I think guilt is something that I am always carrying, but I’ve learned that it is really not helpful,” she continued. “What I know is I always go back to, ‘what would my husband want for me?’ He would want me to have a big, fun bash. He would want me to celebrate my life with my friends and family, and that is what I always think about when guilt of any sort comes in front of me.

“I’m really happy that I did - we brought together my friends, some family, and it was a really lovely, intimate night. On top of it, it was the Knicks final and they won! It was a great celebration.”

Bruce stepped away from the spotlight over his health in 2022, and his loved ones - including Emma and his ex-wife, Demi Moore, issued a public statement the following year, announcing his diagnosis.

‌



During a recent appearance on the Bossticks podcast, Emma clarified his symptoms, sharing that his memory has not been impacted.

"The one that Bruce has affects language. But there’s another variant that will affect behaviour and another one that could affect movement,” she said.

"That’s a different part of the brain. So when people say, ‘Oh, does he remember who you are?’ Well, he does because he doesn’t have Alzheimer’s, he has FTD. I think that’s a very common misconception that, when you think of dementia, we think of memory loss.”

Article continues below

Bruce was initially diagnosed with aphasia in 2022, and retired from acting shortly after. Emma explained that she first noticed his FTD signs when his childhood stutter returned.

She added: “I think what you experience with any form of dementia is it just takes. You know these diseases they take and they take, sometimes very slowly and you are grieving different losses all the time. So you are constantly in grief. I’ve just learned how to navigate it.”

News.title: Families slam funeral director Robert Bush's apology letter as 'slap in the face'
News.content:
Families slam funeral director Robert Bush's apology letter as 'slap in the face'

Bush failed to bury or cremate people and gave grieving families the ashes of strangers. He offered those affected a written apology, but some reacted angrily today.

Robert Bush: Families give statement following sentencing

A letter of apology from disgraced funeral boss Robert Bush has sparked fury from the families of his victims.

‌



Bush was jailed after he failed to bury or cremate people and gave grieving families the ashes of strangers, and in at least one case, an animal. Now, he has offered those impacted by his actions a written apology, but today some have reacted in anger at his latest actions.

‌



Bush, 48, was jailed for 20 years at Hull Crown Court on Friday. Police found about 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes after raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024, following a tip-off. Jasmine Beverley, 40, whose son's remains were discovered at the funeral parlour nearly two years after he was stillborn, told The Mirror the letter was “cold and condescending”.

‌



View 4 Images Robert Bush has been jailed for 20 years (Image: Humberside Police)

She said: “The letter was read to us after he was jailed at Hull crown court and we were all in total disbelief, everyone in that room was - you could hear a pin drop. There were five families in the room.

"It’s not an apology. He’s not apologising for what he’s done but how the families feel about what he’s done. It sounded empty and hollow. It sounded like ChatGPT had helped him out a bit. "

‌



Jasmine points out the start of his letter which reads; 'I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that wish to say something directly to you...' She said: "That was the first line and he hadn't even bothered to check it for mistakes. It's just an insult, I really wouldn't have bothered.

“It was the last line that really got me though: ‘I hope that in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved ones for who they were rather than the circumstances that have followed.' There's no acknowledgement of what he's done.

View 4 Images Jasmine Beverley's son, Sunny, was stillborn in May 2022 - his remains were found on the floor of Bush's funeral directors (Image: Andy Commins)

‌



"I’ve got no good memories, Rob is the memories of my son. He haunts me and I still can’t sleep. I thought I would be able to rest easy after he was jailed but I haven’t. I just want a public inquiry now, we all do.”

In his open letter to victims, Bush wrote: "I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry. There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced.

‌



"I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you. I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so."

View 4 Images The victims of Robert Bush outside court (Image: Scott Heppell/PA Wire)

‌



The former undertaker admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities. Prosecutors said Bush ran a "shambolic and chaotic" operation at the Hessle Road premises and his "appalling" offending had caused "extreme emotional pain, anguish and upset".

Jasmine told the court how learning that her baby Sunny Beverley-Conlin was found in a brown paper bag on the floor of the funeral parlour "will stay with me for the rest of my life". Sunny's remains were recovered from the Hessle Road premises one year and 10 months after he was stillborn on 13 May 2022, the court heard.

She was given a set of ashes by Bush the following March. Jasmine added: "Reading the letter has left me feeling nothing but anger. I don't have the luxury of separating my memories of Sunny from what happened because the memories I do have are tied directly to the mismanagement of the final act of love I tried to give him - his funeral. This will haunt me for the rest of my life."

‌



Karen Dry, who has been supporting some of the families, said: "There was no sorrow or remorse in the letter . It's a slap in the face, he's just out for himself."

View 4 Images Karen Dry acted as a spokesperson for the bereaved families during the court hearings (Image: Scott Heppell/PA Wire)

Robert Bush's letter in full:

‌



"To everyone who has been affected by my actions.

"I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that [sic] wish to say something directly to you. I know that many of you entrusted me and my business with the care of someone you loved during one of the most difficult times in your lives.

"I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry. There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced. I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you.

Article continues below

"I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so.

"I do not expect forgiveness, nor do I write this letter in the hope of reducing the seriousness of what has happened. I simply wanted you to know that I genuinely regret the consequences of my actions, and the impact they have had on so many people.

"I appreciate that every family's experience has been different, and I respect that some people may never wish to accept my apology. That is entirely understandable. I hope that, in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved one for who they were rather than for the circumstances that have followed. I am truly sorry."

News.title: Monster shark '25ft long' spotted in UK waters as sightseers stunned
News.content:
Monster shark '25ft long' spotted in UK waters as sightseers stunned

An enormous shark has been spotted lurking off the coast of the Isle of Man - the beast is believed to be a basking shark measuring around 25ft

Moment a 'monster' shark spotted patrolling just off British Isles

An enormous shark has been spotted patrolling the waters just off the coast of the British Isles.

‌



Footage of the monstrous creature captures it cruising just beneath the surface near Peel on the Isle of Man.

‌



One dramatic clip shows a huge dorsal fin slicing through the water, while another captures the giant shark heading directly towards sightseers aboard a boat.

‌



Yet despite its terrifying appearance, the giant fish was in fact a harmless basking shark. Nicholas Lewis, of Casey J Fishing Trips, said: "It's been years since we've seen so many basking sharks. They were 25-foot long.

View 3 Images The huge creature was spotted lurking beneath the waters in the Isle of Man (Image: Jam Press/Casey J Fishing Trips)

Shark sighting closes St Ouen's Bay beach on Jersey for the first time READ MORE :

"It can be hard to judge but when they're next to the boat you know."

‌



Basking sharks are the second-largest fish in the world, surpassed only by the whale shark.

They are also one of only three shark species that feed on plankton, alongside the whale shark and the elusive megamouth shark.

The gentle giants are regularly seen swimming alone or in small groups as they slowly glide through coastal waters with their huge mouths open to filter-feed.

‌



View 3 Images The Isle of Man is recognised as a global hotspot for the basking shark (file) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Despite their enormous size and fearsome appearance, basking sharks pose no danger to humans.

Recent years have seen the Isle of Man become recognised as a global hotspot for basking sharks, with hundreds of sightings reported each year. It is believed that at least 90 individually recognised sharks reside in the waters, which appear to be a breeding ground for the gentle giants.

‌



There is a relatively long history of basking shark research in the Isle of Man. In the 1980s and 1990s, The Basking Shark Project, run by Ken Watterson and supported by many local volunteers, carried out basking shark research and awareness-raising.

View 3 Images Basking sharks can grow to be 40ft (Image: Jam Press/Casey J Fishing Trips)

The organisation helped to raise the global profile of basking sharks, and played an important role in influencing the government to include them on the protected species lists in the Isle of Man and the UK.

Article continues below

Basking sharks typically measure around 25ft long, although some can grow as large as 40ft. The lumbering creatures can weigh up to six tonnes (6,000kg), and their huge mouths filter around 2,000 tonnes of seawater per hour.

Many tales of sea serpents and monsters are said to have originated from basking shark sightings. In one notable case, a basking shark carcass discovered by Japanese fisherman was initially thought to be the remains of a pre-historic plesiosaurus.

News.title: Melanie Sykes stars in first modelling shoot since going public with alopecia battle
News.content:
Melanie Sykes proudly shows off her shaved head in a powerful new modelling shoot, which is her first since going public with battle against alopecia.

The TV presenter, 55, cut her hair earlier this summer after revealing that the condition had progressed significantly. Back in June, she debuted her new look on Instagram saying 'Thank God I can laugh.'

Now the star has taken to the streets of Manchester to model a new sunglasses campaign in her hometown of Manchester.

Posing up a storm in the Northern Quarter, Mel head turned to the side so that her shaved head was on full display, and beamed as she wore a pair of Cubitts sunnies and a black leather jacket. Two other pictures, taken from the front, saw the star grinning from ear to ear and she looked just as happy in a close up of her face.

‌



Alopecia signs and symptoms as Melanie Sykes shares update READ MORE :

Melanie Sykes proudly reveals completely bald head after opening up about alopecia battle READ MORE :

7 View 7 Images She showed off her shaved head in the pictures (Image: Niall Hodson/Cubitts) 7 View 7 Images Melanie Sykes in her new Cubitts campaign (Image: Niall Hodson/Cubitts)

The star changed into a white suit and green shirt for more pictures and could be seen lifting her face towards the sun. She also brandished several pairs of sunglasses, and, in one image, adopted a more serious pose, with her collar coolly turned up against the breeze.

The shoot comes after Melanie spoke openly about her health. Prior to shaving her head, she said: "I'm two-thirds bald, really. Every time I say I'm bald I laugh, I don't know why… Thank God I can laugh."

‌



7 View 7 Images She returned to Manchester for the campaign (Image: Niall Hodson/Cubitts) 7 View 7 Images Mel Sykes has opened up about her battle with alopecia (Image: Dave Benett/Getty Images)

There are several different types of alopecia. Alopecia areata is the most common and is an autoimmune condition that causes sudden hair loss on the scalp and other other parts of the body, including eyebrows and eyelashes. It occurs when certain immune cells mistakenly attack hair follicles. As well as hair loss, it can cause inflammation, itching or burning along the scalp, though that is less common.

While anyone can develop alopecia, it is more commonly diagnosed before the age of 40 and is often linked to other autoimmune conditions. Stress, genetics and family history are also thought to play a role, although the exact cause is not always clear.

‌



7 View 7 Images Melanie decided to shave her head after losing two third of her hair to alopecia (Image: Niall Hodson/Cubitts) 7 View 7 Images Melanie previously revealed that she kept "having crazy inflammation" because of her alopecia (Image: Niall Hodson/Cubitts)

When Melanie revealed she had the condition, she explained: "I've got an autoimmune condition, I am losing my hair, I keep having crazy inflammation all over and I am working on healing."

She added that she had to step back from a meditation teacher training course she was doing as she was too unwell. "I was too ill to finish it like. The last two days of it I couldn’t do. It’s meditation teacher training, I don’t necessarily want to teach, but I can do…," she said. “Mostly I’ve been living a very, very very spiritual existence."

‌



Melanie first spoke publicly about her diagnosis last year. The star said she developed an irregular heartbeat and “rapid” hair loss after being “harassed” when allegations surfaced against TV chef Gino D’Acampo, whom she worked with on the ITV series Let’s Do Lunch with Gino and Mel from 2011 to 2014.

“I went into the New Year with so much energy. I’ve slowed things down because I got a heart problem, which I developed during the whole Gino D’Acampo bull**** that happened in the news,” she said in the video. “And suddenly, the stress levels in my life shot up because I left that industry years ago but it won’t leave me alone."

News.title: Girl, 9, 'sexually touched' at Butlin's as police release description of man
News.content:
Girl, 9, 'sexually touched' at Butlin's as police release description of man

Police have given a description of someone they want to trace following reports that a man 'sexually touched' a girl, nine, at a Butlin's in Skegness

View Image The incident took place a the Butlin's site in Skegness (file) (Image: MEN MEDIA)

Police have launched an investigation after reports a nine-year-old girl was "sexually touched" at Butlin's.

The incident took place at the Butlin's site in Skegness shortly before 10am on Monday this week, where the girl was approached outside the family's accommodation on Pelican Court.

Officers from Lincolnshire Police were called following a report that a man touched the child over her clothing and put his hand on her face.

An investigation has now been launched. The man is described as being white, between 30 and 40 years old with dark hair, and he had been wearing a green T-shirt.

Lincolnshire Police has appealed for anyone who saw the incident or was in the area at the time to get in touch.

A spokesperson for the force told the Mirror: "Incident 104 of Monday 3 August refers to a report that just before 10am a 9-year-old girl was approached by an unknown man at Butlins in Skegness.

"The man is reported to have touched the child over her clothing and put his hand on her face; we are investigating an offence of sexual touching.

"The incident is reported to have happened outside of the family’s accommodation which was at Pelican court. The man is described as white, aged 30-40 years old, with dark hair and wearing a green t shirt.

"We are appealing for anyone who was in the area or anyone who witnessed the incident to get in touch. Anyone with information is asked to email force.control@lincs.police.uk, alternatively you can contact the independent charity CrimeStoppers at CrimeStoppers-uk.org or call 0800 555111. Please refer to Incident 104 of 3 August."

Article continues below

A Butlin's spokesperson said the company was "deeply concerned" about what had happened and had provided "support" for the family.

"We’re deeply concerned to hear about this incident on resort," they said.

"As soon as we were made aware we supported the family and have been in direct contact since. We’re working with Lincolnshire Police and will further support however we can."

News.title: Young women tell BBC of rape, assault and harassment at Army training college for teenagers
News.content:
Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assault

Four young women have told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed at an army training college for teenagers - with one saying she was raped by several fellow junior soldiers in an attack that lasted hours.

The women all attended the Army Foundation College (AFC) at Harrogate, North Yorkshire, over the past five years and say the incidents happened when they were aged 17.

The college has a dangerous culture of misogyny and sexual violence, say the women, who are all speaking out for the first time.

These reports are "extremely distressing and serious", said an Army spokesperson in a statement.

The BBC can also reveal that North Yorkshire Police received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, according to a Freedom of Information request.

Those reported offences include allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault. No information was provided as to whether they had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

Thirty-two allegations were against permanent staff and 144 against junior soldiers.

"Unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our Armed Forces," said the Army spokesperson.

"People join in the hope of having a fantastic career and any such reports are unacceptable and go completely against everything the Army stands for."

AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits. There are currently 70 female junior soldiers at the Harrogate site out of a total of 889.

We have changed all the women's names to protect their identities.

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
A University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect".

On Wednesday the university said it had launched an investigation into Professor Jason Arday "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

Arday - who became the university's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his work, but said he had faced "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack" and was not a "liar".

It came after a series of media reports questioning some of his achievements and allegations of plagiarism in his PhD thesis.

Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

In the statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life".

But he added: "There comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great."

He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal".

"When that time comes, I will return," he added.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist", whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

Cambridge had initially described allegations made against Arday as a "vile campaign to undermine his credibility".

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated allegations of plagiarism in his thesis that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.

The BBC has contacted the university for further comment.

News.title: Meredith Kercher's sister criticises Amanda Knox's Edinburgh comedy show
News.content:
The sister of Meredith Kercher has criticised a solo comedy show by Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering the British student in Italy in 2007.

The Edinburgh Festival Fringe website says Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain what happened in Perugia to her daughter.

Stephanie Kercher, addressing Knox directly on BBC Breakfast, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Her comedy show's title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed she did cartwheels in the police station after her friend's death.

Knox told the Telegraph newspaper, external last week: "I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder."

Asked if Meredith Kercher would have found her comedy funny, she added: "Yeah, I think so. I mean, it is funny!".

Responding to that suggestion, Stephanie Kercher told the BBC: "Meredith absolutely wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value."

She said: "Our family's pain is immense. I can't explain to you how much pain our family have been through, and also we're talking two decades later now, this pain."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women by making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail new environmental review
News.content:
The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".

It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".

She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.

Much of the debate about the state of England's waters has centred on water companies and the sewage they release into rivers.

But campaigners and scientists also point to agriculture as an equally large source of pollution - one that attracts far less public attention.

Erica Popplewell, of the campaign group River Action, said some farming, particularly intensive poultry units - vast sheds housing hundreds of thousands of birds - were a growing threat to rivers such as the Wye and Severn.

"There's a lot of poo that comes out of the chickens," she said. "If it goes straight into a river, it causes eutrophication. The whole ecology of the river is damaged, and the river is dying." She called on the government to tackle sewage and farming "with the same urgency".

The National Farmers' Union of England and Wales has been approached for comment.

Other types of pollution affecting England's bodies of water, the Environment Agency pointed to, include petrol, garden pesticides and contaminated water running off roads picking up microplastics.

News.title: Families' anger at jailed funeral boss's apology letter
News.content:
Natalie Smith's grandfather Norman Bridger was one of the bodies found at Legacy.

He had been there for 11 months and was 95 when he died, with a funeral held for him before they found out his body was still at the site.

Smith said Bush's letter was a "tick box exercise to try and make himself look like he'd approached the families".

She said she reacted with "disbelief" when she received the letter, which contained "no real substance, no emotion, nothing".

"They're just words and there was nothing behind them," she said, adding she would never forgive Bush for what he had done.

Robert Bush's letter in full:

To everyone who has been affected by my actions.

"I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that [sic] wish to say something directly to you.

"I know that many of you entrusted me and my business with the care of someone you loved during one of the most difficult times in your lives.

"I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry.

"There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced. I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you.

"I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so.

"I do not expect forgiveness, nor do I write this letter in the hope of reducing the seriousness of what has happened.

"I simply wanted you to know that I genuinely regret the consequences of my actions, and the impact they have had on so many people.

"I appreciate that every family's experience has been different, and I respect that some people may never wish to accept my apology. That is entirely understandable.

"I hope that, in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved one for who they were rather than for the circumstances that have followed. I am truly sorry."

If you have been affected by issues surrounding bereavement, information is available via BBC Action Line, including contact details of organisations that can help.

Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
News.content:
More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.

The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least Â£41,700.

But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.

More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."

It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.

There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a Â£611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of Â£1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.

Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least Â£38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.

The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.

News.title: Meta becomes latest firm to say its AI hacked another company
News.content:
Facebook owner Meta has become the latest tech firm to say one of its AI models was able to connect to the internet and hack into another organisation's systems, during testing.

The incident, which Meta says occurred during an evaluation by an independent company, is the fourth recent incident of its kind disclosed by AI companies.

Similar breaches by OpenAI and Anthropic models have raised cyber-security concerns and prompted calls for tougher safeguards and more rigorous testing.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it was investigating the hack, which it said had been caused by a "misconfiguration" by its independent tester.

It also described what happened as similar to previously reported incidents at other firms.

Meta said the security trials were conducted by Irregular, the same AI security vendor that carried out tests for Anthropic's AI model that had gained access to three other companies' systems.

An Irregular spokesperson said the Meta incident "is the exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week."

Irregular is working on a report on how to securely run cyber-security tests involving AI agents, the firm's spokesperson told the BBC.

Meta also said it will publish more information on the incident "once we have all the facts."

In the past two weeks, AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported incidents in which their models hacked into other organisation's systems during testing.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said in a series of announcements that its agents attacked several publicly available services, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

OpenAI's disclosure prompted rival Anthropic to conduct its own checks, leading to the discovery that its Claude AI model had carried out similar attacks on several firms after a "misconfiguration" gave it access to the internet.

Daniel Hulme, global chief AI officer of advertising firm WPP, told the BBC that such AI models "are not conscious â they're not deliberately doing something devious".

"What they're doing is coming up with very sophisticated strategies or cyberattacks to be able to achieve the goal that they've been given," he told the Today programme.

"When you give an AI a goal, if you don't think of all the ways it might be able to achieve the goal, it will find a way to achieve a goal that you haven't thought about."

News.title: Why playing your phone out loud in public might become the new normal
News.content:
Listen to Angus read the story here

Most days on my commute, I am treated to the contents of strangers' phones.

It could be a teenage boy slouching on a seat on the top deck of the number 29, holding his device inches from his face, either unaware or indifferent that everyone else can hear what he's watching too.

Or a woman taking a phone call on loudspeaker before scrolling at volume through her social feed.

Surveys suggest that many do find this modern phenomenon - known as loudcasting, sodcasting, or headphone dodging - similarly frustrating.

In recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it. TfL has just relaunched its Travel Kind campaign across the London transport network this summer, reminding people to use headphones.

The phenomenon has grown as we become ever more connected. Figures published in July by Ofcom show that mobile data use has increased by 13% year-on-year in the UK. 5G is being rolled out across the country, meaning that more people can get faster connectivity while travelling. And research has found that many data packages have become cheaper, meaning customers are less likely to have to ration their data use when out and about.

So as we become ever more online in public, will we see increasing attempts to clamp down on loudcasting? Or will it end up becoming as normal a part of our soundscape as the hum of passing traffic or the roar of a plane's engine thousands of feet above us?

News.title: Half of vaccines are binned - 'fridge-free' versions could change that
News.content:
Prof Saul Faust, the director of the NIHR Clinical Research Facility in Southampton, said it gave "equivalent" immune responses to the conventional vaccine as well as being "safe and well tolerated" in the early stage studies.

Faust added: "This obviously has potential to remove cold chain dependence, reduce wastage and improve access."

A larger trial involving 160 people is already due to start in the coming months.

This would be the final stage of research as the original vaccine is already approved and licensed so there is no requirement to perform large-stage trials needed for a novel vaccine.

The studies are being done to meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) goal of a vaccine that survives at 30C and 75% relative humidity.

But the research team say separate data shows the components of their vaccine also survive cycling between temperatures of -20C and +40C. That could mean the vaccine being viable after transport in a cold aircraft hold and then in the back of a truck in the heat.

There is not one single reason vaccines are wasted and disposed of, but the WHO estimates this is the fate of half of all vaccines globally. This can include damage in transport, passing the expiration date, and unused doses from multi-dose vials, but a major factor are failures in the cold chain.

News.title: Walk-in mental health centres to open in banks and libraries across England
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Nobody should be left to struggle with their mental health alone. But every day, thousands of people are waiting months for help, then finding the only door open to them is a busy A&E.

"These new centres will be a lifeline for so many," he said.

"They will bring NHS services closer to home, making it easier to get support before problems get worse and ensuring those in crisis get the right care in the right place."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "This is how we can turn the tide on mental ill health - preventing more people from reaching crisis, cutting waits for care, and building an NHS which is there for everyone when they need it.â

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Cooper said there would be a "continual programme" of rolling out these mental health centres - with the first ones set to open this autumn.

"It will take a bit of time in some areas but 100 right across the country I think will make a real difference to getting people mental health support early," she said, adding that "prevention can be much more effective to provide healthcare".

She said the government has already increased mental health staffing, but said "what these services are going to be doing is bringing together existing teams of staff to work together in a different way".

The chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, Andy Bell, said he welcomed the announcement on the whole - although was concerned that the mental health emergency departments had not been properly tested yet.

He also said children and young people, who will be able to use these services, needed their own dedicated hubs.

But he said he was "delighted" that the government was taking action on mental health after it had been neglected by successive governments for too long.

"This must now be backed up by investment, most crucially in the workforce needed to provide effective mental health care," he said.

Stephen Jones, of the Royal College of Nursing, said he agreed investment in staff would be crucial if the new centres were going to cope with demand.

"More services closer to people's homes are a crucial step towards more humane care," he said.

But he added: "To succeed, both will need specialist mental health nurses at the centre."

The Department of Health said that the initiative is backed by Â£343m and the first sites will open in autumn this year, with "further facilities following from March 2027".

News.title: Raleigh owner starts insolvency proceedings
News.content:
The company that owns iconic Nottingham bike manufacturer Raleigh has begun insolvency proceedings.

Accell, based in the Netherlands, bought Raleigh for $100m in 2012 but said on Wednesday it had "exhausted all the available options" and was "no longer able to meet its financial obligations".

It comes after a difficult period for Raleigh, which saw redundancies in 2024 and losses of Â£30m in accounts released the following year.

Jonas Nilsson, chief executive of Accell, said it was "a deeply sad and frustrating situation".

News.title: Reform UK pledges to jail bosses employing illegal workers
News.content:
Reform UK has pledged to imprison the bosses of companies employing illegal migrants and said it would fine larger firms 10 per cent of their global revenues.

The party said its aim was to stop delivery and gig economy companies profiting from illegal workers "without consequences".

Home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said "young British people are being shut out of entry level jobs and our whole economy is being undermined".

The Home Office said it was already increasing penalties for companies hiring illegal workers. A source within the department called some of Reform's proposals "empty posturing".

Reform said that if it won the next general election, it would pass a law making chief executives and directors of large companies profiting from illegal workers personally and criminally liable.

That would be regardless of their knowledge of workers' legal status.

The party said this would be similar to the personal liability of senior managers for the financial misconduct of their firms under Financial Conduct Authority rules.

Reform would also introduce a phone line for the public to report suspected illegal working or organised criminal activity, which police and other authorities, such as trading standards teams, would be required to follow up.

Reports resulting in successful prosecutions would be rewarded with a share of any fines generated.

Yusuf said the party "would introduce the toughest penalties anywhere in the world for illegal working".

News.title: When your child is dying you shouldn't have to beg for help
News.content:
One of the main problems the Cookstown family experienced was taking Lila out in the car, which had a huge impact on family life and their ability to attend hospital appointments.

In Northern Ireland, a child cannot qualify for the higher rate mobility component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA), external - which is required for the Motability Scheme - until they reach three years of age as it depends on a child's ability to walk.

Lila could not roll, sit, or stand and, according to a paediatric physiotherapist, was completely dependent for all care.

She received a specialised buggy, but the family still needed a wheelchair-accessible vehicle to transport her and the buggy.

Hayley said this was "denied" to Lila "due to her age, not clinical need".

Robert said not having a safe vehicle to transport his daughter in was "terrible" and he had to sit in the back of the car and hold Lila's head up "just so she could breathe".

A charity which helps disabled children did step in to assist and provided the family with a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, just before Lila's second birthday. Her father said that was a "lifeline".

"She was able to be safe and she got the life that she deserved eventually because she was fit to get out of the house," her mother said.

Lila's third birthday would have been on 1 August.

The family spent what turned out to be Lila's final weeks of life filling in forms so she did not miss the deadline for applying for mobility DLA before her third birthday.

Hayley said she felt her daughter was not "entitled to basic human rights that other kids are entitled to because she was born different".

"I would like the departments to work with healthcare professionals and look at diagnosis and clinical need and the expert opinions of medical professionals rather than age and a birthday," she said.

News.title: Michelin-star restaurant regains top hygiene score after previous one-star inspection
News.content:
Wales' only two-Michelin-star restaurant that received a one-star food hygiene rating after inspectors found flies, broken equipment and a dirty knife has had its top score restored.

Ynyshir Restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales was ordered to stop serving raw lobster after Ceredigion council had found "significant hazards" were not properly identified.

Ynyshir serves Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its nearly Â£500 a head 30-course tasting menu, and had accused inspectors of not understanding its specialised procedures.

The council has now awarded it a hygiene rating of five after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

"This outcome demonstrates the effectiveness of the food hygiene inspection process and the positive results that can be achieved through constructive engagement between regulatory officers and food businesses to improve standards," the council said.

Chef Gareth Ward previously said he had not been embarrassed when the restaurant had been given a 1-out-of-5 score.

Ynyshir has been asked to comment.

News.title: PC Harper widow 'won't give up' early release fight
News.content:
The widow of a police officer has said she hopes people will share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison, insisting she "will not give up".

PC Andrew Harper, from Wallingford, died in 2019 when he was dragged by a car as three teenagers fled the scene of a Berkshire quad bike theft.

Under updated plans to tackle prison overcrowding, two of PC Harper's killers - Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers - would be eligible for release next year.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

Lissie Harper said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets.

"Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."

As of just after 08:30 BST, the petition had over 440,000 signatures. It was started by Aileen O'Connor, chair of Thames Valley Police Federation.

News.title: Our daughter's death at 18 left us shattered - but she saved two lives
News.content:
A couple whose daughter died from a cardiac arrest brought on by an epileptic seizure say she has saved "lives in her death".

Beth and Malcolm Owen's daughter Menna, 18, donated her heart and lungs after she collapsed at the family's home in Tonteg, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 1 March 2025, dying in hospital.

The couple have since received letters from the man and woman who Menna saved, with both doing "incredible well".

"Perhaps Menna's purpose was to make an incredible difference to us every day of her life, and to save lives in her death," Beth said.

Figures show that family consent for organ donation across the UK has dropped by almost a fifth in five years, from 69% in 2020/21 to 57% in 2025/26.

Amid this decline, the NHS wants a million more people in the UK to 

Beth said that on the day her daughter died, Menna - who had "well controlled" epilepsy - had been at work and went for a lie down.

"That was a bit out of the ordinary, but she'd been working long hours, I assumed she was tired," Beth said.

She later found Menna in the bathroom.

"She was in cardiac arrest when I got in there," Beth said, adding that Menna had suffered a catastrophic brain injury which she would not recover from.

A two-Michelin star restaurant that received a one-star food hygiene rating has found its way back to the top.

Ynyshir Restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales specialises in Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its 30-course tasting menu, which comes to nearly £500 per person.

Ceredigion council had initially found "significant hazards" were not properly identified, ordering the restaurant to stop serving raw lobster in October 2025.

However, Ynyshir said the inspectors did not understand its “specialised procedures”.

open image in gallery Ynyshir Restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales specialises in Japanese-inspired raw dishes ( Instagram )

Dirty floor, inadequate hand-washing facilities in some areas and broken equipment were also identified by the inspectors.

The results of the inspection, published by the Food Standards Agency (FSA), had declared that the management of food safety in Ynyshir requires “major improvement”, while the cleanliness and condition of the facilities and building also need to be improved. Hygienic food handling was rated as “generally satisfactory”.

Chef Gareth Ward, who has featured as a guest judge on Masterchef: The Professionals, previously said he was not embarrassed by the one star.

He told the BBC at the time that Ynyshir is working “at the highest standard in the world”, arguing that it is merely doing “something different” in its approach to raw ingredients and techniques.

open image in gallery The restaurant’s owner and chef, Gareth Ward, has featured as a guest judge on Masterchef: The Professionals ( BBC )

He added: “We buy in the best ingredients from around the world, and a lot of it I serve raw.

“I’m buying sashimi-grade fish from Japan, and they’re questioning, ‘Well, we don’t know the water, so how do we know it’s sashimi grade?’ Well, it is sashimi grade, this stuff’s eaten raw all over the world, and just because our rules don’t fit their rules, they’re questioning it.”

The council has now awarded the restaurant a hygiene rating of five following a re-inspection in February after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

open image in gallery The council has now awarded the restaurant a hygiene rating of five ( Ynyshir )

The council added:"This outcome demonstrates the effectiveness of the food hygiene inspection process and the positive results that can be achieved through constructive engagement between regulatory officers and food businesses to improve standards.

“Ynyshir was immediately notified of its revised rating and the updated score was published on the Food Standards Agency website, where it has been available for public viewing since March 2026.”

Ynyshir has been approached for comment.

An ex neo-Nazi who was has been appointed as an adviser for the Conservative Party on tackling radicalisation is embroiled in a fresh row over claims he has government certification for his counter-extremism work.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was selected by the Tories to fight a council election next year but withdrew his candidacy on Wednesday after backlash. He was convicted in 2015 of racially aggravated harassment of former Labour MP Luciana Berger, ⁠who is Jewish, and had ​also ⁠been jailed for stirring up hatred against a north London Jewish community.

Mr Bonehill-Paine insists he has put his past behind him and now works to combat anti-semitism and extremism. He said this month in a post on X that he holds “Home Office certification for my counter-extremism work”, which he claims has taken him “across the country delivering training to police officers, probation services, schools, universities and many other organisations”.

This claim was repeated by Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, who said on that Mr Bonehill-Paine would work to deliver “training certified by the Home Office” for the Tories.

But the Home Office has now thrown doubt on these claims. In a statement on Thursday, a government spokesperson said: “The Home Office does not certify individuals to deliver training.”

open image in gallery Joshua Bonehill-Paine ( Joshua Bonehill-Paine/Facebook )

They added: “We do provide funding to Civil Society Organisations, who may use individuals to deliver training on preventing extremism that is commissioned by local authorities.”

The Conservative Party has been approached for comment.

Mr Bonehill-Paine also runs a satirical media outlet in support of the Tory party that produces AI videos of famous politicians, called The Crewkerne Gazette. While some are humorous, others are more invasive, such as a recent AI rendering of Andy Burnham crying on the floor in his underpants.

Others, such as recent videos of fake interactions between Mr Burnham and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch at PMQs, are also less obviously AI-generated.

open image in gallery Joshua Bonehill-Paine, 23, claimed Labour MP Luciana Berger was responsible for Jesus's death ( Social media )

Mr Bonehill-Paine withdrew as a Conservative election candidate after Ms Badenoch offered him a role as a cultural adviser to the party.

He will be an adviser to the Tory party’s culture and integration commission, where he will focus on “how young men become radicalised”.

He said in a statement on Wednesday that he will “support the work the party is doing to rebuild trust with the British people”, adding: “I intend on making a meaningful contribution to tackling extremism and promoting social cohesion”.

open image in gallery Baroness Luciana Berger said Bonehill-Paine’s appointment as a Tory advisor was an insult ( PA Media )

Baroness Luciana Berger, who now sits in the House of Lords, reacted to the news that Mr Bonehill-Paine will advise the Conservative party, saying it was “no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate.”

She added: “It is a privileged and influential national role. As a victim of this man’s heinous crimes this appointment is an insult”.

Foreign secretary Ed Miliband said the Tories had questions to answer, telling broadcasters: “He should never have been a candidate for the Conservative Party, given the harassment that he positioned upon Luciana Berger, a colleague and a friend of mine.

“I think the Conservative Party is going to have to answer for why he’s a candidate in the first place, and also any future activities he might be undertaking on behalf of the Conservative Party.”

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Mrs Badenoch had shown an “outrageous lack of judgment, doubling down on her support for a former neo-Nazi”.

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson also questioned Mrs Badenoch’s judgment, saying: “It beggars belief that Kemi Badenoch was happy for a former neo-Nazi to stand in the first place. That she has gifted him a plum job further adds to that shame.

“It speaks volumes about Badenoch’s judgment and even more about the state of the Conservative Party under her leadership.”

Confidence in Fifa is being restored. How do we know? Because Fifa has told us. And Fifa’s integrity is such that attacks on it cannot be tolerated... Fifa, in between plotting to sell off the World Cup, has said it wasn’t doing that. Not that many people in Fifa knew for sure, as Fifa didn’t bother consulting them.

But then, as Fifa said a statement about a “constructive and positive meeting held in Rabat, Morocco”, its only official elected by the 211 member associations is the president. Although, admittedly, many of those associations are calling for Gianni Infantino to go and plenty of others came out in opposition to what – according to the governing body, anyway – was called the “Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal”.

And now that is off the table, again in Fifa’s words, a statement that tested the boundaries of Orwellian doublespeak, the only remaining issues, in Fifa’s world, are the horrible “attacks” on it.

open image in gallery Gianni Infantino showed minimal remorse in his letter after the Fifa crisis meeting ( Getty Images )

A global sport was plunged into crisis by one man, Infantino, who either had an idea he forgot to fully communicate with virtually everyone – Fifa’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, its chief of global football development Arsene Wenger, the various confederations, clubs, national associations, players, fans... – or tried to stage a coup against the sport as a whole.

But now Fifa have met, Infantino and Mattias Grafstrom, the secretary general, have released a joint letter and everyone can be reassured, thanks to these 19 words that highlight the depth of the delusion. “Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will help restore confidence in the organisation,” they said.

And why wouldn’t it? Infantino wants to stay in charge and either he is the most divisive man in football or he has succeeded in uniting vast numbers of people and contrasting interests against him. “Mistakes made were acknowledged,” came the message otherwise littered with credibility-defying optimism.

open image in gallery Infantino’s letter was littered with credibility-defying optimism ( PA Wire )

open image in gallery He appeared to take a leaf out of the Donald Trump playbook by portraying himself as the victim of unfair attacks ( PA )

“It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process,” read the closest thing to a mea culpa. In which case, then, why exclude them? A scheme of such secrecy that only members of the Kushner family were informed was sprung upon the footballing world; FAs who were going to vote for it would get more funds from Fifa than those who would not, which struck some as tantamount to bribery; not that the word crops up in Infantino’s letter.

Still, he has pledged there will be no repeat and that a review will be conducted; but presumably the Infantino faction of Fifa will conduct the review and present the conclusions it is supposed to present.

Though that may be another unfair assault on the good names of Infantino and Fifa; the touchiness that was apparent in the 56-year-old’s Instagram posts appears to have extended to an entire organisation.

“It was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation,” came one of the more delusional sentences. Entirely coincidentally, Donald Trump portrays himself as the victim of unfair attacks; so Fifa did too.

open image in gallery Infantino (centre) and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom (left) attended a women’s AFCON match together after the crisis meeting in Rabat ( AP )

It is, of course, too late to safeguard a reputation dragged into the mud by the Infantino regime; by quashing suspensions to Cristiano Ronaldo and Folarin Balogun, by twisting the rules to put Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami in the Club World Cup, by letting the United States ban Somali referee Omar Artan from entering the country, by cosying up to Trump, by creating a peace prize to give to a man who then started an illegal war.

Fifa became a byword for greed; it was notable in the United States that ordinary Americans blamed Fifa by name for the sky-high ticket prices. They did not stand for impartiality; not when preferential treatment was given to the Trump administration and decision-making seemed influenced by the White House. They did not represent the global game; not when, as the strategy of selling off the World Cup showed, they tried to do so without most of it knowing.

If Fifa is serious about restoring its reputation, it requires more honesty and new leadership. The latest dispatch from Infantino world offered none of that.
