As Iran and Oman close in on a deal to open the Strait of Hormuz, hopes are growing that the main hurdle preventing peace talks to end Donald Trump’s war may be cleared.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesperson for Iran’s foreign ministry, said an agreement is in its “final stages”, while US president Donald Trump said an "all-day negotiation" had taken place with Tehran on Tuesday.

Senior Trump administration officials, including secretary of state Marco Rubio and treasury secretary Scott Bessent, suggested a deal was imminent earlier this week - but an agreement had not been reached as of Thursday morning.



open image in gallery Trump will likely sell any Iran-Oman deal as a success for the US ( Getty )

The contents of the current agreement remain unclear. Tehran says the proposed deal would give it control over ships entering the Gulf through ​the ⁠Strait, in what would represent one of Trump’s biggest ‌concessions yet.

Iran’s attacks on ships since the war began in late February have severely disrupted oil supply and caused chaos in the global energy market, leading to higher prices for consumers.

Despite optimism growing over a deal, US officials have been clear that they will not Iran to control the world’s most important waterway for energy supplies.

The Independent looks at three key scenarios that could take place in the event of a deal - or a collapse in negotiations.

The deal holds and Hormuz reopens

Throughout the war, Trump has consistently oscillated between threats of escalation against the Iranian regime and talking up diplomacy.

After five months of conflict, much now hinges on whether Oman can negotiate a deal on Hormuz which is acceptable to Washington.

In the event that Muscat’s negotiators succeed, it would bring an end to a long stalemate. Tehran established its blockade in response to the launch of the US-Israeli war on 28 February - and attacks on ships continued even during a fragile US ceasefire deal that collapsed earlier this month.

While it may take time to restore shipping to pre-war levels, the free flow of vessels would undoubtedly bring crude oil prices down after they soared to a peak of $114 a barrel in May.

open image in gallery People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Wednesday, Aug. 5 ( AP )

While they dropped to $71 following the the Iran-US memorandum of understanding in mid-June, oil prices increased again after the resumption of heavy strikes between Washington and Tehran. It is hoped that a new deal could bring prices down more permanently.

Brent Crude, the international benchmark, is currently priced at $80.

A cold peace and return of proxy war

The US and Iran could drop back into a phase of cold peace, with limited military operations on both sides hindering further progress towards a peace deal.

This limbo phase has defined much of the US-Iran war: periods characterised by tit-for-tat strikes and contained aggression that have not escalated into full-scale conflict. Recently, the US has carried out operations in Hormuz, while Iran has struck targets in Gulf neighbour states.

Such strikes continued even during a supposed ceasefire deal between the US and Iran, leading UN secretary general Antonio Guterres to suggest in June that the agreement was actually “a lesser fire” with the constant risk of escalating.

Meanwhile, a war being fought between Israel and Hezbollah in southern Lebanon has also struggled to reach its conclusion - defined similarly by flare ups and both sides claiming ceasefire violations.

The two countries agreed in June to a US-brokered security arrangement intended ⁠to ease hostilities along the border.

But on Thursday, Israel said two of its soldiers were killed in southern Lebanon while Lebanese authorities said Israeli retaliatory attacks killed at least one person - suggesting the conflict remains unsolved.

open image in gallery People and journalists stand at a site hit by Israeli strikes that occurred in the early hours of Thursday, according to Lebanon’s state news agency NNA, in Burj al-Shamali ( Reuters )

The deal falls apart and fighting resumes

The risk of full-scale fighting between the US and Iran feels ever present - particularly after the failure of an earlier peace agreement to halt the war.

The glimmer of hope after the 17 June memorandum of understanding was signed, followed by an increase in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, was dashed in early July when merchant ships were reportedly attacked and the ceasefire began to unravel.

Trump declared the ceasefire was “over”, referring to Iran’s leadership as “scum” and “sick people”.

It would likely take a major compromise on both sides - or a major concession from one - for the negotiations to produce an agreement which will see lasting peace around the strait.

Dr Neil Quilliam says one such deal would see “services” disguised as “environmental fees” being paid to Iran. This would be a major concession from Washington, which has rejected the premise of Iran collecting a fee for passage through the strait.

“[Trump] just needs the Gulf Arab states to sign up and live with the services fees - and given the alternative - a continuous war of attrition, this looks increasingly likely now,” he said.

Life on Earth may have first emerged from complex chemical reactions in two different ways near a deep-sea hot spring, a new study claims.

One of the biggest mysteries rattling the scientific community is to understand where and how life first emerged on the planet from a primordial soup of non-living chemicals.

Previous studies hint that the rich chemical environment around deep-sea hydrothermal vents – hot springs on the ocean floor – most likely served as the breeding ground for the emergence of the first living cells.

A radical new theory suggests that the two main lineages of early life – bacteria and archaea – independently emerged from the primordial soup around deep-sea vents.

“The new data leave only one conclusion. The bacterial and archaeal lineages made the transition to the free-living state independently... We are looking at one origin of the genetic code, but two origins of life,” said William Martin, a biologist from Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany.

open image in gallery Hydrothermal vent type called 'black smokers' ( Ocean Exploration Trust via Eurekalert )

In the study, scientists probed the network of chemical reactions that the very first cells may have used to make life-building block molecules.

They also looked at the likely energy sources around thermal vents that drove those early metabolic reactions.

Researchers assessed genomes, protein structures, and chemical reactions near deep-sea vents that were likely behind the emergence of the first living cell.

They looked into a known set of about 420 chemical reactions that cells may have used to make the building blocks of life, such as amino acids, from compounds present on the early Earth, including hydrogen, ammonia, and carbon dioxide.

Scientists found that the enzymes speeding up these reactions differ between ancient bacteria and the single-cell life form archaea that live in extreme places.

This means bacteria and archaea most likely evolved into the first living cells following separate pathways, concluded the study published in the journal Science Advances.

“We can see cases where the ancestors of bacteria and archaea independently evolved structurally distinct enzymes to catalyse the same essential metabolic reaction,” explained biologist Natalia Mrnjavac, another author of the study.

open image in gallery Hydrothermal vent on the Niua underwater volcano in the Lau Basin, southwest Pacific Ocean ( Pacific Coastal and Marine Science Center )

Some of the early life forms seemed to have relied on metal catalysts, scientists found.

These metals, like palladium, are “excellent catalysts” and are naturally occur in hydrothermal vents, researchers say.

“We found that the last universal ancestor of all cells, LUCA, possessed enzymes for only about half of the reactions of metabolism. The other half was catalysed by metals in the environment where LUCA arose,” Dr Martin said.

“Metals that naturally occur in hydrothermal vents can replace a surprisingly large number of enzymes in metabolism,” explained Harun Tüysüz, another author of the study.

Scientists could reconstruct four phases of early metabolic chemical reactions: one that relied on metal catalysts only, one that needed a metal-enzyme hybrid, as well as reactions that drove early bacteria and archaea.

In modern life forms, metabolism is driven by the energy-currency molecule ATP, or adenosine triphosphate.

A chemical process attaches phosphate to organic molecules, and is a crucial form of energy transfer within life forms.

But in early Earth, instead of ATP, this reaction may have been driven by palladium and phosphite molecules, researchers say.

“When we react phosphite, a form of phosphorus that naturally occurs in hydrothermal vents, with organic compounds, we get metabolic phosphorylation reactions overnight in water,” Dr Schlikker says.

“Such parallel inventions could have paved the way to the independent emergence of free-living bacteria and archaea,” Dr Mrnjavac said.

A conference on Tibetan studies scheduled to be held this month in Nepal was called off at the request of government officials who gave no reason for the decision, organizers said Thursday.

The International Association for Tibetan Studies seminar was scheduled to be held in Nepal Aug. 23-26, to be attended by delegates from many countries and hosted by the Himalaya Centre for Asian Studies at Kathmandu University.

Prof. Sagar Raj Sharma of the Center confirmed they made the decision to cancel after top government officials asked them not to hold the conference. No specific reasons were given.

There was no immediate comment from the government, but Nepal has long maintained good relations with China and has disallowed any pro-Tibetan activities.

China has ruled Tibet since 1951, when Communist forces occupied the Himalayan territory. Decades of political repression followed, including the demolition of some Buddhist monasteries and the suppression of all forms of political or cultural expression outside Communist Party control.

Thousands of Tibetan refugees live in Nepal and pass through the territory to reach their spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India. However, Nepal has maintained it will not allow any protests, rallies or activities against any friendly countries.

There have been several protests by refugees living in Nepal where police have been used to quell them.

The birthday celebration of Dalai Lama is held every year in Nepal, but within the boundaries of monasteries or schools and police keep a close watch.

News.title: Boardmasters Festival: Police defend controversial live facial recognition technology used on thousands of attendees
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A police force using live facial recognition at a young persons’ festival insist the controversial technology is “not mass surveillance or mass data capture”, but is being used to keep people safe.

Devon and Cornwall Police will use a police van with the biometric camera for the first time on people attending Boardmasters Festival this weekend. The event, with headliners including Fatboy Slim and Lily Allen, is expected to draw in a crowd of 50,000 across the three three days.

The unit will be positioned in Killacourt, close to the stage, and will be manned by six police officers. The camera will read the faces of passers-by, and issue an alert if anyone matches a “watch list” of thousands of known criminals or those wanted for crimes.

The “watch list” will include suspects, people with sexual harm prevention orders and those suspected of dealing drugs in the area.

Use of the live facial recognition technology has prompted concern from liberty groups, however. Earlier this year, two members of campaign group Big Brother Watch lost a High Court challenge against the Metropolitan Police over concerns it could be used arbitrarily or in a discriminatory way.

The government has already signalled plans to increase the number of vans with the technology from 10 to 50 for forces across England and Wales, despite a strict rules on its use, and although currently being set up, is not yet being in place.

Speaking to The Independent, Chief Inspector Peter Shabytah, who will be leading the live facial recognition operation at the festival, said deployment of the technology was not something the force did “willy-nilly as they fancy”, but was to support a specific policing purpose to keep people safe.

open image in gallery A live facial recognition unit used by the Met Police, which has already deployed the technology at a protest in the capital ( PA )

He said anyone whose face was scanned but did not match the “watch list” was deleted within a few tenths of a second, with no record of the face kept afterwards.

He said: “I would reassure them [attendees] that it's not something that we deploy lightly and where we do deploy it, it's essentially to keep them safe from people who are there to commit crime.

“Sadly, people will be coming to Boardmasters with the sole intention of selling drugs to people there and we know it's young people. And of course, as a police officer, my worst fear is that a bad batch of drugs goes in and cause serious harm to youngsters.

“And so I feel if we have tactics that will allow us to in some way prevent that happening then we should be using those tactics. I would reassure the community that it's not mass surveillance, it's not mass data capture. It is entirely trying to keep communities safe from being victimised.”

Chf Insp Shabytah said that a legal framework from the government on use of the technology would “certainly help all sides”, but that the force was already following legislation on data protection and human rights. The force, he said, had also developed safeguards around deployment of the technology.

open image in gallery The Kaiser Chiefs headlined last year’s Boardmasters festival ( Will Bailey )

He said success from using the kit would be measured on the number of people arrested for serious offences, and also the providing of a visible presence which could deter antisocial behaviour, with the event historically bringing a spike in crime in the area. Last year, six people were arrested by Devon and Cornwall Police.

He added: “Rather than a police officer having to remember in their head these faces and then go ‘is that the person I saw’, now we have a piece of technology that can hold thousands of images in its database and it can match with almost 100 per cent accuracy much better than a human can.”

Across the UK, the technology is also being used find missing and vulnerable individuals. In setting out the plan to increase the number of vans in January, home secretary Shabana Mahmood said forces were "fighting crime in a digital age with analogue methods".

This week, Tory shadow home secretary Chris Philp said he wanted to bring in greater use of facial recognition technology to investigate crimes.

A major new study has found that just a single dose of magic mushrooms could significantly ease depression.

Results found the psychedelic could help with symptoms that is resistant to other treatments.

Symptoms went into remission in four in 10 patients taking part in the first publicly-funded trial of the therapy.

One person described the treatment as “very emotional” at times, but said it helped them to understand their depression more.

The patient said: “It got very intense two or three times… one part that got very emotional for me I felt like I was in a ribcage of some sort and in that I saw my dad holding my sister and that image stays with me because those are two people I have lost.

“I felt like it was a way of them saying we are here and that was definitely a point of emotional release.

“I think afterwards I felt pretty tired and broken. It has taken me a while to reflect and I think it just helped me understand my depression more and just ‘feel’ my feelings – I think I am glad I did it.

“It was very difficult – very painful – but I think that was what I needed and it came at the right time.”

The trial, led by King’s College London and published in Nature Medicine, included 60 people with depression that had not responded to two prior treatments at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust.

Half were given 25mg of psilocybin, while the other half were given a placebo.

Both groups received psychological support throughout the study.

open image in gallery Psilocybin mushrooms stand ready for harvest in a humidified ‘fruiting chamber’ in the basement of a private home on July 28, 2023 in Fairfield County, Connecticut ( Getty )

More than four in 10 people (43%) taking psilocybin met the threshold for treatment response after three weeks, rising to 56% after six weeks.

This is compared to 3% of patients in the placebo group.

Meanwhile, psilocybin helped 40% of patients enter remission, meaning their symptoms of depression fell low enough to no longer meet clinical criteria, within three weeks compared to 3% in the placebo group.

Remission was sustained at six weeks, the trial found.

Professor James Rucker, of King’s College London’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and consultant psychiatrist at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust, said: “Here, we show that a randomised trial design of psilocybin compared to a true placebo was feasible in participants who had often failed many different types of treatment.

“People who were randomised to receive a dose of 25mg of psilocybin were much more likely to improve than those who were randomised to placebo up to six weeks of follow up.

“As is often the case in clinical depression, individual responses were very variable and some of the difference seen between groups will be due to non-drug factors.

“Publicly funded clinical trials are an important part of the jigsaw of evidence needed for a new intervention to find its place in the real world.

“Meanwhile, the wider evidence base for psilocybin therapy is growing rapidly, and looks increasingly promising.”

Recruitment for the trial started at a research facility before moving to a community mental health building.

Catherine Bird, senior clinical trials manager at the IoPPN, said the move shows “psilocybin, unlike many psychiatric drugs, can be administered safely outside a hospital ward” and requires a “calm, supported environment and trained staff rather than medical monitoring”.

Prof Rucker added: “This trial makes a strong case for larger publicly funded trials of psilocybin therapy in community settings, which are often more convenient and less anxiety-provoking for patients than hospital settings.”

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

News.title: What I saw in a week on the front line of Afghanistan’s hunger crisis
News.content:
May 15 and 16, 2026

It is the weekend, a small moment to rest, although there is still a lot of work waiting for me. A week in the field does not mean that work in Kabul stops. I try to catch up on my emails and have a planned online interview for an international staff position – since in Europe, Friday is a normal working day. I also review parts of new proposals for donors and our financial planning.

On Saturday, however, I take a short break. Together with the base management team in Helmand, we visit a historical site called Qala-e-Bost, believed to have been built around 3,000 years ago. It is a rare moment to step away from work, followed by lunch with the team.

May 17, 2026

Sunday morning, the first working day of the week, we visit Basrhan Sub Health Centre, run by one of our local partners. As a nurse and former nurse trainer, I feel very much in my element in these health centres. It allows me to engage easily with the team and discuss their work.

I speak with the outreach officer and the vaccinator. They explain that this facility supports 18 outreach locations, each visited at least once a month. They provide vaccinations, raise awareness, and connect communities to the health centre. These visits often take place in simple settings, like mosques.

Immunisation is now well accepted. In the beginning, there was some resistance, but trust has grown over time. Every child is tracked, and if a child misses a vaccination, community health volunteers follow up at home. For extra polio vaccinations, this is carefully recorded by marking a finger of the child – helping ensure that no child is missed. The goal is clear: a polio-free Afghanistan.

I also speak with a mother. She is wearing a burka, so I cannot see her face. She tells me she is 22 years old and holds her 12-month-old son on her lap. She came because he has a fever, but I see a healthy child – something that stands out after my time in the TFU.

She brings her child regularly for follow-up and growth monitoring and the child has never been in a treatment program for malnutrition. She speaks positively about the services. “We are lucky,” she says. “The staff treat us well, and we have access to care in our community.”

News.title: World’s first seahorse hospital fights to protect them from extinction
News.content:
With careful precision, marine biologist Linda Albonetti extracts a 10cm-long injured seahorse – a heavily pregnant male – from an aquarium tank to apply healing ointment to its wound.

Linda, 29, coordinator at the world’s first specialist seahorse hospital, is currently caring for around 50 of these tiny creatures, all of which were brought in by local fishing crews after becoming snagged in their nets.

The seahorse will be kept for a few more days before it is released back into the Adriatic Sea, giving it time to recover from the cut to the soft, bony plates that form its outer carapace.

What the team here are doing is a literal drop in the ocean, a small attempt to fight back against the potential extinction of these remarkable fish.

In Europe and around countries like Indonesia, they are being poached in their millions for sale to a voracious Asian traditional medicine market where they are consumed as an aphrodisiac and alleged cure for impotence, asthma and kidney problems.

“There is definitely a downward trend in the overall seahorse population because they are being collected for the Asian market,” says Linda. “Technically, they cannot be exported to countries such as China, but there is no specific law preventing that trade. They do not have the same protections as sea turtles, for example.

“It is not happening in this part of Italy yet, but it is further south, off the Mediterranean coast. That is why it is so important that we monitor their numbers and maintain a good relationship with the local fishermen.”

News.title: The 13 best castle hotels in England
News.content:
Few places capture the imagination quite like a castle, and England is home to some of the most remarkable places to spend the night. If it’s not the romance of waking up in a canopied four-poster bed, or losing ourselves in centuries-old tapestries and visceral oil paintings, we are lured by tales of brave knights and plotting dignitaries, duplicitous royals and ghosts parleying secrets in the hallways.

Part of the magic is spending an afternoon wandering grounds and gardens followed by evenings in front of a roaring fire, or dining in a banquet hall that may have hosted medieval kings and queens. While not every castle has crenellated battlements, glistening moats or royal connections, each stony stronghold on our list has something special that makes it worth travelling for. In this modern age that might include a spa, fine-dining restaurant or extra touches like free admission to exhibitions and museum tours. Here’s our pick of the best castle hotels in England.

News.title: Careless Liverpool concede same goal twice in second-half capitulation against Leeds
News.content:
Soldier Field in Chicago hosts an all-Premier League tie encounter as Liverpool take on Leeds as both sides bring their US tours to a close. Both Premier League encounters between these sides last season ended in draws; a 3-3 draw at Elland Road was followed up by a 0-0 stalemate at Anfield. The draw at Elland Road was immediately followed by Mohamed Salah speaking to the media, claiming he had been thrown under the bus.

It is a new era at Liverpool as former Bournemouth boss Andoni Iraola has replaced Arne Slot at Anfield. They kicked off the Iraola era in Nashville, Tennessee, with a 4-2 win over Sunderland, following that up with another victory in New York on Wednesday night, beating Wrexham 1-0, and will be aiming to make it three wins from three on their US tour.

“I think it [the US tour] has been really, really useful,” Iraola said in an interview on the official Liverpool website. Obviously, you spend a lot of time with the players, with the staff, you get all the information you can. And I think there is also an evolution, it has to be. We start to understand each other better, what we need to do. Every game, I hope we can get closer and closer and put ourselves in a position where the few players that still are not here start to train also, they are helped by the others.”

Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo resumed training back on Merseyside whilst Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson and Victor Munoz are yet to return to training following their World Cup exploits. The trio of Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch are all set to feature for the first time this pre-season.

Leeds’ pre-season campaign began with a 3-2 loss to Championship Wrexham in Tampa, Florida before beating Sunderland 1-0 in New Jersey courtesy of a long-range strike from Lukas Nmecha. Former Liverpool man Harry Wilson joined Leeds on a free from Fulham this summer.

“Really tough but that is expected,” Wilson said. That is what pre-season is for, building up a base for when the season starts, making sure you are in the best physical position you can be to attack the season. It has been good. I played against them [Leeds] twice last year when I was at Fulham. Both games were really, really tough games.

“I think when the fans have got a good team to support, I think that [the atmosphere at Elland Road] goes up a notch. I think the size of the club was a massive part of me coming. Then speaking to the guys, the chairman, the sporting director, and seeing kind of the plans and the aims for the club, it is something I wanted to be a part of.”

Team news to follow shortly.

Sports.title: David Beckham and Gary Neville funding major Salford stadium revamp as Paul Scholes reveals plan for 12k-capacity ground
Sports.content:
SALFORD owners David Beckham and Gary Neville are funding a revamp of the club’s stadium amid a raft of changes at the League Two club.

The pair completed a consortium takeover of Salford last year after buying out the rest of their old Manchester United Class of 1992 pals.



Some of the players have stayed on, including Paul Scholes, who is the club’s football director.

But Beckham and Neville are leading the efforts to restructure the club from top to bottom after their agonising League Two play-off final defeat to Notts County.



According to the Athletic, the duo are set to overhaul their Moor Lane stadium, which is now known as the AIG Stadium, to ensure Salford remain competitive.

The ground currently has a capacity of 5,108 but Scholes says the dream is for Salford to reach 12,000.



He told the outlet: “Salford has a community of 300,000 people. We just need three per cent of our city coming to Salford week in, week out and you get 10,000 attendees.

“When we talk around the reality of maybe one day being like a Bournemouth, we live in a community in the part of the world where we have all of the tools at our disposal.”

Scholes adds: “I felt that growth coming last year. Can we get to a 12,000-seater stadium and fill it? That’s the dream. But it’s a long way to go.”

Salford are also renovating their Littleton Road training ground, owned by Scholes’ old club Manchester United.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Scholes added: “This building is going at a level where you are thinking Championship football club.

“It’s something we needed to do because the last five or six years we’ve probably still acted a little bit like a non-League club.”

Their medical department is getting an overhaul too as the US-backed ownership plot a path through the EFL.

The major changes aligns with their total rebrand as a club, which has also seen Beckham and Neville change the kit colours from red to their original orange.



And a new club crest has also been created featuring a lion facing forwards inside a ring and a rose.

The ring represents the gas works in the city, while the rose is a reference to Salford Lads Club.

It’s not just the facilities that are getting an upgrade at Salford.

The club have swapped out their manager after sacking Karl Robinson following the 3-0 defeat in the play-off final this summer.

Salford have since brought in Australian Peter Cklamovski, who previously managed the Malaysia national team and once worked under Ange Postecoglou.

“My heart was pounding,” Paul explained when asked about his experience of watching the Champions League final between Arsenal and PSG. “When that final whistle went, I was just absolutely drained.

“Usually, I imagine people would be jumping up and down for joy. But I was just so…it was such an emotional rollercoaster watching the game and just huge, huge relief when I won.”

“I don’t want to make it a sob story but it’s been a pretty crazy 12 months. I became a father in August last year for the first time. And then we’ve had a bit of a rough year in terms of the family.



“We’ve had a couple of family members that have passed away this year. And so to win this money…I had people messaging me saying, ‘After the year that you’ve had you really, really deserve this.’”

The Champions League final may have been the emotional crescendo but a series of smart decisions throughout the season earned Paul victory.

When quizzed on his process, he explained: “The way I play the game is very much further down the line. I don’t look at what’s happening this weekend, necessarily. I look at what’s happening in a couple of weeks’ time, three or four weeks’ time.

“It’s just a lot of forward planning. It’s not looking in the short term.”



Many Dream Team bosses get disheartened if they start slowly but Paul’s triumph is a reminder that our fantasy game is a marathon, not a sprint.

The Liverpool fan started without Erling Haaland in his XI and didn’t switch tactics until the striker had raced to five goals from his first four outings.

“The reason why I didn’t go with him [Haaland] is that I often think, at the start of the game, it’s important to build your budget. And I think if you go for players that are really, really expensive then they are expected to do well every week and if they don’t, their price is going to drop.”

Prioritising budget is a smart strategy for the first few months of the season but it’s important to recognise when top-tier performers such as Haaland become must-have assets.

Paul balanced long-term planning with reactive adjustments to lay a solid foundation during the first half of the campaign.



One would assume that to amass a jackpot-winning points total you must deploy your Boosters at the optimum moments but that wasn’t the case last season.

“I wasted them,” Paul admitted. “None of them worked out for me.”

Just two players scored the Gameweek he activated Goal Bonus (for a minimal gain of six points) and his 12th Man, Mohamed Salah, delivered a measly seven points from what appeared to be a juicy double header on paper.



“The 12th Man on Salah… I was swayed by people on that one. I think at the time Salah was out of form. But there was that fear that it’s Mo Salah. He could go off and get you a lot of points. It just didn’t work out at all.

“All season, I thought if I’d have used those Boosters a lot better I probably wouldn’t have knocked off ten years of my life watching the Champions League final!”

Paul’s triumph is evidence that smart, consistent decisions over the the course of several months can lead to a life-changing sum of money, even if the Boosters fail to deliver.

One such smart move involved bringing in Lewis Hall amid a flurry of bonus points.



And captaining Anthony Gordon for his four-goal rout against Qarabag in the Champions League was the moment Paul realised he had a legitimate chance of winning Dream Team.

“That was another turning point. Liverpool had played Qarabag and beaten them 5-0 at Anfield. I watched the game and thought Qarabag were awful. I thought they looked like a League One side.

“And when I saw that Newcastle had got them, I thought, I’m targeting them. And I think Gordon had just started playing up front as the No9. I just thought, I really fancy him this way, I’m going to captain him. And he shot me up from 30th to second.”

Sports.title: Arsenal players left ‘fuming’ by pre-season humiliation as Gunners ‘given a hard time’ in woeful defensive showing
Sports.content:
ARSENAL players were left “fuming” in the dressing room after being thumped in their latest pre-season outing.

The Gunners lost 3-1 to Real Betis in front of a bumper crowd in Dublin.



Rodrigo Riquelme gave Manuel Pellegrini‘s side the lead on nine minutes, before Nelson Deossa thumped in a second from range.

Piero Hincapie pulled one back for Arsenal just after the half hour mark, only for ex-West Ham star Pablo Fornals to restore Betis’ two-goal advantage before half-time.



The Gunners looked awful defensively, despite fielding a senior back four featuring the likes of Cristhian Mosquera, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Hincapie.

After the match, boss Arteta said: “We know half of the squad is still not with us.

“We had four players joining three days ago so we know the context but that’s what we have.

“We have to maximise every day that we are with them. We put a lot of work into them the last 10 days.

“Back to London now, we’re going to have two games at home before we play the Community Shield so we’re ready for that.”

Quizzed about the mood in the dressing room, Arteta was brutally honest.

The Spaniard admitted: “They are very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

They will then face former midfielder Cesc Fabregas‘ Como on August 12 in their final pre-season friendly.

Sports.title: Top international footballer murdered in street attack as gang beat him to death with paving stones before robbing him
Sports.content:
FOOTBALL star David Owori has died at the age of 27 after being horrifically attacked by a gang outside of his home.

The Ugandan was one of his nation’s most recognisable stars, but was murdered in a shocking attack by robbers near his home in the capital, Kampala.



Police said Owori was fatally assaulted after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone.

Witnesses then described him being attacked with paving stones before he was robbed of his belongings.



Owori was rushed to a nearby medical clinic and was later transferred to a private facility in the city, but died of his injuries on Wednesday.

The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief and public anger over violent crime in Uganda.

His club, SC Villa, released an emotional statement paying tribute to their late captain.

It said: “Sports Club Villa has called upon the relevant security and law enforcement agencies to urgently investigate and bring to justice those responsible for the tragic death of club captain David Owori, who succumbed to injuries sustained following a brutal assault by unknown assailants.

“’We call upon the relevant security and law enforcement agencies to urgently pursue, apprehend, and bring to justice the perpetrators of this heinous crime.’

“The club described Owori’s passing as a devastating loss, noting that Uganda has lost not only an accomplished footballer but also an exceptional leader and role model.



“This senseless act has robbed the club and the country of a committed captain and a promising sportsman, and it must not go unanswered.

“David Owori will be remembered as a dedicated servant of SC Villa, a respected leader on and off the pitch, and a player whose commitment, professionalism, and passion for the badge inspired team-mates and supporters alike.”

They continued: “As the football community continues to mourn one of its finest leaders, SC Villa once again calls upon the authorities to deliver justice and ensure that those responsible are held accountable.



“The thoughts and prayers of everyone at Sports Club Villa remain with David Owori’s family, friends, team-mates, and all who had the privilege of knowing him.

“May his soul rest in eternal peace.”

Owori had helped the club achieve a record-extending 17th league title in 2023/24 and skippered the side to the Fufa Super 8 trophy last season.

The Ugandan Football Federation said he was “a true leader on and off the pitch”.

Sports.title: International footballer, 27, beaten to death in shocking street attack as thugs ambush him
Sports.content:
International footballer, 27, beaten to death in shocking street attack as thugs ambush him

Ugandan footballer David Owori was reportedly attacked with paving stones outside of his home before dying with an outpouring of grief taking place in his home nation

View 2 Images David Owori died on Wednesday after a brutal attack (Image: SC VILLA)

An international footballer has died aged 27 after being ambushed by thugs and beaten. David Owori was rushed to a medical facility after being left unconscious from a brutal attack and died on Wednesday.

‌



Police say the fatal assault saw Owori resist an attempt to steal his belongings, while witnesses reportedly saw attackers hit the Sports Club Villa captain with paving stones. An SC Villa spokesperson said that Owori was targeted just outside his home in Makindye, a Kampala suburb in Uganda.

‌



"The player was ambushed by thugs as he approached his home, leaving him with life-threatening injuries before he was rushed to the medical facility," they said.

‌



Owori's club posted a short tribute following their captain's passing. "Our hearts are broken," it read.

"SC Villa mourns the tragic passing of our beloved captain, David Owori, following a brutal attack. We have lost more than a player—we have lost a leader, brother and friend. Our deepest prayers are with his family. Rest well, Captain."

One dead and 12 injured after horrific lightning strike during football match READ MORE :

Uganda's football association also paid tribute to Owori, who wore national team colours during the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign. They said he 'carried the hopes of a naiton'.

‌



"The Federation of Uganda Football Associations mourns the untimely passing of Owori David, Captain of SC Villa and Uganda Cranes player," a statement read.

"David was not just a footballer. He was both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.

View 2 Images David Owori died after being brutally beaten (Image: GADLEE/Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International)

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook pag

"On behalf of the FUFA Executive Committee, Delegates, Members, Secretariat Staff and the entire football fraternity, we extend our deepest condolences to SC Villa, his family, teammates, coaches and all Ugandans on the loss of Owori.

"We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.

‌



"We pray that the Almighty grants Owori David eternal rest and gives his family and SC Villa the strength to bear this great loss during these trying times. Rest in peace, Captain."

Uganda's parliament held a minute of silence for Owori on Wednesday.

The midfielder helped SC VIlla to a first league title in 20 years in 2024 after joining the club for the second time in 2023. The earlier parts of his career saw spells as Proline FC, Spanish side Velez CF and Swedish team Utiskitens BK, in addition to SC Villa.

Sports.title: Liverpool weigh up hijacking £60m Arsenal transfer to appease desperate Andoni Iraola
Sports.content:
Liverpool weigh up hijacking £60m Arsenal transfer to appease desperate Andoni Iraola

Andoni Iraola is desperate for a signing in central defence, where Liverpool are "very thin", and the club could beat Arsenal to Aston Villa and England star Ezri Konsa

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola is desperate for defensive reinforcements (Image: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Liverpool could rival Arsenal for the signing of Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa as Andoni Iraola desperately seeks a solution to his injury crisis. Pre-season has shown just how short Liverpool are in central defence, providing some urgency to their search for a new centre-back.

‌



An injury to Joe Gomez in a friendly against Sunderland has highlighted the lack of depth in the position, with £55million signing Jeremy Jacquet yet to feature in pre-season as he's eased back from a shoulder injury and Giovanni Leoni still recovering from his ACL injury.

‌



With Virgil van Dijk given time off after the World Cup, Iraola has been forced to turn to youth, starting Ifeanyi Ndukwe, 18, and Luke Chambers, 22, in the 4-2 defeat by Leeds on Sunday, while Mor Talla Ndiaye, 18, has also featured in pre-season.

‌



The departure of Ibrahima Konate means Liverpool need an experienced player to partner Van Dijk and the Guardian reports that Konsa has emerged as a target. The England international is also on Arsenal's radar after William Saliba suffered a back injury at the World Cup, but Villa's £60m valuation is thought to be beyond the Gunners' means.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Jamie Carragher criticises Mohamed Salah's Turkey move after Liverpool exit READ MORE :

Konsa has two years left on his contract at Villa, where he has played since 2019, making 286 appearances in all competitions. The 28-year-old has a wealth of Premier League experience and could fit the bill for Iraola, who has voiced frustrations at the lack of depth in the squad he inherited this summer.

‌



Jacquet, who signed in January from Rennes, and Victor Munoz (£35m from Osasuna) are the only two major deals done so far and the issue is shown by the fact Iraola's assistant, Tommy Elphick, had to fill in at centre-back in a recent training drill.

Iraola admitted recently: "With the centre-back, with the right-back situation, in terms of defensive depth, we are, I think, very thin right now so I think it's a solution that we are trying to find, yes."

View 2 Images Ezri Konsa is a target for Liverpool and Arsenal (Image: Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

‌



Gomez will miss the Premier League opener against Newcastle on August 23, leaving Van Dijk as the only fit senior centre-back in the squad. The Dutchman did not join his team-mates on the United States leg of their pre-season, leaving Iraola will less time to work with him before the campaign kicks off.

"When the market is open, you have to be always open to new options to improve the squad," Iraola said last month. "There are obvious situations where we need to sign players."

Liverpool are undergoing a summer of transition, with Iraola arriving to replace Arne Slot after a disappointing campaign, which saw Konate, Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson leave. To complicate matters further, Fenway Sports Group chief Michael Edwards has also left, piling more pressure and responsibility onto sporting director Richard Hughes to get deals done.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino 'held secret talks' to get FIFA involved in European Super League
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino 'held secret talks' to get FIFA involved in European Super League

A leaked document reportedly shows that FIFA and Gianni Infantino were not just aware of the European Super League plans in 2021, but wanted in on the failed scheme

View 3 Images The European Super League sparked a huge backlash in 2021 (Image: Getty Images)

Gianni Infantino tried to get FIFA involved in the failed attempts to establish a European Super League, according to a leaked document.

‌



Infantino is currently desperately trying to cling onto power as FIFA president following the humiliating U-turn over his plans to sell stakes in tournaments like the World Cup. Infantino has now apologised for secretly plotting to welcome private investment, while insisting that he will continue as president.

‌



But UEFA and their allies are understood to remain determined to oust the Swiss from his position. They have encouraged their members to backtrack on their previous support for Infantino ahead of his attempt to be re-elected for a fourth term in March.

‌



And the revelation that the recent plot was not the first time that Infantino had used football's governing body to try to usher in outside money will pile further pressure onto him and strengthen his detractors' resolve. The Guardian reports that Infantino held talks about branding the European Super League as "FIFA Super League".

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Gianni Infantino issues grovelling apology for botched World Cup plot after crisis meeting READ MORE :

The European Super League fell flat in a matter of days in the spring of 2021 after becoming public knowledge. The 12 clubs involved in trying to form a closed-shop breakaway league from UEFA were forced into an embarrassing climbdown after fan protests.

‌



It has now emerged that Infantino and FIFA were also involved, having created a 'term sheet' for the league in October 2020. Infantino reportedly wanted a 'golden share' in the breakaway, while a 12-year partnership, which would've seen FIFA run the commercial operation, was proposed.

There were also plans to tie FIFA's Club World Cup to the Super League. It is reported that, like with the private investment scheme, FIFA's federations were not consulted in the early stages of the scheme.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino is trying to hold onto power at the top of FIFA (Image: Getty)

‌



In response to the article, a FIFA spokesperson replied on X, writing: "The FIFA President, Gianni Infantino, in his address to the 45th Ordinary UEFA Congress in Montreux, Switzerland in April 2021, clearly expressed FIFA’s strong disapproval of the proposed European breakaway league project: 'At FIFA, we can only strongly disapprove the creation of a super league which is a closed shop, which is a breakaway from the current institutions, from the leagues, from the associations, from UEFA and from FIFA, which is outside of the system. There is no doubt whatsoever of FIFA’s disapproval for this'."

Those words from Infantino came after it was clear the European Super League was doomed to be a spectacular failure. All six of the Premier League's 'Big Six' - Arsenal, Chelsea, Tottenham, Manchester United, Manchester City and Liverpool - pulled out quickly following the backlash, while Inter Milan, AC Milan, Juventus and Atletico Madrid soon joined them.

View 3 Images The European Super League collapsed almost immediately due to the backlash (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Barcelona and Real Madrid held on longer to the pipe dream before quietly backing out in 2025 and 2026 respectively. A company called A22 Sports Management is still trying to pursue the idea through the courts, but it largely been consigned to the history books until now.

Meanwhile, Infantino has gone on the offensive in his attempts to secure his position at the head of FIFA, where he has sat for 10 years. After holding a meeting in Morocco, he issued a letter with FIFA general secretary, Mattias Grafstrom, which outlined the new approach to sweeping the ordeal under the carpet.

It said: "With the project withdrawn, FIFA will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation."

Sports.title: One dead and 12 injured after horrific lightning strike during football match
Sports.content:
One dead and 12 injured after horrific lightning strike during football match

A tragic incident has unfolded during a football match, where a lightning strike caused the death of one player and 12 others

View Image A footballer in Thailand has been killed by an airstrike (Image: Facebook/@FCYala)

A man has been killed after being struck by lightning while playing a football match. The freak incident happened in the small Thai town of Sungai Golok on Tuesday August 4th.

‌



The Golok FA Cup clash between Abu x Nong Sirin and SAMCOLT was suddenly halted by a gigantic lightning strike which forced the match to be abandoned. However, the terrifying bolt claimed the life of 24-year-old Sofwan Awae who was struck at the Santiphap Stadium.

‌



Team-mates desperately tried to revive him on the pitch with emergency services being called immediately. Tragically, neither his team-mates nor the emergency medical team were able to save his life.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook pag

Sungai Golok police chief Thun Sirikhunt announced in a statement: “Although the emergency medical team made every effort to save him, the victim succumbed to severe injuries sustained in the incident."

Local police forces also confirmed 12 others were injured by the strike and taken to hospital. Video footage of the chilling incident has since gone viral.

‌



His fellow players could be seen pushing him onto his back to begin resuscitation efforts after the terrifying blast.

The Football Association of Thailand released a statement after the tragedy which said: "The association joins in mourning this loss and offers its condolences to the family, those involved and the football club during this time of sorrow."

Yala FC, the opposing team to the one Awae was playing for, also said: “We extend our condolences to the family of our new FC Yala player, Sofwan Awae."

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The incident has similarities to another tragedy in 1998 which was caused by lightning. A football match in the Democratic Republic of Congo saw 11 players from one team be killed by a blast.

Lightning strikes are understood to have claimed the lives of 283 people in Thailand between 2020 and 2024. The Department of Disease Control has also claimed the majority of those people died on the spot, immediately after the strike.

Article continues below

As recently as May, an engineering student and his auntie were killed by lightning when a bolt struck a hut in the province of Lampang. A 30-year-old pregnant woman was also killed by lightning in Uthai Thani province as she took shelter beneath a tree, after returning from a fishing trip with her husband.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher criticises Mohamed Salah's Turkey move after Liverpool exit
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher criticises Mohamed Salah's Turkey move after Liverpool exit

Mohamed Salah was given a hero's welcome after touching down in Turkey before his official unveiling as a new Trabzonspor player, but Jamie Carragher thinks he's made a mistake

View 2 Images Mohamed Salah was greeted by Trabzonspor fans on Wednesday (Image: Seyit Ahmet Eksik/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Mohamed Salah is "too good" to be playing for Trabzonspor and should have stayed in a top European league after leaving Liverpool, according to Jamie Carragher. Salah is poised to sign a two-year deal with the Turkish side after being mobbed by excited fans at the airport on Wednesday.

‌



Salah is a free agent after walking away from Liverpool - and his £400,000-a-week contract - at the end of last season. He has ended up in the north of Turkey, where he will play for the side which finished third in the Super Lig last season.

‌



Trabzonspor, who have Manchester United loanee Andre Onana in goal, last won the title in 2022 and will play in the Europa League next season. They have won the race to sign Salah, who will be officially unveiled on Thursday evening, having already been given a seismic welcome by thousands of fans at Ataturk Airport in Istanbul and then later at Trabzon Airport.

‌



There had been speculation that the 34-year-old would end up in Saudi Arabia, due to his sky-high wage demands. But Carragher is disappointed he didn't end up in Italy, where he could have continued to play at a high level and prolong his career like Cristiano Ronaldo.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Liverpool exploring Ibrahim Mbaye transfer as PSG star's stance on move emerges READ MORE :

"I never believed he was going to go to Saudi, because number one, he's too good for that. I think he can be playing in Serie A. Turkey for me feels a level too low," he told the Football Ramble.

‌



"I was convinced he'd end up at an AC Milan or Juventus or somewhere like that, maybe his wages were a problem. Looking at him, I don't know him, obviously have never spoken to him.

"But he's like Ronaldo, he's so driven, his numbers mean so much to him. I thought, he can still do this in Turkey by the way, but I thought he'd want to play at a real prestigious club."

View 2 Images Mohamed Salah got a hero's welcome at Trabzon Airport (Image: Hakan Burak Altunoz/Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Salah's wages were always likely to be a barrier for interested clubs and it seems the Egyptian was an unrealistic signing for many big clubs. While Trabzonspor haven't had to pay a transfer fee, they have completely altered their wage structure to make the biggest signing in their history.

"Obviously his wage demands have put a few people off but I thought he might almost curb those demands a little bit to almost get a better club," Carragher added.

"To go to an AC Milan or Juventus or whoever it may be, play at the San Siro, still playing in big games, still playing in Europe. Turkey just feels like... I just think he's better than that."

Article continues below

Salah will now embark upon a new stage of his career after leaving behind Liverpool, where he scored 257 goals in 442 appearances over nine years and won two Premier League titles, the Champions League, the Club World Cup, the UEFA Super Cup, FA Cup and two Carabao Cups.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta gives blunt response to Bruno Guimaraes question after Newcastle transfer agreed
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta gives blunt response to Bruno Guimaraes question after Newcastle transfer agreed

Arsenal are poised to announce the signing of Bruno Guimaraes in a £75million deal from Newcastle in a significant boost which comes after a friendly defeat by Real Betis

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta spoke after a friendly defeat by Real Betis (Image: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)

Mikel Arteta kept his cards close to his chest when asked about the impending arrival of Bruno Guimaraes at Arsenal following their friendly loss against Real Betis.

‌



The Gunners were beaten 3-1 by their Spanish opponents on Wednesday night in a disappointing performance. Piero Hincapie's header from a corner was the only consolation for Arteta's side, who appeared rusty in Dublin.

‌



Arsenal have been relatively quiet in the summer transfer window so far, with a £34million deal for Christos Tzolis and a free transfer for Illan Meslier the only major done deals. But they are soon to be boosted by the arrival of Guimaraes, who is set to undergo his medical in the coming days after a £75m fee was agreed with Newcastle.

‌



The Brazil international is due in north London after leaving Newcastle's pre-season training camp in Spain and will replace Christian Norgaard, who joined Everton for £7m. The deal was agreed on Wednesday before Arsenal's defeat by Betis, but Arteta would not discuss it.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Vinicius Jr takes extreme measures amid Arsenal transfer interest and Real Madrid meeting READ MORE :

How Arsenal could line up after signing Bruno Guimaraes and completing Vinicius Jr transfer READ MORE :

"I'm not going to talk about any players who aren't Arsenal players," he said when first asked in his post-match press conference.

‌



When pressed, he added: "Well, I can tell you at the moment that something happens and we can announce it. I will give you my straight answer."

While he won't yet say it, Guimaraes' arrival will come as a significant boost for Arsenal. The 28-year-old has 30 goals and 26 assists in 153 Premier League appearances for Newcastle and will add competition for places and leadership in midfield.

It is understood that he has had his heart set on Arsenal since hearing of their interest and his insistence forced Newcastle to sell. Arsenal initially offered £60m, while the Magpies wanted £80m for their captain, who had two years left on his contract. A compromise was reached at £75m.

‌



View 2 Images Bruno Guimaraes will soon be an Arsenal player (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Once Guimaraes has joined, Arsenal will turn their attention to signing a centre-back and another attacker. William Saliba's back injury has forced the Gunners into the market, with Aston Villa's Ezri Konsa a key target. However, the England international has two years left on his deal and is valued at £60m by Villa.

Meanwhile, a move for Vinicius Junior hangs in the balance, with Real Madrid in delicate negotiations to try and extend his contract. Vinicius' current deal expires in June 2027 and he wants a pay increase to bring him closer to Kylian Mbappe's level.

‌



Real are understood to have offered him an increase, but short of what the 26-year-old Brazilian was looking for. It remains to be seen if a compromise can be reached, but while Vinicius has raised eyebrows by deleting his Instagram posts, he has not stated a desire to leave this summer.

Sports.title: Why Jimenez’s Wolves return means so much to fans
Sports.content:
The most romantic signing of the summer came early. Raul Jimenez is back at Wolves. And for the club's supporters, they are not so much welcoming back a former favourite but revisiting a chapter of their own lives. For a generation, Jimenez is the Wolves No 9.

He was the striker who arrived just when Wolves were rediscovering themselves. Promotion became Europe. The best came to Molineux and were beaten. Now, he is returning with Wolves at a low ebb. But this second coming has rejuvenated the club.

The evidence has been overwhelming since Jimenez's signing was confirmed after three seasons away. It was not just the emotional announcement video, although that certainly captured the imagination, instantly transforming the mood after relegation.

Consider the social media numbers. Since signing for Wolves, each of the club's top 10 most engaged posts have been about Jimenez. The club has been blown away by the response across platforms. Their most engaged Instagram post anyone can remember.

And that is just social media. Out in the real world, Jimenez shirts are everywhere. Not Wolves shirts, Jimenez shirts. For the pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad, where his name was chanted even in his absence, there were Mexico tops - home and away.

Inside the club shop, the Jimenez jersey is outselling last year's most popular player by more than 250 per cent. You probably need to go back to Steve Bull to find a figure so beloved by the supporters but the shirts did not have names on the back in those days.

None of which should come as much of a surprise. Jimenez's name has been sung regularly by supporters in recent seasons and it had little to do with the hope that he would come back. He, along with others, had come to symbolise what had been lost.

It was a lament to Wolves' decline, sometimes accompanied by another chant aimed at owners Fosun. "You sold the team, now sell the club." But when Fulham visited Molineux in the final home fixture of last season, the tone became more celebratory.

It was only after that game that Jimenez revealed to a local journalist that there had been talks over a deal to bring him home. The giddiness that greeted that revelation helped make it happen and sustained supporters in the wake of a miserable relegation.

If all this still seems a bit much for a player who scored 40 Premier League goals for Wolves, the context is key. Jimenez was the club's top scorer as the club finished in the top seven in consecutive campaigns for the first time since Stan Cullis was in charge.

Image: Raul Jimenez's Premier League goal map during his career in England

You have to go back to 1989 to find a Wolves player who has beaten Jimenez's 27 goals in the 2019/20 season. That was Bull, the folk hero of all folk heroes, in the third tier. To find a player doing it in the top flight you are going back to 'King' John Richards in 1973.

Jimenez's 40 goals are more than anyone else has scored for Wolves in the Premier League era. It is 57 in all competitions and those other competitions are all part of the story. He scored at Wembley, not just away to Tottenham, but in an FA Cup semi-final.

More than that, he is the club's all-time top scorer in European competition. That is about the memories as much as the numbers for the fans who travelled. Two goals away to Crusaders in Northern Ireland. Two goals away to Pyunik Yerevan in Armenia.

Jimenez scored home and away against Torino, a trip that fans talk about to this day. He scored home and away against Slovan Bratislava. He scored in the torrential rain in Braga, another adventure still sung about by Wolves supporters. This stuff matters.

Image: Raul Jimenez celebrates scoring for Wolves against Man Utd in the FA Cup in 2019

It was later that year that Jimenez suffered a fractured skull in a collision with David Luiz away to Arsenal. The silence in the stadium was eerie enough during that period of the pandemic. That day it took on a more ominous tone. A sickening blow in every sense.

The road back was long and arduous, the scars mental and physical. Jimenez arguably never did recapture his best form in a Wolves shirt. He is yet to score a headed goal for the club since. That could soon become another cathartic Molineux moment to relish.

But if the injury hampered his performances on the pitch, it only solidified the bond with the club off it. Jimenez and his family have been open about how much the support that they received meant to them. The emotions of that experience have led them back here.

Image: Wolves favourite Raul Jimenez is back at Molineux after three years away

And this is a family move. Daniela, Jimenez's wife and mother to his two children, has long embraced the city, endearing herself with her efforts to repeat the 'Wolves Ay We' mantra. The pair even did the gender reveal of their second child on the Molineux pitch.

That first exit, after Jimenez had fallen out of the first-team line-up under Julen Lopetegui, never did feel like a satisfactory ending for such a hero. He was crying that day against Everton in May 2023, saying his goodbyes after being an unused substitute.

This is a chance to correct that and to underline Jimenez's status as a figure woven into the emotional architecture of the club. That Diogo Jota, his old strike partner, is no longer with us only adds poignancy. All parties are determined to cherish this reunion.

Image: Raul Jimenez is Wolves' top Premier League goalscorer from his first stint

Can he still deliver? There will be optimism based on a World Cup in which he found the net three times in four games. Jimenez looked sharp enough this summer to suggest that he is still close enough to his best to cope with the demands of the Championship.

Jimenez is the bookmakers' favourite to be the competition's top scorer. So reliable from the spot - he has scored more Premier League penalties than anyone else with a 100 per cent record - he is surely a safe bet for at least 20 goals this season if he can stay fit.

Whether he will receive the service required to fire Wolves back up is another matter. Under new coach Cesar Peixoto, there is still uncertainty over the makeup of the squad and the ability to implement a shift in style. Success is far from guaranteed.

But, in a way, all of that is to miss the point. Bull himself spent 10 long years playing for Wolves in the second tier without achieving the promotion that his efforts deserved. He still garnished his legend during that decade, plundering goals and making memories.

Bull stayed. Jimenez has returned.

And Wolves have their No 9 back.

Sports.title: Bethell to miss Pakistan Test series as Pope recalled
Sports.content:
Jacob Bethell will miss the entirety of England's upcoming Test series against Pakistan, while Ollie Pope and Brydon Carse have been named in the 16-man squad.

England are preparing to return to action following their series defeat to New Zealand and the departures of head coach Brendon McCullum and captain Ben Stokes.

Joe Root, reinstalled as skipper following Stokes' international retirement, will lead a team seeking to turn the page on a difficult spell on and off the field.

England's new head coach Stephen Fleming will not take charge until after the three-match series, which begins at Headingley on August 19, live on Sky Sports Cricket.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England have made multiple changes to their side following the departure of Ben Stokes

Bethell sustained a knee injury during England's ODI series against India in July, causing him to miss The Hundred.

He will remain sidelined for the Pakistan series, with Essex wicketkeeper Jordan Cox replacing him at No 3, having made his Test debut earlier this summer.

Pope, formerly vice-captain under Stokes, and Carse return to the Test squad for the first time since England's dismal Ashes tour of Australia last winter.

Dan Lawrence has also been recalled to the side two years after his last Test appearance and is set to enter the starting XI to bat at No 6.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player New England Test coach Stephen Fleming will not take charge until after the three-match Test series

England national selector Marcus North said: "We have selected a squad for the first two Tests that balances rising talent with the experience needed against a quality Pakistan team.

"Dan Lawrence returns following an exceptional season so far with Surrey and we believe he has the right level of experience, maturity and skill to complement our middle order.

"Jordan Cox is well regarded as one of the most exciting talents in English cricket and will have the opportunity to bat at 3 in place of Jacob Bethell, who sadly misses this series through injury."

Sports.title: 'Relieved, excited, and energised!' - Parker's plans revealed after drug ban lifted
Sports.content:
Joseph Parker is 'relieved' after a ban was lifted for a failed drug test and he will return to the ring this year, says manager David Higgins.

The New Zealander returned traces of cocaine in a Voluntary Anti-Doping Agency test on the day of his defeat by Fabio Wardley in October, but Parker denied taking any banned substances and the British Boxing Board of Control confirmed the suspension has been lifted.

Parker's manager Higgins is planning the next career move for the former WBO world heavyweight champion, who could fight twice before the end of 2026.

Image: Joseph Parker has started preparing for his next fight

"A combination of relieved, excited, and energised," said Higgins when asked about Parker's current mindset.

"Joseph is champing at the bit to get back into the ring. He was up early to go for a run this morning.

Sports.title: Joe Ward: The unluckiest man in Irish boxing
Sports.content:
Joe Ward had the world at his feet. He was an amateur boxing sensation, he had a golden future laid out before him. Until disaster struck, over and over again.

In 2011 Ward made history, becoming the youngest Irish boxer to win a gold medal at the senior European Championships.

Even at that early stage hype was building for what Ward could accomplish at the London Olympics. But at the 2012 qualification event, tucked away in Trabzon in Turkey, the teenage Ward lost a contentious decision to the host nation boxer.
