Sports.title: Why Honda only realised the scale of its F1 problems in January
Sports.content:
Heading into Formula 1's major technical overhaul, expectations at Aston Martin were high. With a state-of-the-art factory in Silverstone, legendary designer Adrian Newey and a works partnership with Honda, all the ingredients for success appeared to be in place.

That may still prove to be the case in the longer term, but the start of the new era has proved far more challenging than anticipated. Mike Krack recently admitted that Aston Martin had barely been racing before the summer break, simply because the gap to newcomer Cadillac amounted to around one second.

That changed when the AMR26 received its first major upgrade package in Hungary, although the chassis is naturally only part of the story. Honda has also encountered numerous problems since officially returning to F1, ranging from vibrations that troubled the drivers during the opening weeks of the season to a significant deficit in outright performance.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with Autosport, trackside manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara explained that the full extent of those problems only became clear in January.

“So, probably at the end of last year, our position was not so bad,” he said. “Still, performance and drivability were in the development stage, but it looked okay.

"But in January, we realised that in some of the areas we found some, not issues, but we realised that performance was always up, down, up, down. So we found some performance, but then we also found some reliability issues."

Shintaro Orihara, Honda Photo by: EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Because reliability is always a top priority, Honda had to take a step back on several performance gains to ensure reliability at that performance level. Naturally, that slowed down its overall development.

"In January, we realised that our performance and reliability would not be competitive,” Orihara added. “When we started running in Barcelona, we realised that our performance was definitely poor compared to the other manufacturers. And also, we found some issues on the battery side."

Those battery-related issues made the development process more complex. They cost valuable track time during winter testing, something that was especially painful given Aston Martin and Honda's need to gather data to recover from their deficit.

"So we realised that we were not in good position, maybe at beginning of this year. Last year, at end of last year, we already saw that we were not competitive, but we didn't expect it so bad," Orihara admitted.

What has been Honda's biggest challenge?

Part of the explanation is that Honda's current F1 project is very different from its successful years with Red Bull, something that ties in with the company's philosophy of transferring F1 knowledge to other parts of the company.

Another part of the explanation is, according to Honda, the complexity of the current regulations. Orihara stressed that there has not been one single stumbling block ahead of 2026, but rather the combination of all the changes introduced at the same time.

Honda Power Unit Launch

"It's difficult to say which component of the power unit is most challenging because in this regulation, everything has changed a lot,” said Orihara. “For example, MGU-K power changed from, let's say, [120] to 350 kilowatts. That is a significant change.

"But also on the internal combustion engine side, we have changed the fuel flow rate. So in this regulation, everything has been changed so much. So, a challenging point for Honda is just the combination of a lot of changes happening at the same time."

That means Honda is lacking outright power from its internal combustion engine, something the long-awaited Zandvoort upgrade is specifically designed to address. It is intended to be the first step towards reducing the brand's still significant performance deficit.

On the electrical side of the power unit, the emphasis is on efficiency. However, Orihara explained that the changes there have also had a major impact on drivability – one of the areas that has been a recurring topic for Honda and Aston Martin in the opening months of the season.

"Removing the MGU-H has also been quite challenging on the power unit side,” he said.

“Probably that is the most exciting point for power unit manufacturers. I have always been mentioning drivability. That is, maybe not mainly, but the majority of that is coming from removing the MGU-H.

"So that is a challenging point for us as a power unit supplier, to keep the boost pressure at a target. Again, it's difficult to pick one component that has been most challenging for us, but it has been the combination of all changes at the same time."

Although Honda knows that returning to the competitive level it is targeting will take time - a lot of time - it hopes to make a first step at Zandvoort. That upgrade is focused purely on improving the internal combustion engine and was already tested during a filming day at the Hungaroring.

Sports.title: Why McLaren has been coy about introducing its rotating F1 rear wing
Sports.content:
McLaren will race its version of the so-called 'Macarena' rear-wing concept – but not until an unspecified point in the future, according to team principal Andrea Stella.

It's understood that the reason for not rushing to race the new rear wing is not linked to Red Bull's well-documented issues with its similar design. Instead, McLaren is being cautiously pragmatic, since the rotating rear wing adds to the complexities of managing car behaviour as it moves in and out of Straight Line Mode (SLM).

McLaren planned to test its new wing in Austria but made a late decision to abandon the evaluation. It then waited until Hungary to run it for the first time in FP1 on Oscar Piastri's car, driven by Leonardo Fornaroli, before parking it for the remainder of the event.

Max Verstappen crashed at the Red Bull Ring and Silverstone, prompting his Red Bull team to temporarily shelve its pivoting rear wing based on suspicions that a delay in airflow reattachment when the wing returned to cornering mode made Verstappen's car unstable.

"I have to say it's been a complicated project," Stella told media including Autosport.

"Which was no surprise because when we saw Ferrari introducing the wing in Bahrain test and testing it in China in the first lap, [Lewis] Hamilton spun. And then it took a few more events to actually being in condition to race it.

"We knew it was going to be a complex project, so I have to say that our engineering department has delivered this project in a way that looks well-behaved – like the wing in terms of mechanical actuation, times of the actuation, because there's some limitations by the regulations, not only for aerodynamic reasons.

Ferrari was the first team to run its rotating rear wing, which operates differently to the McLaren and Red Bull examples Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"And then the overall behaviour from an aerodynamic point of view, reattachment – so the time it takes for the car to regain the load, not only the load on the wing, the load on the entire car as driven from the wing.

"All this I have to say has been pretty consistent with expectation, so it's been a positive sign off of this concept and we look forward now to introducing this concept at some future events."

These concepts are a classic example of thinking-outside-the-box creative engineering that is possible for the first time this season because the regulations are relatively open. F1 first adopted the principle of legally shedding drag in a straight line with the Drag Reduction System (DRS) in 2011, which permitted the upper rear wing plane to flatten in prescribed areas of the track.

The speed and actuation procedure for this was clearly defined, along with the dimensions of the wing planes themselves. But under the new ruleset introduced this season, in which front and rear wing flaps can open in specified Straight Line Mode zones, the speed of transition from one state to the other is defined (within 0.4s), but not the means by which it moves between open and closed.

McLaren's pivoting rear wing is closer to Red Bull's than Ferrari's, in that it uses a central actuator to manage the rotation rather than having a mechanism built into the endplates. Also like Red Bull's, it pivots forwards rather than backwards.

The means of actuation gives it an element of air braking as it closes. The trade-off between the two concepts is that Red Bull and McLaren accept a degree of aerodynamic blockage from the actuator and its shroud in exchange for having a wider space between the upper and lower planes when SLM is active.

Ferrari's also has to take a longer path between open and closed because of the angle of rotation.

Verstappen shunted in qualifying in Austria, and a delay in airflow reattachment to the rear wing was cited as one possible contributory factor Photo by: Getty Images

One of the less predictable effects of the new regulations has been the shift in tyre loading during the transition between SLM being on and off. This is because the airflow doesn't reattach to the wing planes instantly, but takes fractions of a second to re-establish its path.

Teams knew ahead of the season that this would be a significant performance factor, but were unable to measure it accurately with simulation tools such as the wind tunnel and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD).

The true extent of the shifts in loadings, and their effect on car behaviour, could only be measured at the track.

This also applies to the theoretical benefits of the rotating rear wings. The airflow around the rear of an F1 car is tremendously busy because of the interaction between the car's aerodynamic surfaces and the turbulent wake of the rear wheels.

Simulating this with great accuracy is very difficult in the wind tunnel, where model size is capped at 60% scale and the wind is generally blowing in one direction. Historically it is difficult to access a car's aerodynamic performance when it's in a state of yaw (i.e. turning), or facing different wind directions. The different deflection properties of the model tyres, as well as their smaller size, also has a tendency to skew results.

Hence McLaren has done a lot of FP1 running with large aero rakes fitted behind the rear wheels to validate substantial bodywork changes such as the latest-spec floor, introduced in Hungary, as well as its pivoting wing. Practical measurements trackside are the real proof (or otherwise) of any theoretical gains.

"There was a question about comparison with Red Bull, but I don't think the wind tunnel is a major factor in terms of determining the aerodynamic behaviour in reattachment," Stella said.

"I think you can use some other tools for that, and then the most important tool, especially when you have this sort of complicated project, even from an aerodynamic point of view, remains what you observe at the track. So it was important for us to acquire data here trackside, because you would have never relied on a wind tunnel only for such a delicate project."

Sports.title: Why the FIA couldn't intervene sooner over F1's 2026 rules
Sports.content:
With the first Formula 1 season under the new technical regulations approaching its halfway point, the summer break provides a good opportunity to take stock. The 2026 rules, with their much greater emphasis on electric power, have sparked considerable debate both in and outside the paddock.

F1 insists that fan ratings – for example in its own Formula 1 Fan Voice programme – have been largely positive, but drivers have been far more critical.

Max Verstappen described the power unit regulations as "Formula E on steroids" during winter testing in Bahrain, while Oscar Piastri spoke at Spa-Francorchamps about the "self-learning elements" of the power units and "qualifying grids being decided by computers behaving or misbehaving".

Asked by Autosport whether the criticism from drivers over the past few months had been stronger than the FIA expected, Tombazis responded: "I think drivers are, by definition, quite demanding clients. I don't think we expected them to have a sugarcoat or to not speak their minds. So to say that it's been more than expected, no, I wouldn't say so."

The complaints from drivers about energy management, super clipping and algorithms were also in line with what the FIA had anticipated, according to its single-seater director.

"We did anticipate a lot of these things that they have complained about in the two years before the launch of the season. We did try to make some adjustments, but we failed with the governance that was in place," Tombazis said. "So I think it was realistically only to be expected."

Energy-starved circuits such as Silverstone and Spa-Francorchamps have highlighted the shortcomings of the 2026 regulations Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

FIA tried to listen to F1 drivers' criticism in build-up to 2026

If it had been up to Tombazis, the changes to the regulations that have now been agreed for 2027 and 2028 – to gradually move to a 60-40 split – would ideally have been introduced much earlier.

"I think it's a bit of a shame that we had to wait until we discussed things in May and get to a package for 2027 and for 2028. I think we could have ideally done that a couple of years before and then there wouldn't have been all of this discussion," Tombazis said.

Several drivers warned about potential problems with the new engine regulations before 2026. Verstappen was the first to do so publicly during the 2023 Austrian Grand Prix, when Autosport asked him about his initial simulator runs with the new engine formula.

That has perhaps created the impression that drivers were not listened to in the years leading up to 2026, but Tombazis insists the reality is different. According to him, the initial feedback was taken seriously, but the governance framework meant the regulations could not be significantly revised.

"When OEMs decide to participate as PU manufacturers, they sign a governance agreement that is binding towards all parties, so the FIA, FOM and the PU manufacturers. It's similar to what the Concorde Agreement does for the team side of things," Tombazis explained.

"And there was a separate governance agreement signed in 2022 in order to basically outline the requirements for the PU manufacturers during the years of 2023, 2024 and 2025. That is before the championship started because there's such things like financial regulations for the first time."

The FIA states that governance, even with new manufacturers such as Audi, has made intervention impossible Photo by: Pirelli

Among other things, that agreement stipulated that new entrants would not be allowed to spend unlimited amounts of money to develop their 2026 power units.

"If a PU manufacturer who was not participating in Formula 1, let's say Audi, they still had to be bound by regulations and not come to us and say, well, we're not participating, hence we can spend five times the money. That would be unfair," he said.

"So that's why there was a governance agreement that on the one hand forced them to be bound by the regulations, including the financial and operational rules and all of that."

At the same time, that document made it much harder for the FIA to reopen the regulations in the years leading up to 2026 without securing a supermajority.

"On the other hand it put limitations as to how much we could change things unilaterally as the FIA. And therefore any change had to be approved by a significant number of the PU manufacturers," Tombazis explained.

"So for the sort of changes we did [in May], we needed at least four of them to agree. And quite simply, four of them did not agree during the years when we discussed some adjustments."

Tombazis had hoped that the changes for the coming years could have been implemented sooner Photo by: Lars Baron / Getty Images

Challenges known since 2022, but races still entertaining

Part of the reason for that was that the reality of the automotive industry looked very different at the time, with manufacturers placing a much greater emphasis on electrification.

"Overall, it was always a challenging target to have a close to 50-50 power split between the two units," Tombazis said.

"But that was a very important position for the OEMs participating, and frankly having to decide whether they want to be in Formula 1 or not. Don't forget that if we didn't have them in, we would have just two power units in Formula 1, which I think would have been a bit of an issue. So that requirement to have a much stronger electrical part did create these difficulties."

Tombazis explained that the FIA had already become aware of these challenges in 2022, a year before Verstappen publicly voiced his concerns, but by then it was simply too late to fundamentally alter the regulations.

"As simulations came in back in 2022 or so, we knew there were these issues, but we were a bit too far down the line there to change things and some people had committed too much resource," he said. "So that left us slightly on the back foot at the start of the season, discussing that."

Tombazis concluded by stressing that, despite all of this, the races themselves have still provided good entertainment during the first half of the season.

Tombazis feels despite the problems with the F1 regulations, the racing has been exciting Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

"Now with that said, I think most races have been pretty exciting, I would say. There's been quite a lot of fighting," he said.

"I would even say that currently we still have, I don't know if I would go quite as far as to call it domination, but we do have a clear advantage for one manufacturer. And in the past when we've had that at the early start of the regulations, races have been very processional.

"Now I think, even despite the fact that Mercedes have been doing most of the winning, I think the races have nonetheless been quite exciting with quite a lot of changes and so on."

Sports.title: Verstappen's mindset going into the F1 summer break: "Of course I can easily stop, but I love racing"
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says he is "feeling good" about his place in Formula 1 as he detailed his mindset about Red Bull and the regulations heading into the summer break.

Verstappen and Red Bull have not had an easy ride this year with a RB22 chassis that has fallen short of expectations and has been tricky to set up and drive. At the same time Red Bull-Ford Powertrains delivered above expectations with its first-ever power unit, although its place atop the pecking order of the convoluted ADUO upgrade system means Red Bull isn't allowed to improve its engine.

As Red Bull heads into the summer break winless and fourth in the standings, which could see Verstappen trigger get-out clauses from his 2028 deal, the other concern has been the Dutchman's bitter discontent with the 2026 power unit regulations, which has been another element to take into account as he weighs up his future.

Despite the usual mid-season speculation around Verstappen's future, little appears to have moved in recent weeks, and with few credible alternatives the expectation is that the four-time world champion will simply stay put at Red Bull for another year.

As he heads into the summer break, Verstappen has offered the latest insight into his thinking, suggesting he can easily walk away tomorrow if he wanted to, but that he's still keen to keep racing on. In that regard Verstappen is still in a different place than 45-year-old veteran Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, who said his enjoyment of the regulations will play a big role in deciding his future.

"Of course, Fernando is 45, so it's probably a bit easier for him to say: 'I quit,'" Verstappen said. "But as a real racer, it's tough, especially when you're not enjoying the regulations and you're not competitive at the moment. Fernando, of course, doesn't deserve to be in P21.

Lando Norris, McLaren, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I'm of course 28 years old, so it's a little bit different. I mean, of course I can easily stop, it's not a problem, but I love racing, and I'm just trying to deal with what we have, even though what we have at the moment is not what I like."

The two sticking points for Verstappen are still the same, with some hope that both Red Bull's own performance and F1's controversial regulations, which will be tweaked further for 2027, can be improved enough for an extended stay in the series to be desirable. But speaking on the eve of the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend, Verstappen insisted his focus was squarely on the former.

A confusing Budapest weekend in which Verstappen and team-mate Isack Hadjar both struggled for confidence in an unpredictable car, but Verstappen still had strong race pace to finish second, perfectly encapsulated Red Bull's 2026 campaign.

"I am feeling good from my side, but I'm saying that there is nothing to say because there is nothing going on," Verstappen explained. "I'm just focused on trying to get the most out of the car and that's already complicated enough to deal with.

"This team is like a second family to me. I'm just trying to understand our car a bit better, and get back to winning ways. We've been close one weekend, I hope of course a little bit more often than just one weekend, but like I said before, it's definitely on an upward trend, so that's good to see."

Sports.title: Audi won’t upgrade F1 power unit again until 2027
Sports.content:
Audi won’t add to its first Formula 1 power unit update by the end of the 2026 season, racing director Allan McNish has revealed.

Having taken over the Sauber squad this year and introduced its very first F1 engine project, Audi rarely troubled the top 10 early in the season but launched a power unit upgrade at the Barcelona Grand Prix, providing “driveability mostly” as per Nico Hulkenberg – as this had been a weakness of the R26’s.

Audi’s progress has been obvious since then, as it has scored points in the last three rounds with Gabriel Bortoleto (eight) and Hulkenberg (two), edging Williams out of eighth place in the constructors’ championship.

However, asked by Autosport when the next powertrain update would be introduced, McNish replied: “It'll be next year.” The reason is simple: staying within the budget cap.

“Everybody has got this trade-off between when you're bringing upgrades – chassis and PU – and also where you spend your money,” McNish continued. “Because you can't spend everything at one time, because then you don't have anything to fight with later. So it's got to be a managed expectation, and not just over one season, but multiple seasons as well.

“And so certainly from our point of view with the ADUO [Additional Upgrades and Opportunities for weaker powertrains], we brought something in Barcelona straight away, which was some small adaption, and that worked well, that helped us on our way. And then I would say the bigger parts are for 2027. So we will not see anything big on the power unit until then.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director of Audi F1 Team Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

When Autosport followed up with how big a step he would expect from the 2027-spec power unit, McNish chuckled: “That’s ‘27. Give us a break. We’re only halfway through ‘26, I need my cup of tea first.

“You've got where you're going, but it's also relative to the competition. And so therefore we're always benchmarking against the competition, and how quickly they move, and how quickly we can evolve.

“You could see that we've evolved in our performance this year so far, which has been definitely power-unit-related as well, making sure that we try to maximise some of the systems on that, but also definitely on the chassis with the upgrades that we spoke about there. And so I think we've definitely done that.

“We will do again in the second half of the year, but for the power unit that’s the ‘27 topic. It’s more hardware than anything, and that’s not a quick thing to change.”

Expanding on the Barcelona update’s “driveability” focus, Hulkenberg had detailed at Spa-Francorchamps: “It is about what you request on the pedal, but how the PU responds, how the torque delivery is. Does it surge, is it consistent, is it smooth? It is very fine stuff.

“We can talk about it, but you need to have experience to feel it. It happens in a blink of an eye, less than a tenth on a corner exit. But with a car on the limit, over the limit, all these things matter a lot.

Nico Hulkenberg, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“If you then have driveability issues on top of that, it is like trying to hit a curveball. The same on the gearbox side with shifting, shift quality.

“As you are all aware and heard of, there can be big differences in terms of shift quality, upshifts and downshifts. And they have an impact on car balance and car behaviour too. So it all goes together.”

Sports.title: The challenge Haas faces in trying to meet F1 budget cap: "Fighting with both hands tied"
Sports.content:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu says the American outfit has been “fighting with both hands tied” relative to wealthier Formula 1 outfits.

Komatsu opened up about needing to find more funding for the team in order to reach the budget cap, which is set at $215m for the 2026 season – excluding the salaries of all drivers and the other top three highest earners, as well as the likes of marketing costs.

The Japanese believes this has been holding the squad back with its approximate 400-person headcount when a number of teams boast more than 1,000 employees.

Asked at Spa-Francorchamps if Haas could now operate at the limit of the budget cap, Komatsu replied: “I wish we can. We're not. It's one of the top priorities on my job list to be able to fund this team so that we can operate at the budget cap. Because that's the baseline, right? We should be achieving that first step.

“We talked about us being outdeveloped. That's not a reflection of, let's say, incapability of our guys. I think our guys are doing, honestly, a fantastic job. Anybody who knows about Formula 1, knowing our size and resource of the team, and then producing what we are producing, I think they will understand this statement.

“But I think they are very capable. They work as a team. Their communication is clear. No-blame culture. I think the culture is getting there, and the capability is there. But I'm not, so far, able to give them enough ammunition for our guys to show what they're capable of.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“What they produced at the beginning of this year is completely unexpected. You cannot expect the smallest team to be performing the way that we've been performing beginning of the season in the year of the biggest regulation change. That's not sustainable for us.

“So it's not a reflection of our guys, it's more a reflection on my side. I need to be able to get better revenue to this team and provide a better environment for our guys. Then, once we've done that, we've got the guys to do it. We've got the drivers to do it. So I'm sure we can come back.”

Above, Komatsu was referring to Haas’ remarkable start to the season, as it lay fourth in the constructors’ standings after the first two grands prix – courtesy of Oliver Bearman’s standout results, with the British sophomore finishing seventh in Melbourne and fifth in China.

But Komatsu hasn’t shied away from the fact his team has been outpaced by its rivals in the development race. Points have grown scarcer with Q3 more elusive, to the extent the squad has been point-less in the latest five grands prix – hence the focus on finding more budget.

“Those things take time. So, I'm really trying to put that in place as soon as possible,” Komatsu added. “But it's not like I just started working on it. We've been working on it. So we're having some very good conversations.

“But really, honestly, it's not fair on our guys to have that constraint, if you like. It's like they're fighting with both hands tied.

“But then when they see our lack of performance or struggles in places like Miami, Barcelona, Spielberg, Silverstone, nobody's hiding from it. Everybody's just talking, ‘OK, what's the problem? How have we missed it? How did we get into this situation? How are we going to improve?’ And that's something I really respect. So I'm really just determined to give them the environment they deserve.”

Sports.title: Hamilton vs Leclerc: 2026 F1 team mates’ head-to-head scores at summer break | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Does Lewis Hamilton have an eighth world championship in him? Has he not recovered from the blow of 2021 or did he simply never gel with the ‘ground effect’ cars of 2022-25?

Those hoping to see the seven-times world champion fight for another title will have drawn great encouragement from what they have seen so far in 2026. Last year, in his first season at Ferrari, he came off badly in comparison to Charles Leclerc , taking a 19-5 pasting in qualifying and making zero podium appearances to his team mate’s seven.

Hamilton has given full credit to team principal Frederic Vasseur for implementing the changes he needed to make a success of his transition to Ferrari, whether that has involved different brake material or swerving the simulator. On the face of it, it has paid off, and Ferrari now have two A-list drivers performing at their peak.

Leclerc is still shading Hamilton on average in qualifying, but the fight between the two has been much closer. Hamilton has delivered more consistently on race day, including that breakthrough victory in Spain.

Both drivers have misfired at times. Leclerc had a spate of errors including costly crashes in qualifying at the Circuit de Catalunya and during his home race.

Hamilton, meanwhile, has picked up a bad habit of incurring the stewards’ wrath, collecting a series of needless penalties in recent races. Though some may not have been his fault or were debatable calls, many others were straightforward, and he was fortunate to avoid a worse penalty for his yellow flag slip in Silverstone.

For all that, Hamilton is Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s closest rival in the championship at the summer break. “Has the time finally come for Hamilton to hang up his helmet?” we asked in May, in what already looks like one of the most poorly-timed polls ever featured on RaceFans.

Sports.title: Antonelli vs Russell: 2026 F1 team mates’ head-to-head scores at summer break | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Early in the season it seemed certain that whichever of the Mercedes drivers came out ahead would be crowned world champion. That remains likely, but the threat posed by rival teams has grown in recent races.

Little about Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s form in his rookie season indicated that 12 months later he would be beating his team mate quite as emphatically as he is. But heading into the summer break, Antonelli holds a valuable 59-point lead over the other Mercedes driver.

It’s a far cry from the situation around 12 months ago. At the end of the ‘European season’, Antonelli was 15-1 down against George Russell in qualifying. He ended the season still with less than half his team mate’s points tally.

But after a difficult mid-season, following a Mercedes upgrade which did not go as intended, Antonelli rebounded impressively with the end of the year in sight. He reached the podium twice over the final four rounds.

So while Russell’s season-opening victory in Australia looked like the shape of things to come, Antonelli shattered those illusions by winning the next five rounds in a row. He got the rub of the green at times – technical trouble hit Russell in qualifying at Shanghai and took him out while he led in Montreal – but he has also seemed fundamentally more at ease with Mercedes’ W17 than his team mate.

The unusually high rate of problems on Mercedes’ cars, and Russell’s particular problems with poor straight-line speed at Silverstone and Spa, have further complicated the picture. Antonelli’s car has not been immune, breaking down in Spain and breaking an aerodynamic component at Silverstone. Overall, Russell has probably had slightly worse luck, but not 59 points’ worth. Antonelli is leading this championship on merit, and Russell will have to dig deep in the second half of the season if he is going to avoid a painful defeat.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: How far is modern F1 like the ‘turbo era’? | Formula 1
Asian Le Mans Series to take place entirely in Europe following war in Middle East | Brief
Sports.content:
The Asian Le Mans Series has announced its 2026-27 season will take place entirely at European circuits.

Since 2021 the series has only raced at the Dubai Autodrome, Yas Marina in the United Arab Emirates and Malaysia’s Sepang International Circuit. Its upcoming championship will take place at Jerez in Spain, Paul Ricard in France and Autodromo do Algarve in Portugal. The championship will be renamed the ‘Winter Le Mans Series’ as a result.

The change is the latest in a series of alterations to the motorsport calendar which have arisen following the war in the Middle East.

“While moving the Asian Le Mans Series to Europe is not ideal, the situation in the Middle East dictated that we worked to find the best solution,” said series promoter Stephane Ratel. “Between SRO, LMEM and the ACO we have a huge pool of experience to draw on, and the consensus was a Winter Le Mans Series in southern Europe was the most sensible option given the mounting external constraints.”

Formula 1 cancelled its races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier this year. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has indicated the series will race in Europe if its final two rounds in the Middle East cannot go ahead.

Sports.title: FIA failed to listen to warnings over its 2026 F1 rules change – Coulthard | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard blames the FIA for the poor state of the series’ 2026 regulations.

The championship revised its rules just four races into the new season after discovering significant shortcomings which left the cars seriously starved of energy on some tracks. This was evident from the first race of the season in Melbourne where cars slowed down significantly approaching fast corners because they could not recover enough energy to keep their batteries sufficiently charged.

Some figures in F1 had warned about this problem years before the new rules were introduced. Coulthard said the FIA should take responsibility for failing to listen to them.

“The new regs came at us with drivers and engineers going, ‘this is not going to be good’, and pretty much silence from everyone else,” Coulthard told Up to Speed. “We get to Melbourne and we go, ‘ah, they have deceleration as they go towards certain corners’.”

Coulthard believes the FIA should have anticipated the shortcomings in the new rules.

“I feel that we saw this coming and nobody really was listening,” he said. “And the fact they had to react to the reality in a sport that simulates the hell out of the future was a bit disappointing and that has to fall really with FIA.

“I know they’ll get sensitive and go ‘well we are a small group of people and the Formula 1 teams have hundreds of people’ but all of the evidence was there that having 50-50 on electrical and battery was going to be challenging.”

He said the series reacted well to the problem by introducing changes after the Miami Grand Prix. F1 will also make further changes to its regulations over the next two seasons in an attempt to improve the cars’ performance.

“What are we doing going forward? We’re going to have more internal combustion next year and it’s suggested even more the year after. So to see the obvious, and then react, is a bit disappointing.”

He likened the new rules to “the halftime show at the [football] World Cup – it was a bit of a disappointment.”

Sports.title: Why Sugar Ray Leonard Remains Boxing’s Gold Standard
Sports.content:
Leonard’s rise reached another level in November 1979 when he stopped Wilfred Benitez to capture the WBC welterweight championship. He never spent his prime protecting a title against limited opposition. Instead, he pursued the defining names of his era, including Roberto Duran, Thomas Hearns, Marvin Hagler and later Donny Lalonde. Few champions have matched that level of opposition while continuing to win on boxing’s biggest stages.

Leonard’s greatest strength may have been his ability to adjust. After losing to Duran in their first meeting by choosing to trade at close range, he completely changed his approach in the rematch. Using movement, sharp combinations and psychological pressure, Leonard frustrated Duran until the Panamanian famously quit in the eighth round. That performance remains one of boxing’s finest examples of tactical adjustment between fights.

Another defining victory came against Hearns in September 1981. Trailing on the scorecards late in the fight, Leonard produced a dramatic rally before stopping the unbeaten champion in the 14th round. After returning from retirement following a detached retina, Leonard outpointed Marvin Hagler in one of boxing’s most debated championship fights. That victory reinforced his reputation for delivering on the sport’s biggest stages.

Leonard retired with a 36-3-1 record, 25 knockouts and world titles in five weight classes. His career was built on victories over Hall of Fame opponents at a time when boxing’s biggest names routinely fought one another. That willingness to chase the toughest available challenges became one of the defining traits of his career.

Leonard’s accomplishments continue to resonate because they were earned against an extraordinary generation that included Roberto Duran, Thomas Hearns and Marvin Hagler. Few champions have defeated that caliber of opposition during a single era, which is why Sugar Ray Leonard remains boxing’s gold standard.

Sports.title: Hamzah Sheeraz’s Pressure Fighter Problem Casts Doubt On Undisputed Hopes
Sports.content:
Adames and Zachenhuber approached Sheeraz in different ways, yet both achieved success by applying constant pressure. Neither man spent much time backing away. Both absorbed punches to close the distance, forcing exchanges while keeping Sheeraz from settling behind his long jab. Instead of controlling the pace with his size and reach, Sheeraz spent long stretches reacting.

That presents a major concern at 168 pounds because the division contains numerous fighters who thrive under those exact conditions.

Christian Mbilli relentlessly marches forward. Kevin Lele Sadjo brings constant pressure. Jaime Munguia keeps throwing punches until opponents break. Lester Martinez keeps pressing forward and makes opponents fight at close range. Osleys Iglesias possesses enough power to make every exchange dangerous. Diego Pacheco controls distance behind his jab and steadily applies pressure. Even Saul Canelo Alvarez, despite being late in his career, excels at cutting off the ring and forcing opponents to fight his fight.

Becoming undisputed is never about defeating a single champion. It requires beating a series of elite fighters across contrasting styles. Pressure fighters, punchers, technicians and counterpunchers all present different challenges. The deeper the division, the harder that task becomes.

The Berlanga knockout looks more like a favorable stylistic matchup than proof that every weakness vanished. Berlanga gave Sheeraz room to establish his rhythm and capitalize on defensive mistakes. Adames and Zachenhuber denied him that comfort, forcing rounds that were far more competitive than many expected.

A single tough fight does not define a career. Sheeraz still possesses the size, skill and punching power to win a world title. His performances against Adames and Zachenhuber, however, show that aggressive opponents who refuse to surrender ground present a difficult style for him to solve.

Until Sheeraz answers that question against top opposition, talk of cleaning out the super middleweight division appears premature. Winning one championship is difficult enough. Sweeping through one of boxing’s deepest divisions is an entirely different challenge.

Sports.title: Teofimo Lopez Leans Toward Conor Benn Upset Over Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
“I think we’re going to get an example of what it is. You always hear the saying where they say it’s easier to get the belt, but then it’s harder to keep it, right? Maybe Ryan right now might find out that. Ideally, in the business aspect, everyone wants to see Ryan win,” said Teofimo to Sean Zittel. “But Conor Benn is hungry. He’s in there. He’s in the gym every day. He’s speaking Spanish to the man, and he’s not even Hispanic. I think those things show the determination and what it means to Conor Benn. When he didn’t look so great against Eubank the first time, he came back with vengeance the second time. Conor Benn is no pushover, man. Look, I said it before, I think Conor Benn might pull the upset. We just have to wait and see.”

Garcia’s dominant performance against Mario Barrios also factored into his thinking. Teofimo said that version of Ryan would be extremely difficult to beat, but he is not convinced the same fighter will appear on September 12.

His support for Benn also comes with a personal incentive. Teofimo said he is rooting for the British contender because a victory would improve the chances of landing a future fight in the United Kingdom. He added that either Benn or Garcia would be an attractive opponent after his August 22 WBA welterweight title fight against Rolando Romero.

Sports.title: Canelo Refuses To Give Crawford Full Credit For Defeat
Sports.content:
“You cannot control the results,” Alvarez said. “Even when you do everything good, things don’t go your way. I learned that. Sometimes we forget the bases, and I forgot the bases in that fight,” said Canelo to CBS Mornings about his loss to Crawford. “Mentally, I was not there. I did everything correct in the training camp, but mentally I was not there. I learned that. If I’m going to still fighting, I need to be there mentally and physically.”

Alvarez’s explanation puts the spotlight on his own performance rather than Crawford’s. He did not point to injuries, problems in training camp or controversial judging. Instead, he argued that his mindset kept him from performing at the standard he expected of himself.

Not everyone will accept that explanation. Crawford spent months crafting a game plan, executed it with discipline and repeatedly beat Alvarez to the punch. His speed, timing and ring IQ played a major role in one of the biggest victories of his career. Because of that, some fans will view Alvarez’s comments as an honest assessment of his own shortcomings, while others will see them as an attempt to soften the impact of a clear defeat.

One thing is certain: Canelo does not believe the fight reflected his best version. Combined with his recent comments about wanting a lucrative rematch, it is clear he still believes he can produce a different result if the two ever meet again.

Canelo still has to get past WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli on October 31 for a Crawford rematch to remain a realistic possibility. Even if he defeats Mbilli, it’s far from certain Turki Alalshikh will want to finance a second fight after last September’s disappointing first meeting. Crawford spent much of the night boxing cautiously, tying Canelo up whenever he closed the distance, while Alvarez faded after the sixth round. Given the lukewarm reaction to the bout, Turki may decide his money is better spent on fresher matchups rather than revisiting a fight that failed to meet expectations.

Sports.title: Remembering Boxing’s Most Unusual Heavyweights
Sports.content:
Dallas Cowboys defensive end Ed “Too Tall” Jones brought NFL fame into the boxing ring during the late 1970s. He finished 6-0 after stepping away from football, although many questioned the quality of his opposition. Jones was knocked down in his professional debut before escaping with a heavily booed majority decision over Abraham Meneses. Only one of his six opponents owned a winning record. Following a first-round knockout of Ricky Gonzalez in his final bout, Jones returned to the Cowboys.

Eric “Butterbean” Esch became one of boxing’s biggest attractions during the 1990s thanks to his enormous size and knockout power. Known as “The King of the Four Rounders,” Butterbean finished with a 77-10-4 record and 58 knockouts. His most memorable performance came in 2002 against former heavyweight champion Larry Holmes. Fighting ten rounds for the only time in his career, Butterbean scored a knockdown in the final round before losing a unanimous decision in the 53-year-old Holmes’ farewell fight.

Chicago’s Craig Bodzianowski won his first 17 professional fights before a motorcycle accident resulted in the amputation of his right leg below the knee. Refusing to walk away from boxing, he returned with a prosthetic limb and eventually challenged WBA cruiserweight champion Robert Daniels. Bodzianowski lost the decision after suffering severe facial damage, yet simply reaching a world title fight under those circumstances remains one of boxing’s most remarkable comeback stories.

None of these men became heavyweight champions remembered for championship reigns. Instead, each earned a lasting place in boxing history because their careers unfolded in ways few other fighters could match.

Sports.title: Cassius Clay vs Doug Jones 1963 The Night A Future Champion Was Pushed To His Limit
Sports.content:
Despite his unbeaten streak, skepticism remained. His speed and reflexes had overwhelmed previous opponents, yet critics remained unconvinced those strengths would survive against a seasoned contender who refused to be intimidated. His habit of pulling straight back with his hands low also invited scrutiny. If Jones timed those defensive lapses, many believed the young contender’s shortcomings would finally cost him.

Clay intensified the spotlight. He first predicted a sixth-round stoppage before changing it to the fourth after spotting a newspaper photograph of Jones reading a book titled The Rise and Fall of Cassius Clay. He mocked Jones throughout the promotion. Jones responded calmly, saying Clay’s boasting increased both purses while maintaining he would win.

Jones immediately justified the pre-fight concerns. He landed clean right hands early, repeatedly timing Clay as he leaned straight back, and absorbed the favorite’s attacks without flinching. When the fourth round passed without the promised knockout, the Madison Square Garden crowd greeted Clay with loud boos. The final rounds remained competitive before Clay finished with a stronger burst of activity to secure a unanimous decision.

The verdict settled little. Two officials scored the fight five rounds to four with one even for Clay, while the referee had him comfortably ahead. Many ringside writers disagreed, with one media poll producing more scorecards for Jones than Clay. The disputed result, combined with Jones’ performance throughout the contest, left many wondering whether Clay was truly ready for Sonny Liston.

History answered those questions quickly. Clay stopped Henry Cooper three months later before defeating Liston in one of boxing’s greatest upsets. Jones never received his own title opportunity despite pushing the future champion harder than almost anyone during his rise. For one night inside Madison Square Garden, Doug Jones forced the boxing world to question whether the sport’s loudest prospect was truly destined to become heavyweight champion.

Sports.title: Robert Garcia Accuses Jaron Ennis Of Targeting Injured Josh Kelly To Avoid Vergil Ortiz Jr.
Sports.content:
“If Boots decides to fight Kelly and take advantage of Kelly being cut and everything, then that’s kind of showing me that you really don’t want to fight Virgil,” Robert said to Sean Zittel. “The fighter will probably do it because he’s a fighter. He’s a warrior, and he’ll probably get the biggest payday in his career, and he could lose to anybody else because, let’s be real, Kelly might not be the best in the division. So, they’re going after him to take advantage of that opportunity to get another belt under his belt.”

The veteran trainer dismissed any suggestion that his fighter needs an interim bout before pursuing the division’s biggest name. Ortiz is already back in camp. He said the former interim champion wants Ennis next.

“We don’t need a tuneup. We want to go straight into Boots,” Garcia said. “If Boots decides to go after him and take advantage of that big old cut, then that’s the way they’re going to do it. I can’t force them either.”

Ennis has repeatedly spoken about adding more world titles, with Kelly and WBC champion Sebastian Fundora mentioned as possible opponents. Garcia rejected that explanation, insisting the larger fight sits across the ring.

“No, that’s a lie. He doesn’t want to fight Virgil,” Garcia said. “The fight against Virgil is three times bigger when it comes to his payday, to a meaningful fight. Nobody’s going to care because you beat Kelly or you beat Virgil. A win over somebody like Virgil means a lot more than Josh Kelly.”

Asked why he believes Ortiz wins the matchup, Garcia offered a brief reply.

“Because I know he beats him,” Garcia said. “I know he beat him.”

Sports.title: Jose Valenzuela Calls For William Zepeda Title Fight
Sports.content:
“Felicidades por la victoria. Sin duda, es otra gran pelea que me encantaría hacer. Ojalá algún día podamos compartir el ring,” Valenzuela wrote on X. Translated, Valenzuela said: “Congratulations on the victory. Without a doubt, it’s another great fight that I’d love to make. Hopefully one day we can share the ring.”

Fresh off his second-round knockout of a ring-rusty Edwin De Los Santos on June 28, Valenzuela (16-3, 10 KOs) is trying to turn that performance into another title opportunity. Before calling for Zepeda, he repeatedly called out fellow Zuffa fighter and WBO light welterweight champion Shakur Stevenson, but those public challenges gained little attention.

Matching Valenzuela with Zepeda presents a different challenge.

Zepeda is promoted by Golden Boy Promotions and competes on DAZN, while Valenzuela is now aligned with Zuffa Boxing and fights on Paramount+. Crossing promotional lines and television platforms is possible, but it usually requires a matchup with significant commercial value.

Unless one side is willing to bridge that promotional divide, Valenzuela may have to keep looking in-house for his next opportunity while Zepeda pursues bigger names at lightweight. Neither promotion has shown interest in working together yet.

Ghana News.title: ‘Democracy under attack’: We’re not against accountability, but against selective justice – Afenyo-Markin
Ghana News.content:
Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has called for an end to what he describes as selective justice and political retaliation, insisting that the opposition is not against accountability but opposed to the unequal application of the law.

Speaking at the "Democracy Under Attack" demonstration on Thursday, August 6, Afenyo-Markin argued that Members of Parliament are being subjected to investigations after making contributions on the floor of Parliament.

"We are not against accountability, but we are against selective justice," he said.

He claimed that an MP makes a contribution on the floor of Parliament and is subsequently invited by investigative agencies, questioning what he described as the selective application of the law.

He also referred to concerns raised by some members of the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) over the conditions under which suspects are held.

According to him, former Minority Leader Haruna Iddrisu has complained on the floor of Parliament about what he described as unlawful conditions, while Interior Minister Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak has also raised concerns on the matter.

Afenyo-Markin maintained that the opposition is merely expressing its views on the way the country is being governed and stressed that criticism of government should not be met with intimidation.

He urged political leaders to end what he called the "you do me, I do you" approach to politics, saying Ghana's democracy would only thrive if successive governments resisted the temptation to target political opponents.

"As a country, we must end this vicious cycle of 'you do me, I do you.' I've been talking about this for quite some time now," he said.

The Minority Leader said his position was not influenced by the fact that members of his party were currently affected but by his long-held belief that politics should be conducted with decency and mutual respect.

"I don't say this because it is my people who are going through this situation. I say this because all my life I've believed that we can do politics in a very decent way. I believe in that decent approach to politics."

He further urged politicians to shift their attention from partisan disputes to addressing the country's development challenges.

"If you leave Accra and go deep into the hinterlands, you see the serious underdevelopment in our country. That should be what should occupy our minds as political leaders," he said.

Afenyo-Markin warned that if the alleged cycle of political persecution continues, it could make it difficult for moderate voices within the New Patriotic Party (NPP) to restrain more hardline elements when the party returns to power.

"For me, if they don't stop, it will be difficult for the moderates in the NPP to calm the nerves of the extremists when the NPP comes to office tomorrow. But is that what we want as a country? No. That's not what we want."

He concluded by stressing that the demonstration was not against Ghana but a call for fairness, justice and the protection of democratic principles.

Ghana News.title: Livestream: Gov’t holds interfaith memorial service for victims of August 6 helicopter crash
Ghana News.content:
The government is holding a national interfaith memorial service in honour of the eight people who lost their lives in the August 6, 2025 helicopter crash.

The ceremony is taking place at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), with President John Mahama, Vice President Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, government officials, families of the deceased and loved ones in attendance.

The crash claimed the lives of Defence Minister Dr Edward Kofi Omane-Boamah and seven others, including officials and crew members, while they were travelling to the Ashanti Region to support efforts in the fight against illegal mining.

The Ghana Armed Forces said the Ghana Air Force Z9 helicopter, carrying three crew members and five passengers, took off from Accra at 0912 GMT on August 6, 2025, and was heading to Obuasi when it crashed in a wooded area at Adansi Sikaman in the Ashanti Region.

The aircraft was destroyed by fire following the crash, which shocked the nation and led to widespread tributes from political leaders, state institutions and members of the public.

The memorial service is expected to provide an opportunity for the country to remember the lives and contributions of the departed and offer support to their families a year after the tragedy.

Ghana News.title: GMTF partners MDS-Lancet, Quest Medical Imaging to expand access to quality diagnostics
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) has entered into a strategic partnership with MDS-Lancet Laboratories Ghana Limited and Quest Medical Imaging to improve access to quality diagnostic healthcare services across the country.

The agreement seeks to combine GMTF’s mandate of supporting the prevention and treatment of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) with the expertise of MDS-Lancet Laboratories Ghana Limited and Quest Medical Imaging in delivering advanced medical diagnostic services.

The partnership is expected to enhance access to timely, accurate and reliable diagnostic testing, supporting early detection of diseases and improving treatment outcomes for patients nationwide.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, the Administrator of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, described the collaboration as a significant milestone in the Trust Fund’s efforts to establish partnerships that strengthen healthcare delivery.

“Today marks a significant milestone as the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, MDS Lancet Laboratories Ghana Limited and Quest Medical Imaging formally establish a partnership that reflects our shared commitment to improving access to quality healthcare for the people of Ghana.

Accurate and timely diagnostics are the cornerstone of effective treatment, and this collaboration represents an important investment in the health and wellbeing of Ghanaians,” she said.

She expressed appreciation to the leadership of both organisations for their confidence in the partnership and reaffirmed GMTF’s commitment to working with key stakeholders to address the growing burden of non-communicable diseases.

The Chief Executive Officer of MDS-Lancet Laboratories Ghana Limited, Dr Paul Sekyere-Nyantakyi, welcomed the partnership, noting that it aligns with the organisation’s objective of providing accessible and high-quality diagnostic services to support improved patient care.

According to the partners, the collaboration will help strengthen Ghana’s healthcare system through innovation, technical expertise and coordinated efforts, while improving access to diagnostic services and supporting better clinical decision-making, particularly for patients managing chronic conditions.

The agreement also reflects a shared commitment to building a long-term relationship anchored on trust, excellence and a common goal of improving healthcare outcomes.

The Ghana Medical Trust Fund, MDS-Lancet Laboratories Ghana Limited and Quest Medical Imaging expressed confidence that the partnership will make a lasting contribution towards achieving more equitable and sustainable healthcare delivery in Ghana.

Ghana News.title: NPP demonstration meant to mar one-year helicopter crash anniversary – Solomon Owusu
Ghana News.content:
The Director of Communications for the United Party, Solomon Owusu, has criticised the opposition New Patriotic Party's (NPP) nationwide demonstration, alleging that the protest was deliberately organised to overshadow the first anniversary of a tragic incident that claimed the lives of 8 gallant men.

Speaking on JoyNews' AM Show on Thursday, 6 August, Mr Owusu argued that the NPP had "no business whatsoever" taking to the streets, insisting that the demonstration, themed "Democracy Under Attack," was politically motivated rather than driven by genuine concerns over Ghana's democratic governance.

His remarks come as the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) stages nationwide protests under the theme "Democracy Under Attack," arguing that recent developments threaten Ghana's democratic governance.

Rejecting the party's justification for the demonstration, Mr Owusu questioned the basis of the NPP's claims.

"They have no business whatsoever being on the street. I say it from the heart of my heart. I think they decided to do this demonstration just to mar the one-year anniversary of our departed souls. That is all they are talking about," he said.

Mr Owusu dismissed assertions that individuals had been arrested merely for speaking their minds, arguing that the claims did not reflect the realities of the country's democratic environment.

"What did we see? That people have been arrested for speaking? Is that the truth? Is that the case? Is that what you believe in?" he questioned.

He further pointed to demonstrations organised by the NPP while it was in government, arguing that the party had previously exercised its constitutional right to protest without interference.

According to him, the party organised major demonstrations, including Save the Judiciary and another under the slogan 'Yɛn Suro Ahunahuna' ("We Are Not Afraid of Intimidation"), during which its members publicly declared that they feared no one.

"They themselves told Ghanaians they were not afraid of anybody, and they embarked on demonstrations to show the whole world that they would not be intimidated," he stated.

Mr Owusu also accused the NPP of hypocrisy over concerns about political insults and intolerance, arguing that the party has historically engaged in some of the harshest political rhetoric in Ghana.

Drawing on his experience as a former member of the NPP, he claimed the party had a long record of using derogatory language against political opponents.

"Fortunately, I have been a member of the NPP before. There has not been any political party that has insulted more than the NPP, and it started long ago," he said.

He cited instances involving the late former President Jerry John Rawlings and John Evans Atta Mills, recalling that political figures associated with the NPP had previously used disparaging language against their opponents.

Mr Owusu specifically referred to comments made in 2002 by Gabby Asare Otchere-Darko, who allegedly described Professor Mills as a "poodle" following the 2000 general election.

"As recent as 2002, Gabby Asare Otchere-Darko referred to Professor Mills as a poodle. So what exactly are we discussing here?" he asked.

Addressing the NPP's concerns over the reported arrest of 21 individuals, Mr Owusu argued that the party had overlooked similar incidents during its own tenure in office.

He referenced the 2024 Democracy Hub #OccupyJulorBiHouse protests, during which dozens of demonstrators were arrested, contending that the current criticism lacked consistency.

"So, for this reason, they have no business whatsoever being on the streets," he said. According to the NPP, the demonstration is intended to draw attention to issues including alleged restrictions on free expression, concerns over the treatment of opposition voices, and what it describes as threats to democratic institutions.

Ghana News.title: President Mahama concludes Jamaica visit with Seville Heritage Park tour
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama last Tuesday brought his four-day state visit to Jamaica to a close with a visit to Seville Heritage Park in St. Ann, where he toured the preserved Ghanaian Village Houses.

The visit formed part of the President’s official engagements and highlighted the historical and cultural connections between Ghana and Jamaica.

It also served to reaffirm Ghana’s commitment to strengthening relations with Caribbean nations in the areas of culture, trade, investment and diplomacy.

Reception

At the heritage park, President Mahama laid a wreath in honour of Africans who were transported across the Atlantic during the transatlantic slave trade.

A Great House Reception was later held in his honour, and was attended by Jamaican government officials, cultural leaders, diplomats and members of the Ghanaian delegation.

The President also toured the Great House, which was constructed in 1745 by the grandson of Captain Richard Hemmings.

Captain Hemmings had participated in the English conquest of Jamaica in 1655 alongside Admiral William Penn and General Robert Venables before establishing the Seville Estate on approximately 2,500 acres of land.

The Great House was originally designed as a fortified two-storey residence without a veranda.

It overlooked the sugar plantations, sugar works, the village of enslaved Africans and the Caribbean coastline. Defensive guns were positioned around the building to protect the plantation owner and his household.

Following hurricane damage after 1745, the upper floor was removed and a veranda was added to improve ventilation and provide shade.

Several architectural features, including decorative architraves surrounding the doorways, have been preserved.

The property was declared a National Monument by the Jamaica National Heritage Trust on May 13, 1999.

Future cooperation

Addressing guests at the Great House Reception, President Mahama said Ghana and Jamaica shared common ancestry, history and cultural traditions.

He stated that both countries should focus on building a prosperous future through economic cooperation, tourism, education, investment and people-to-people exchanges.

The President reiterated his call for the establishment of a direct air link between Ghana and Jamaica, stating that improved connectivity would enhance tourism, trade, business, academic collaboration and cultural exchange between West Africa and the Caribbean.

One family

Jamaica’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, said Ghana and Jamaica were one family connected by shared ancestry and history.

She emphasised the need to deepen cooperation and translate historical ties into stronger diplomatic and economic partnerships.

Jamaica’s Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport, Olivia “Babsy” Grange, expressed gratitude to President Mahama and the people of Ghana for the support extended to Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa.

She called for greater collaboration in tourism and cultural development to drive economic growth.

Later in the day, President Mahama attended a State Dinner hosted by the Governor-General of Jamaica, Sir Patrick Allen, and Lady Allen at the Ballroom of King’s House.

The dinner marked the official conclusion of the President’s state visit.

Ghana News.title: The August 6 tragedy and Ghana’s Galamsey fight: Any lessons learnt?
Ghana News.content:
It was meant to be another chapter in Ghana's war against galamsey. Instead, August 6, 2025, became one of the darkest days in the nation's recent history.



Eight of the country’s citizens, including senior government officials, the Defence and Environment ministers, tragically lost their lives in a helicopter crash when they were travelling to an event in Obuasi aimed at confronting illegal mining.



One year after the tragic incident, what lessons has the country learnt in the quest to mitigate against illegal mining that continues to ravage natural resources?



Their death shook the core of the nation. A routine mission ended in unimaginable loss.



For weeks, the country brooded over the sudden demise of eight of its gallant citizens, including cabinet ministers.



A helicopter carrying men committed to national duty never completed its journey.



The defence minister, Dr Edward Omane Boamah, the environment minister, Murtala Mohammed, three other top government officials and three crew members never returned.



The painful demise left behind grieving families, shattered dreams, and a nation searching for meaning in tragedy.



Time has moved on. The pain has not.



For many Ghanaians, the echoes of that tragic day still linger.



The memory of those who perished continues to inspire solemn reflection on the national fight against illegal mining.



The Departed 8 were on a national assignment in a renewed fight to eradicate illegal mining through the Responsible Community Mining and Skills Development Programme.

The Responsible Cooperative Mining and Skills Development Programme (RCOMSDEP) is a national initiative that empowers mining cooperatives and small-scale miners through training, innovation, and responsible practices.



The goal is to transform mining into a force for safe, inclusive, and environmentally responsible development.



But a year after its launch, has the country won the Galamsey war at all?

Convener for the Coalition of anti-Galamsey campaigners, Ken Ashigbey, is distraught that the blood of these individuals has not been avenged.



“Dr Omane Boamah, and what I know that he stood for and the support he gave to the lands minister, unfortunately we have failed them. The best tribute to have given them was to make their blood count,” he said.



While the government touts its achievements in the Galamsey fight, many rivers snaking through the country remain dirty and forest reserves dotted with open pits.



Across Ghana, in the Western, Western North, Ashanti, Central, Eastern Bono and Ahafo regions, illegal mining is eating life away from the lands, water bodies and other natural resources.



Illegal miners continue to operate with impunity – excavating the earth crust close to roads and in forest covers while local authorities watch on.



A recent video which surfaced on social media showed some youth in one of the coastal communities fetching and washing sand along the beach in search of gold.



An aerial view of the country’s water bodies reveals major rivers, once crystal clear, suffocating with heavy siltation and discoloured effluent from the mining activities.



Aquatic life and biodiversity are at the mercy of humans’ unrelenting quest for wealth.



“We have to honour their memory by doing what is right for our fight against illegal,” environmental journalist Erastus Asare Donkor noted.



But perhaps the greatest tribute to these eight gallant souls will not be found in wreaths, monuments, or anniversary ceremonies.



It will be found in rivers that run clear again… in forests that breathe once more… and in a nation that finally finds the resolve to protect the land that sustains us all.



Their mission ended in the skies above Adansi. But the journey they began remains firmly on the ground—unfinished, and now entrusted to every Ghanaian.



Until the scars of galamsey fade from our rivers and our forests, August 6 will remain more than a day of mourning. It will stand as a solemn reminder that the price of inaction can be painfully high.



Rest in power, our fallen heroes.



Damirifa due… Mmarima mma.

Ghana News.title: ‎Police intercept 866 parcels of suspected cocaine hidden in bags of gari, 3 suspects in custody
Ghana News.content:
‎The Police in Tema have intercepted 866 parcels of a white powdered substance suspected to be cocaine. They were concealed in sacks of gari.

The seizure followed an intelligence-led operation conducted by the Police at about 8 pm on Wednesday, August 5, 2026.

‎Three suspects, including a Dutch national and two Ghanaians, have been arrested in connection with the consignment.‎

Sources close to the operation told Graphic Online's Benjamin Xornam Glover that the suspects were picked up while supervising a group of men loading sacks of gari and 'konkonte' into a 40-foot container for export at a warehouse within the Tema Port enclave.

‎The suspects, together with the truck and the intercepted parcels, are currently in police custody for further investigations.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
