After denying the charges, his defence team told the court that Mauti is a young man and a law student at Chuka University whose fees are paid by a church.

The lawyers further informed the court that Mauti is an orphan and has no parents to assist him in securing his release, asking the court to grant him a lenient cash bail.

“We are looking at the charges and when we look at it and the consequences that come from that, and if it goes on this particular way we know what the sentence is and what the consequences are. The court has got the right before passing the sentence to be able to reconsider when he changes his plea,” his lawyers told the court.

The defence also told the court that they had advised Mauti that the earlier position he had taken by pleading guilty carried serious consequences and offered to represent him in the matter.

The prosecution did not oppose his release on bail.

Magistrate Onsarigo granted Mauti a cash bail of Sh5,000 and directed him to provide one contact person.

The matter will be mentioned on August 18, 2026, for pre-trial directions.

World.title: Ruto calls for national dialogue to shape Kenya's vision
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto has invited Kenyans to take part in what he described as the country's most significant national conversation since the adoption of the 2010 Constitution, saying the discussions will help chart Kenya's next long-term development agenda.

Speaking on the country's development trajectory, the President said the conversation should move beyond partisan politics and election cycles to focus on a shared national vision.

"I invite every Kenyan to what I believe will become the most consequential national conversation since the adoption of our Constitution in 2010," Ruto said.

"A national conversation about Kenya's development. This conversation must rise above politics, transcend electoral cycles and unite us around a shared destiny."

The President acknowledged that while Vision 2030 had set an ambitious goal of transforming Kenya into an upper-middle-income country by 2030, the country remains off course to achieve that target.

"Vision 2030 set a target of Kenya becoming an upper-middle-income country by 2030. So far, we are off target. This is not a criticism of Vision 2030, nor is it a reason for disappointment; rather, it is an opportunity to learn from our successes proudly, reflect with honesty on where we have fallen short, and define together Kenya's next long-term vision," he said.

At the same time, Ruto announced that the government will formally launch a nationwide conversation on August 12 to develop Kenya's next long-term development blueprint as Vision 2030 nears its end.

"Accordingly, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, we shall formally launch the National Conversation on Kenya's Future Beyond Vision 2030; the most consequential exercise in national reflection and public participation since the promulgation of our Constitution in 2010," he stated.

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth, citing improvements in key macroeconomic indicators.

"We have stabilized our currency, inflation has fallen, borrowing costs have declined, and investor confidence has returned," he said. "Last year Kenya attracted a record $3.2 billion in foreign direct investment, more than double the amount recorded in 2022."

He added that Kenya's improving investment climate had earned international recognition.

"The 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Ranking placed Kenya as the most competitive economy in Africa, reflecting the confidence our reforms have restored," Ruto said.

At the same time, Ruto also highlighted the establishment of the National Infrastructure Fund and the Sovereign Wealth Fund, saying the two institutions would help finance strategic investments while safeguarding the country's wealth for future generations.

According to Ruto, Kenya must now confront difficult questions about its development path to unlock its full potential.

"The question we must ask ourselves candidly and honestly is why other nations have fulfilled so much of their potential while we have repeatedly fallen short. What must we now do differently to ensure that the next chapter of Kenya's development story is fundamentally different from the last?" he posed.

He urged all Kenyans to help shape a new long-term national vision, saying the country's future depends on collective commitment rather than political divisions.

World.title: Egypt’s FM participates in 5th R-4 group meeting
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty participated on Wednesday, Wednesday 5, 2026, in the fifth meeting grouping the Foreign Ministers of the Quadrilateral Group (R-4 Group) comprising Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia besides Egypt.

Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud were present at the meeting.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting on Jerusalem in the Jordanian capital, Amman.

The talks addressed regional developments amid the military escalation in the region and efforts to reduce tensions and achieve de-escalation, particularly regarding the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.

The ministers stressed the importance of ensuring freedom of navigation in the strait as a key pillar of global economic stability and international trade security.

They also highlighted the importance of returning to the memorandum of understanding signed between the United States and Iran on June 18, 2026, and supporting efforts to reach a sustainable agreement that enhances regional security and stability while preventing further escalation and tensions.

During the meeting, the ministers reaffirmed the centrality of the Palestinian cause, stressing that the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and ending the occupation are indispensable foundations for achieving a just and comprehensive peace and should remain a goal for the entire international community.

The consultations also covered ways to enhance cooperation and coordination among the four countries within the quadrilateral mechanism, the future of regional security arrangements, and mechanisms to strengthen the framework’s effectiveness and ensure regular meetings at various levels to maintain consultations on issues of common regional interest.

World.title: PM reviews plans for two $5bn medical cities in New Capital, New Alamein
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly reviewed a proposal to establish two integrated medical cities in the New Capital and New Alamein City as the government moves forward with plans to develop large-scale healthcare projects backed by foreign investment.

The meeting was attended by Minister of Health and Population Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Minister of Housing, Utilities and Urban Communities Randa al-Minshawy, senior government officials and representatives of an international consortium of private companies.

Madbouly reviewed the proposed financial framework for the projects and stressed the importance of completing the necessary procedures to begin implementation as soon as possible.

Abdel Ghaffar said that the projects have been developed in cooperation with one of the world’s leading international healthcare consortiums and will be financed entirely through foreign direct investment (FDI).

He added that the two medical cities will include specialized hospitals, medical schools, research centers, training institutes, administrative facilities and advanced healthcare infrastructure built to international standards.

The minister noted that the projects are intended to expand specialized healthcare services, strengthen medical education and training, and support Egypt’s position as a regional destination for healthcare, medical research and medical tourism.

He also said the government will receive a significant share of hospital beds under the agreement to support the Universal Health Insurance System, increasing access to advanced medical services.

Representatives of the international consortium said total investment in the two projects will exceed $5 billion, including approximately $2.8 billion for the New Capital medical city and $2.5 billion for the New Alamein project.

They said that the projects will rely mainly on Egyptian doctors and healthcare professionals and are expected to strengthen Egypt’s medical tourism sector. The consortium added that the New Capital medical city could attract more than three million medical tourists during its first three years of operation.

The developers also said they are evaluating several locations in New Alamein before selecting the final site, adding that the project will include hotels and integrated facilities designed to support medical tourism.

At the end of the meeting, Madbouly directed the formation of a joint working group comprising representatives of the relevant Egyptian authorities and the international consortium to finalize the technical, financial and legal arrangements ahead of the start of construction.

World.title: FM reaffirms Egypt’s support for Palestinian legitimate rights
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s steadfast support for the Palestinian people and their legitimate rights during a meeting on Wednesday, August 5, 2026, with Palestinian State Minister for Foreign Affairs and Expatriates Varsen Aghabekian Shahin.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting on Jerusalem in Jordan’s capital, Amman.

Abdelatty stressed Egypt’s complete rejection of all illegal Israeli measures in the occupied Palestinian territories, including attempts at annexation or forced displacement, ongoing violations in East Jerusalem, and infringements on Islamic and Christian holy sites that undermine the existing historical and legal reality.

The talks also addressed developments in the Gaza Strip following the announcement of a roadmap to complete the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s comprehensive peace plan.

Abdelatty stressed the importance of fulfilling all commitments under the roadmap and ensuring the full delivery of humanitarian aid, paving the way for the next phase of the plan and ultimately the establishment of an independent Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

World.title: Egyptian, Qatari FMs meet on sidelines of ministerial meeting on Jerusalem in Amman
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty and Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani held talks on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting on Jerusalem, held in Jordan’s capital, Amman.

The two ministers praised the depth of Egyptian-Qatari relations and stressed the importance of preparations for the upcoming meeting of the Egyptian-Qatari Joint Higher Committee, scheduled to be held in the city of El Alamein on Aug. 20, in a move aimed at boosting bilateral cooperation.

They also discussed regional developments, stressing the importance of ending the war and de-escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, while preserving energy security and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

The meeting also addressed the latest developments in the Gaza Strip following the announcement of a roadmap to complete the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s peace plan.

The two sides stressed the importance of continued coordination between Egypt, Qatar, and Arab and Islamic countries, as well as Israel’s fulfillment of its commitments, paving the way for moving to the second phase of the plan’s implementation.

World.title: ‘Black widows’: Women accused of marrying Russian army recruits to claim death payouts
World.content:
When a Russian soldier is killed in battle, his next of kin receive lump sums from the military starting from 5 million rubles ($64,000), compensation intended to reassure recruits that if — and often when — the worst happens, their loved ones will be looked after.

But there are mounting concerns in Russia that the benefit is increasingly being exploited by ruthless scammers, whom Russian officials and state media dub “black widows.” They dupe vulnerable men into sham marriages before seeing them off to war, then claim compensation if their new husbands are killed, cutting out other relatives.

Deathbed weddings

In recent months, Russians have been scandalized by multiple stories about recruits being allegedly honey-trapped into marriage before perishing on the front lines, or even getting married on their deathbeds.

In one widely reported “black widow” case last year, a nurse working at a military hospital was fired after being accused of marrying five soldiers in her care before they succumbed to their injuries in order to collect their death benefits.

It’s an abuse that has touched a nerve in a society that is increasingly alarmed at how the ongoing war in Ukraine — which the Kremlin still calls a “special military operation” — is taking its toll on life back home.

Against a backdrop of a worsening economy, fuel shortages, the ever-growing human cost and damaging Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil, condemnation of the scammers is getting louder, with mounting public calls for an official crackdown.

“The families of Special Military Operation participants need protection from brazen criminals, from so-called ‘black widows,’ from financial and telephone scammers and predators who target those who have received monetary payouts,” said Leonid Slutsky, a prominent lawmaker in Russia’s usually uncritical parliament. Such “crimes” are now reaching “serious proportions,” he added.

Cynical advice

After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin actively encouraged Russian recruits to get married, perhaps to bolster family support or to instill an additional motivation to fight. The pro-marriage campaign was also in line with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s promotion of so-called traditional values, amid demographic decline in Russia.

The authorities sought to facilitate speedy marriages for newly enlisted soldiers that would avoid the usual notice period, while state television broadcast mass wedding events arranged by local officials to further streamline the process.

Pedestrians walk past a billboard praising a member of the Russian armed forces in a street in Moscow on April 1. The board bears the slogan “Pride of Russia!” Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters

Marrying a soldier, especially a soon-to-be-deployed recruit — for whom life expectancy on the “meat-grinder” front lines is now catastrophically short — has even been cast as a way onto the Russian property ladder.

In a video podcast recorded in the Siberian city of Tomsk last year, one Russian real estate agent offered astonishingly cynical advice to would-be property buyers.

“I’m a 30-year-old woman, but if I want to buy an apartment, where am I supposed to get the money?” the host, Darya Cherdantseva, asked.

“It’s simple,” the agent, Marina Orlova, responded. “Find a man who’s serving in the Special Military Operation and when he gets killed, you get 8 million rubles,” or $102,000, she said with a laugh.

“Lots of women are buying cheap apartments like that these days. It’s business,” Orlova added.

Both women were eventually prosecuted, handed long community-service sentences and forced to apologize to soldiers and their wives.

Servicemen of the 148th Separate Artillery Zhytomyr Brigade fire a self-propelled howitzer toward Russian troops at a position on the front line in Dnipropetrovsk, Ukraine, on June 23. Reuters

Widespread outrage

Russian courts have intervened in other high-profile cases, too, such as the very public spat between the mother of one Russian soldier from Ryazan and a local woman he met and married during a short period of leave from the front lines.

The soldier, Georgy Kostyrko, met Angelina Varyukhina online and married her 10 days later, before rejoining his unit.

According to Kostyrko’s mother, the new wife soon began posting photographs and videos of herself with other men on social media, and her son filed for divorce. But he was killed in action before the paperwork was finalized, leaving her as the legal recipient of the death compensation.

Varyukhina offered a different account, saying accusations about her brief marriage were an attempt to “blacken” her reputation, and that she and Kostyrko reconciled after falling out. She said images of her online with other men were intended to make Georgy jealous.

Varyukhina’s next-of-kin status was eventually overturned in the courts, but the scandal provoked widespread outrage.

But there have also been shocking incidents where members of the Russian security forces appear to have been involved in orchestrating “black widow” scams, conspiring with women to send their newly recruited husbands on dangerous missions in exchange for a share of the compensation if they are killed.

In one case last year, Russian media reported on an investigation in Primorsky Krai, in the country’s far east, into an alleged scheme involving a warrant officer, a sergeant and a military accountant. The three were accused of recruiting vulnerable men, including orphans and people with no close relatives, and arranging marriages for them. The recruits were allegedly then sent to high-risk front-line positions where they were more likely to be killed in combat. There have been no public updates since on the case.

Back in St. Petersburg, Maria took CNN to her father’s old apartment, which has now been sold. She is convinced he was also scammed out of his home.

Maria took CNN to her father’s old apartment. It was sold after his death, and she says she has none of his possessions to remember him by. CNN

Behind a broken door, the new owners insisted it was a legitimate sale and that they had never even met the seller. But the money and the widow, like Maria’s dad, are now long gone.

“There is absolutely nothing left, and that is incredibly painful,” Maria sobbed.

“I don’t have a single thing to remind me of him, just the keys to his apartment, which don’t even work anymore, and that’s it.”

Katharina Krebs and Ana Archen contributed reporting.

World.title: Unpaid wages and deadly risk: Why health workers are threatening to abandon the Ebola response
World.content:
Every morning, Micheline Kayimpa pulls on layers of protective gear before stepping into an Ebola isolation ward in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), knowing that one small mistake could cost her life.

At the Elikya Ebola Treatment Center in Bunia, the nurse spends her days caring for patients infected with Ebola — one of the world’s deadliest viruses — administering medicine and assisting those too weak to feed themselves.

Because Ebola spreads through bodily fluids, even routine care exposes health workers to constant risk — from treating patients to cleaning contaminated spaces.

“I am very afraid for my safety,” Kayimpa told CNN. “Sometimes, a small detail we overlook can prove fatal.”

But as the outbreak grows at an alarming pace, health workers say they are battling more than the virus.

After months of treating Ebola patients, Kayimpa says she has yet to receive a single government paycheck. The mother-of-four is among dozens of health workers who have protested delayed wages and threatened to boycott work.

Micheline Kayimpa stands outside Elikya Ebola treatment center in Bunia on July 27, 2026. Prosper Heri Ngorora

The timing couldn’t be worse.

Kayimpa is working on the front line of what the World Health Organization says is now “the largest Ebola outbreak ever reported” in the DRC. Since the virus emerged in mid-May, it has infected at least 3,874 people and killed 1,751, according to figures released Wednesday by the Congolese health ministry.

The outbreak was jointly detected in both the DRC and neighboring Uganda. While Uganda has since declared itself Ebola-free, transmission has continued to accelerate in eastern Congo.

The flare-up has reached that scale in just over two months, surpassing the country’s last major Ebola epidemic, which spanned nearly two years between August 2018 and June 2020. Only the 2014–16 Ebola epidemic in West Africa has been larger and deadlier, infecting more than 28,600 people and killing 11,325 across Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia.

Deep mistrust fuels hostility

Bunia, where Kayimpa works, is the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak, where more than 90% of confirmed cases have been recorded. The response is already struggling to keep pace even without the threat of healthcare workers walking out in protest.

Unlike previous Ebola outbreaks, this one is caused by the less common Bundibugyo strain, for which there are no proven vaccines and treatment options remain limited. Ongoing fighting in eastern DRC has also made it harder for health workers to reach affected communities.

“This outbreak took hold in communities already worn down by conflict and displacement, with weak health, water and sanitation systems to begin with,” said Lancelot Mermet, director of humanitarian programs at Mercy Corps.

“When people can’t get to care quickly, or don’t trust the system enough to come forward, the virus moves faster,” he told CNN, adding that health officials are still identifying cases that cannot be linked to known infections.

A doctor provides care to a patient with Ebola virus disease at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre in Bunia, Ituri, in eastern DRC on July 13, 2026. Benediction Murhabazi/AFP/Getty Images

Aid agencies say mistrust, misinformation about Ebola, and resistance to restrictions on traditional burial practices have fueled hostility toward health workers and complicated efforts to contain the outbreak.

That hostility erupted into full view in late May, when demonstrators seeking the bodies of two relatives forced their way into an Ebola treatment facility. It was the third such attack since the outbreak began, forcing health workers to move patients to safety as gunfire erupted nearby.

The violence has continued. Similar attacks were reported in June and July, and the United Nations said last month that “at least a dozen facilities have been attacked, largely due to fear, misinformation and deep community mistrust of outside authorities.”

‘We’re sacrificing our lives’

Inside Bunia’s Elikya Ebola Treatment Center, the response is stretched thin.

The 90-bed isolation ward, run by international humanitarian organization Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders, or MSF), is already operating at full capacity, with many patients arriving only after they are critically ill.

“We do not have enough staff,” Kayimpa said. “There are just two or three of us nurses looking after patients with more than 10 different conditions.”

Even with protective equipment, the danger never disappears.

“Accidents can happen whilst I’m working here,” she said. “Some aggressive patients may attack you and infect you. We’re sacrificing our lives for the people.”

Health care workers already paid a heavy price in the early days of the outbreak, she said.

“When the disease first broke out, we didn’t know it was Ebola,” she recalled. “We were treating patients without any protection. Many of us became infected, and some died.”

Despite those risks, Kayimpa says it isn’t the virus that has pushed many health workers to breaking point.

MSF provides bonuses, she said, but those payments do not replace the government wages she relies on.

“I’ve been working here since June, but I haven’t received a single penny in wages,” she said, adding that her name was misspelled on payroll records. “I was told that processing my file would take a long time.”

She stopped work for three days in protest, she said, but has since resumed in the hope her case will be resolved. If there’s no progress, however, Kayimpa – who worked for a private health organization in Bunia before joining the Ebola effort – is ready to walk out again.

It remains unclear whether the delays are linked to broader funding pressures affecting the response.

DRC communications minister Patrick Muyaya Katembwe acknowledged that delayed payments had triggered staff protests at several Ebola treatment centers but told CNN the outstanding payments were now being processed.

Rubble is set on fire as health workers involved in Congo’s Ebola response go on strike as they protest over payment issues in Bunia, on July 15, 2026. Constant Same Bagalwa/AP

He said the delays were largely caused by the administrative process of verifying which workers had been deployed to the Ebola response and ensuring payments reached the correct recipients.

“Anyone officially listed will be paid,” he said.

MSF, which runs several Ebola treatment and isolation facilities across the DRC, said the protests were related to government compensation rather than payments from the humanitarian organization.

“MSF is continuing to meet its obligations towards staff working in the response,” it said in a statement to CNN, adding that “health workers play an essential role in responding to this outbreak, and it is important that they receive compensation in a timely manner for their work under extremely challenging conditions.”

‘Chasing a wildfire from behind’

Aid workers say the success of the Ebola response depends on the people risking their lives to keep it running.

“These are the people carrying the greatest burden of the outbreak, caring for and treating patients, preventing infections and holding together public confidence in the health system, all while taking significant risks themselves,” an aid worker familiar with the response told CNN.

Health workers disinfect an ambulance at the Ebola Treatment Center at Bunia General Hospital in Ituri, on July 22, 2026. Dirole Lotsima Dieudonne/AP

He said, “With this outbreak moving this fast and spreading further from the epicenter, frontline workers need the equipment, protection, timely payment and support required to do their jobs safely.

“Every interruption gives the virus more time to spread and leaves the response chasing a wildfire from behind,” the aid worker added.

Whether health workers like Kayimpa receive that support could determine how many remain on the front line, fighting to keep patients alive and contain the virus.

“As long as I don’t receive my wages, I will boycott work until I’m paid,” she said. “Better still, I will leave this job to try my hand at other activities that will bring me money.”

World.title: Four wounded, two IDF soldiers killed as southern Lebanon conflict flares up
World.content:
Israel has launched attacks in parts of the Lebanese city of Tyre, wounding at least four, according to Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA).

Drones struck the nearby town of Al-Burj Al-Shamali, which was subsequently hit by a strike from a fighter jet, NNA said on Thursday, adding that people were seen fleeing toward Tyre.

Israel also launched three airstrikes on the town of Al-Mansouri and surrounding areas, south of Tyre, NNA reported.

US-mediated talks in Rome between Israel and Lebanon ended earlier than expected on Wednesday amid the renewed Israeli strikes.

While Israel has ramped up attacks, the Israel Defense Forces earlier said two soldiers died in operations in southern Lebanon on Wednesday.

World.title: An agreement on the Strait of Hormuz is taking shape – but not one Trump wants
World.content:
Like shifting winds, plans for the future of the Strait of Hormuz – and their chance of success – change almost daily.

US President Donald Trump said an agreement could be reached this week.

“It could happen. Tomorrow or the next day,” Trump said Tuesday. “A lot of progress has been made. And they called me and they said, ‘Please let’s talk.’”

But he again threatened to attack Iran should no deal be reached.

Even so, there’s no consensus even on who is talking to who. Iran has persistently said it is talking solely with Oman on a temporary arrangement for the vital waterway.

And others are less confident that a deal is imminent and are skeptical about its longevity.

Iran and Oman have agreed on the geographical coordinates of a proposed safe shipping route in the strait, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Wednesday. But he tempered expectations by adding “provided that certain third parties do not obstruct the process.”

A senior Gulf official familiar with the talks suggested there is about a 50:50 chance of a deal by Friday. One issue is that the Iranian delegation does not include the voice of the hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which would have to sign off on the details, the source said.

Iran blames Washington for delays

Trump’s optimism may have surprised Tehran.

“The main reason for the delay in reaching an agreement with Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz is US interference and Trump’s threats,” the semi-official Iranian news agency Tasnim cited “an informed source” as saying on Wednesday.

Another semi-official outlet, Fars, struck a similar tone. It said some US officials had “sent mixed signals and, either directly or through regional partners, have disrupted the course of the negotiations. There remains concern that obstruction by the United States or certain regional parties could prolong the negotiations or otherwise interfere with the process.”

Fars reiterated that Iran is negotiating only with Oman and those talks “are focused on a middle corridor that would safeguard Iran’s rights while taking Oman’s concerns into account.”

“Iran’s rights” is the term that raises many questions.

There are competing routes through the strait and what’s on the table appears to involve merging them – with Iran retaining a level of control that would be at odds with US wishes.

The negotiations should “establish Iranian arrangements because security, de-mining, and maritime services are handled by Iran,” according to Saeed Ajorlu, a member of Iran’s negotiating committee.

Tehran’s goal “is to set temporary arrangements” between one and three months “where Iran is dominant,” Ajorlu told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB this week.

“Where Iran is dominant” may not fly in Washington or Gulf capitals.

“The negotiations have focused on transforming the southern route, which passes through Omani waters, and the northern route, which passes through Iran’s territorial waters, into an intermediate route that serves the considerations and interests of both coastal states,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei earlier on Monday.

“We are now talking about a corridor that will have a two-way route, not two or three separate routes,” he said.

Baghaei, Ajorlu and every other Iranian official insist the legal regime at the strait will not return to its pre – war state, when no country controlled shipping through the critical waterway.

Control or supervision over the chokepoint has become just as much a red line for Tehran as the right to nuclear enrichment.

How the US sees the strait

The prospect of such leverage is unacceptable in Washington, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has repeatedly said any form of state control over international waters is against international law.

“If we create a precedent in the Middle East where a nation state can decide that they are going to control an international waterway,” he said recently, “charge a toll and if you don’t pay them blow up your ships, we have created a very dangerous precedent, which will repeat itself in other parts of the world,” he said last month.

Marco Rubio warned that charging fees in the strait creates a “dangerous precedent.” Tierney L. Cross/AP

Qatar suggested Tuesday that negotiations were moving forward, but it’s hard to square the circle when the goals and demands of the two adversaries are so far apart.

Key questions remain: Will the Revolutionary Guards accept reduced control over the Strait of Hormuz, and under what conditions would it intercept vessels? Would reopening extend to foreign – including American – naval ships? How much information would Iran demand about ships’ cargoes and destinations?

It is also unclear whether the arrangement would lift the US blockade on Iranian ports, restore waivers to permit Iranian oil exports, and revive or replace parts of the US-Iran memorandum signed in June and declared dead a month later.

The June agreement left key provisions deliberately vague. Article 5 committed Iran to using its “best efforts” to ensure safe commercial passage for 60 days, while also saying Iran and Oman will “define the future administration and maritime services” in the strait.

It also said that any future arrangement must be “in line with applicable international law.”

But that qualification resolved little. “Given the well-known disagreement between Iran and most of the world over what international law requires in the Strait of Hormuz, this formulation does little more than kick the can down the road,” noted the Lawfare blog.

Preserving ‘durable’ influence

Ultimately, Tehran “is seeking to convert the leverage it gained during the war into a durable political and institutional role in governing one of the world’s most strategically important waterways,” says Trita Parsi at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

“By embedding a lasting role in the governance of Hormuz, Iran could preserve much of the influence it gained during the war without relying on continual military coercion,” Parsi posted on X Wednesday.

That is a much greater gain than any fees or tolls it may want to collect at the chokepoint.

“From day one, it was clear that restoring the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-crisis status would have required either regime change in Iran or a sustained military effort to impose control over the waterway,” said Israeli security expert Danny Citrinowicz.

“Neither option was politically or strategically acceptable to Washington, given the enormous costs and long-term commitments they would require. Sometimes, the least desirable option is the only realistic one.”

While agreement remains elusive, the world’s oil markets must confront draining crude reserves.

If the Strait of Hormuz were opened today, it could still take up to 18 months to replenish depleted inventories, Amin Nasser, the chief executive of the world’s largest oil producer Saudi Aramco, said Tuesday.

For every day there is no agreement, some 15 million barrels of crude oil are not travelling through the narrow waterway to world markets.

World.title: Ballot Papers Arrive in Mongu
World.content:
Ballot papers for the August 13 General Elections have safely arrived in Mongu District, Western Province, marking another key milestone in the country’s electoral preparations.

The ballot papers were received under the supervision of electoral officials and other stakeholders before being offloaded and secured for distribution to polling stations across the district.

Speaking shortly after the arrival of the materials, Mongu District Electoral Officer Oswell Mpofu confirmed that all ballot papers for the district’s three constituencies Mongu Central, Nalikwanda and Mongu East had been received in good condition.

Mr Mpofu said the electoral materials arrived intact and assured the public that the ballot boxes and other election materials had not been tampered with.

He further encouraged representatives of political parties and other accredited stakeholders to inspect the ballot boxes and election materials in line with the Electoral Commission’s transparency measures aimed at enhancing public confidence in the electoral process.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) Mongu District Secretary Bright Masialeti expressed satisfaction with the successful arrival of the ballot papers, describing the process as transparent and well-coordinated.

Mr Masialeti said his party remained confident of victory in the forthcoming elections, adding that many people in Western Province continue to support President Hakainde Hichilema, whom he said has delivered on a significant number of his campaign promises.

And Zambia Must Prosper (ZMP) Campaign Manager Mayor Musiabosia appealed to all political parties, candidates and their supporters to uphold peace before, during and after the elections.

Mr Musiabosia urged voters to exercise their democratic right responsibly and reject all forms of violence, saying peaceful elections are essential for preserving national unity and democracy.

The arrival of ballot papers in Mongu forms part of the Electoral Commission’s nationwide distribution of election materials ahead of the August 13 General Elections, as preparations continue across the country.

World.title: How Copper Queens exited WAFCON despite beating Malawi ‎
World.content:
The Copper Queens were eliminated from the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) on Wednesday night despite beating Malawi 2-1 in their final Group C match in Rabat, Morocco.

‎

‎The result also means Zambia has missed out on qualification for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

‎

‎Zambia, Malawi and Nigeria all finished the group stage on six points each. However, the Copper Queens exited the tournament due to an inferior head-to-head record among the three teams.

‎

‎Tournament rules stipulated that results against bottom-placed Egypt, who lost all three matches, were not considered when separating the teams.

‎

‎With Egypt removed from the equation, Zambia were eliminated for scoring only two goals in matches involving Malawi and Nigeria.

Malawi scored four and Nigeria three in those same fixtures.

‎

‎It was a cruel exit for a Zambian side that finished with six points but could not progress to the knockout rounds.

‎

‎BANDA STRIKES EARLY

‎

‎The Copper Queens made the perfect start at the stadium. Captain Barbra Banda opened the scoring inside the first minute with a powerful long-range strike her fifth goal of the competition and enough to keep her as the tournament’s leading scorer.

‎

‎Zambia continued to press and nearly doubled their lead in the 18th minute. Irene Lungu’s well-taken free-kick was pushed away by Malawi goalkeeper Mercy Sikelo.

‎

‎The second goal came eight minutes before halftime. Margaret Belemu picked out Prisca Chilufya with a cutback from the right, and the forward calmly fired home to give Zambia a comfortable 2-0 lead.

‎

‎TENSE FINISH

‎

‎Malawi pulled one goal back in the second half, setting up a tense finish.

Both teams created chances in the closing minutes, with Zambia pushing for more goals knowing that goal difference in the mini-league would prove crucial.

‎

‎Despite securing all three points, the 2-1 victory was not enough.

Malawi and Nigeria progressed from Group C on the tournament’s tiebreaker rules, ending Zambia’s WAFCON campaign at the group stage.

‎

‎The early exit marks a setback for the Copper Queens, who had aimed to build on their 2022 semi-final run and secure a second straight World Cup appearance.

‎

‎Zambia skipper Banda was named player of the match.

World.title: Kasama Teacher Advances Literacy Through Book Donations
World.content:
A Kasama based teacher and writer, Clement Shula, has continued to make strides in his literacy project following his recent donation of supplementary books to schools in the district.

Mr Shula, who teaches at Kasama Central Day Secondary School, returned to his former school, Kasonde Chisuna Primary, earlier this month with the gesture aimed at strengthening the reading culture among pupils in rural areas.

In a follow up spot check conducted at Kasama Primary School, both pupils and teachers testified that the donated books have already begun to transform learning outcomes.

They noted that reading confidence and general school performance have improved among learners.

Kasama Primary School Headteacher, Emelda Mwaba confirmed the development, describing the initiative as a timely supplement to government’s Competence-Based Curriculum (CBC).

During the visit, grade six pupil Astrida Chimfwembe and her counterpart Mwape Mulusa confidently demonstrated their reading abilities by fluently reading from one of the donated books, offering clear evidence of the project’s positive impact.

“I can now read better because of these books. They make learning easier and more enjoyable. The books are helping us understand our lessons more clearly,” the pupils said.

Mr, Shula explained that his long-term vision is to roll out the distribution of books across the province and eventually extend the initiative countrywide, ensuring that every child whether in town or in the remotest village has access to quality learning materials.

“The idea is to tackle the low reading culture among pupils, especially in rural areas. These books are meant to give children the confidence to read and catch up with their peers,” Mr Shula said.

Teachers and pupils alike expressed gratitude, saying the project is already inspiring learners to embrace reading and improve their academic performance.

World.title: Don’t Whitewash UPND’s Violence–Mr. President Please Act
World.content:
By Katoka Mweenda

On August 4, 2026, Lusaka Times published Michael Lombe’s commentary, The Dangerous Return of PF: Staged Political Violence. Either Mr. Lombe lives on another planet—or he assumes Zambians are fools.

To reduce the thuggery terrorizing Zambians to “PF cadres” is not analysis; it is a disgraceful distraction. We have lived under President Hichilema’s administration for five years. Who has criticized him and escaped his iron fist? Fear and insecurity have pushed many Zambians into silence. If citizens are arrested for expressing themselves on social media, then opposition “thugs” cannot operate freely in the streets without protection from President Hichilema.

Is Mr. Lombe seriously suggesting that the people beating women, targeting independent candidates, and repeatedly attacking Mr. Nkombo in Southern Province are PF cadres? Public writing requires accountability, not whitewashing. The evidence points not to victims—but to UPND cadres/perpetrators. Pretending the violence is not happening will not stop it; it will only embolden those responsible.

Who does not know what is happening? There is no credible evidence that anyone other than UPND cadres is driving this wave of political violence. If President Hichilema did not authorize these tactics, those responsible would have been arrested long ago. Instead, the police claim to be helpless against “UPND thugs” because they enjoy political backing. They assault people openly—often in full view of cameras and the police—a reality that should alarm every patriotic Zambian.

Lombe ignores that the opposition does not control the police. Where was he when the military was deployed in Mumfumbwe, where lives were lost? If the government can deploy that kind of force there, why has it failed to arrest the “opposition thugs” Mr. Lombe now blames? And what about the official UPND vehicles being used by violent groups? Were those vehicles stolen to embarrass the President—or is the President so weak that his own assets can be misused with impunity?

These individuals are not invisible. Zambians see them. They watch the perpetrators on television and social media as they terrorize fellow citizens while the President stays silent. That silence has strengthened their resolve–they are untouchable—because they have political protection.

Sadly, Mr. Lombe writes as if UPND is still an opposition party rather than the governing party. We have not seen opposition supporters disrupting UPND campaign events. Yet even former UPND members have been assaulted—and even killed—and Mr. Lombe refuses to acknowledge those incidents.

Fear may be human, but this violence reveals character.

By the way, who introduced the label “commanders” for UPND cadres? Who approved military-style berets for them? Symbols and titles are never accidental. They project authority—and many Zambians now believe these “commanders” function as a political militia in defense of President Hichilema. Blaming PF for their actions is unpatriotic.

As a nation, we have witnessed repeated acts of political violence attributed to the “angels” of UPND since 2021. The violence did not intensify because voters wanted it—it intensified because citizens were intimidated into silence. Violence weakened the opposition. But when the “coalition of voters” began turning against President Hichilema, violence became the preferred tool.

What followed was predictable. These so-called commanders have descended on innocent Zambians. Southern Province has been overwhelmed by violence the President has failed to stop. How can violence in Southern Province be blamed on Bembas? How can violence during UPND’s own adoption processes be blamed on outsiders? Mr. Nkombo, like many others, was attacked by people from within his own political space.

The good news is simple: violence will not win UPND any additional votes. If anything, it will harden public anger—and citizens will respond at the ballot box. Zambian elections are not won through intimidation and those who believe otherwise are deluding themselves.

The responsibility for ending this violence rests with President Hichilema as Commander-in-Chief. If Mr. Lombe’s allegations are true, then the government should arrest the alleged opposition thugs. They appear at public gatherings. If they truly exist, they should be brought to justice. Yet those thugs wearing UPND berets and openly supporting the President continue to operate freely.

If political violence is to end, those responsible—regardless of party—must be held accountable. If not, Zambia faces a serious danger: even greater instability after the election. But my hope remains–Zambians will never surrender their democratic rights to intimidation and violence.

World.title: BBC Interview Raises Questions About Mundubile’s Readiness to Lead
World.content:
The recent BBC interview featuring Brian Mundubile has sparked discussion among Zambians about leadership, governance and the qualities required of those seeking the nation’s highest office.

While Mr. Mundubile used the interview to criticize the performance of the current administration, many observers were left wanting more than criticism. They expected detailed policy proposals and a clear vision for addressing the country’s pressing challenges, including economic growth, debt management, job creation, governance reforms and cyber legislation.

Political analysts note that international media platforms often serve as an important stage for aspiring leaders to articulate their plans and demonstrate their readiness for office. Such appearances provide an opportunity not only to identify national problems but also to present practical solutions and a roadmap for implementation.

In the interview, Mr. Mundubile highlighted concerns about the government’s performance. However, critics argue that his responses lacked sufficient policy depth and did not clearly outline how his proposed administration would tackle Zambia’s economic and social challenges.

For many voters, leadership is measured not only by the ability to identify shortcomings in government but also by the capacity to offer credible alternatives. As Zambia prepares for Elections, expectations remain high for political leaders to move beyond criticism and present comprehensive policy frameworks that can be scrutinized by the public.

Zambians increasingly want to hear detailed plans on issues such as reducing the cost of living, creating employment opportunities, managing public debt, strengthening democratic institutions and balancing national security concerns with civil liberties in the digital age.

The debate surrounding Mr. Mundubile’s BBC appearance underscores a broader question facing Zambia’s political landscape: what level of preparation, policy clarity and leadership vision should Zambians expect from individuals seeking the presidency?

For some viewers, the interview did not provide sufficient evidence that Mr. Mundubile possesses the depth, clarity and policy direction required to govern effectively. They argue that until a more coherent and comprehensive governing agenda is presented, questions about his readiness for national leadership are likely to persist.

As Zambia’s political discourse continues to evolve, Zambians will ultimately judge aspiring leaders not only by their critiques of the current administration but by the strength, credibility and practicality of the alternatives they offer.

World.title: Late Dr Katema’s Body Arrives Thursday, Burial Friday
World.content:
The body of the Late Joseph Katema, former Cabinet Minister in the Patriotic Front Government, will be repatriated to Zambia from India on Thursday, 6th August, 2026.

According to a statement issued by Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa, the remains will arrive at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport in Lusaka at 14:35 hours aboard Emirates Airlines.

Dr Katema died in India.

Mr Kangwa said President Hakainde Hichilema has accorded the late former Cabinet Minister an Official Funeral in honour of his distinguished service to the nation.

Mr Kangwa has further stated that the burial will take place on Friday, 7th August, 2026 at Leopards Hill Memorial Park in Lusaka.

“The burial will be preceded by an Official Funeral Church Service at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus at 10:00 hours,” he said

He also said President Hichilema has also declared Friday, 7th August, 2026 a Day of National Mourning in honour of Dr Katema and the mourning period will be observed from 06:00 hours to 18:00 hours.

During this period, all flags will fly at half-mast, Mr Kangwa said.

Dr Katema served as Cabinet Minister during the Patriotic Front administration.

World.title: President Hichilema Urges Luanshya Votes To Protect Development Gains
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on the residents of Luanshya to vote for the UPND on 13th August in order to continue with the developmental projects that his government delivered in the last four years and 11 months of being in power.

President Hichilema cited free education, the school re-entry policy, the increased Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and the Social Cash Transfer as some of the incentives that his administration delivered to the Zambian people.

Speaking at Mikonfwa grounds in Luanshya district on the Copperbelt Province this afternoon, President Hichilema stated that his government has enhanced the economic status of the district through the revitalisation of the shaft 28 mine.

President Hichilema has also promised to complete paying ex RAMCOZ workers, serials and Mpelembe drilling employees when re-elected on August 13.

The Head of State has advised the residents of Luanshya not to listen to political parties that he said had no proper vision to lead the country.

“Do not listen to the people that have joined other political parties to disguise themselves as different people,” said President Hichilema.

President Hichilema stressed that the residents of Luanshya should vote for UPND so that they continue working on the township roads such as Roan -Mpatamatu which is in a deplorable state.

The Head of State also noted that he is aware of the challenges that small scale miners face saying that he is going to resolve them when re-elected in office.

“We are going to legalise mining because we need to protect all the citizens across the country. There is no parent who will allow their children to die carelessly,” said President Hichilema.

President Hichilema also stated that he is going to work on the sewerage system in Roan Township.

“I am aware of the poor sewerage system in Roan township and we are going to work on it, ” said President.

President Hichilema stated that Miners are facing a lot of problems and has designated a day specifically for the miners to discuss their challenges.

“I am aware of the challenges that miners are facing, so I have designated a day specifically for these miners so that we can discuss their challenges,”

World.title: President Hichilema Orders Swift Payments to Farmers
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has directed the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) to ensure that farmers are paid through mobile money within two to three days after delivering their maize.

‎Speaking during a public rally at Mishikishi Grounds in Masaiti District, President Hichilema said farmers should no longer experience lengthy delays in receiving payment after supplying maize to the FRA.

‎The President said the directive is intended to ensure timely payments, to allow farmers to reinvest in their farming activities and improve agricultural productivity.

‎He noted that prompt payments will strengthen the agricultural sector by enabling farmers to adequately prepare for subsequent farming seasons and improve household incomes.

‎Meanwhile, President Hichilema has assured the people of Masaiti that Government will construct the Munda Wanga–Mukushi Road, describing it as an important economic route that will provide a shorter link to the Great North Road.

‎He said the road project will improve connectivity between communities, ease the transportation of agricultural produce and other goods, and stimulate economic growth in the district.

‎The President further directed that volunteer teachers and nurses who attended the rally in Masaiti District be employed as Government remains committed to strengthening the country’s education and health sectors through increased recruitment of frontline workers.

‎President Hichilema reaffirmed Government’s commitment to improving infrastructure and implementing policies aimed at enhancing agricultural production, creating employment opportunities, and improving the livelihoods of Zambians.

‎Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) aspiring candidate for Kalalangabo Constituency, Michael Katambo, has expressed confidence that the newly created constituency will experience accelerated development under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema.

‎Mr Katambo said the people of Kalalangabo and Masaiti constituencies are committed to supporting President Hichilema and the UPND in the August 13 elections.

‎He said the Government has demonstrated its commitment to improving the welfare of citizens through investments in road infrastructure, agriculture, education, and health, adding that continued support for the ruling party will accelerate development in the area.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 6, 2026
World.content:
Nigeria Rescues Over 300 Kidnap Victims in Major Security Operation

More than 300 people abducted in separate attacks in Nigeria have been rescued in what the presidency described as the country's largest single-day rescue operation. The joint operation by the military, police, intelligence agencies and the National Counter-Terrorism Centre. Those freed include 163 people abducted during a February attack on the Woro community in Kwara State, where scores were killed. At least 145 others had been taken in Niger State. The victims were receiving medical care at a military site before being reunited with their families. President Bola Tinubu praised the operation as evidence of improved coordination among security agencies. The rescue comes amid growing concerns over the spread of kidnappings and militant violence beyond Nigeria's traditional conflict zones.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

WHO Defends Uganda's Early Ebola Declaration

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has defended Uganda's decision to declare the end of its Ebola outbreak in Bundibugyo before completing the conventional 42-day waiting period. It said that the country remained focused on the primary objective of halting transmission and protecting public health. The move sparked debate, with some observers questioning why the country did not wait the standard 42 days after the last confirmed case before making the declaration. WHO Regional Director for Africa Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi said Uganda's response should be judged by its success in containing the outbreak, which recorded just 20 confirmed cases, mostly imported from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo). It recorded a case fatality rate of about 10%, compared with 44% in the DR Congo. Uganda has since deployed health workers to support the response in eastern DR Congo. WHO and Africa CDC praised the country's handling of the outbreak as a regional model. Africa CDC also criticised the United States for maintaining travel restrictions on Uganda despite its successful containment of the virus.

El Niño Could Push 49 Million More Into Acute Hunger, WFP Warns

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that the strengthening El Niño weather phenomenon could push nearly 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of 2027. This will raise the number of food-insecure people in vulnerable countries from 225 million to 274 million. Southern Africa and Central America are expected to be among the hardest-hit regions, with droughts, floods and extreme temperatures threatening food production and livelihoods. WFP and its partners have already stepped up early action in more than 50 countries. They stressed that investing in preparedness can significantly reduce humanitarian losses and response costs.

Mutharika Makes Fourth Private South Africa Trip in Seven Months

Malawi's State House has confirmed that President Peter Mutharika has travelled to South Africa on what it described as another "private visit. This is his fourth in seven months without disclosing the purpose or duration of the trip. The announcement followed conflicting media reports about his whereabouts, prompting renewed questions over the President's repeated absences and the lack of transparency surrounding them. Critics argued that while the President is entitled to privacy, the public deserves reassurance about his health, availability and who is overseeing government affairs during his time away.

Nigeria Approves $4.5bn Oil-Backed Refinancing Deal

Nigeria's National Economic Council has approved a new $4.5 billion oil-backed financing facility for NNPC Limited to refinance an existing $3.3 billion pre-export loan and unlock an additional $3 billion in liquidity. The government said the deal, known as Project Gazelle 2, will strengthen foreign reserves, improve NNPC's cash flow and free up funding for infrastructure. The refinancing comes as Africa's third-largest economy seeks to shore up its foreign reserves and fund fiscal priorities amid persistent pressure on the naira and efforts to attract foreign investment through economic reforms launched by President Bola Tinubu's administration. The move forms part of broader efforts by Tinubu's administration to stabilise the economy, support the naira and attract investment.

Close 

Mnangagwa's Daughter-in-Law Held Over Drug Charges

Kelsea Tadiwa Tafirenyika, the second wife of President Emmerson Mnangagwa's son Collins Mnangagwa, spent a night in custody following her arrest on allegations of dealing in dangerous drugs. Prosecutors opposed her bail on charges of dealing in dangerous drugs. Police allege they recovered pethidine, morphine and dagga worth US$204 during a raid at her Harare home and vehicle. The State argued that releasing the 22-year-old could jeopardise investigations into an alleged drug supply network and increase the risk of her fleeing or reoffending. She was remanded in custody pending a bail hearing.

World.title: South Africa: Calls to Ban Foreign Teachers Rejected - South African News Briefs - August 6, 2026
World.content:
NAPTOSA Rejects Calls to Bar Foreign Teachers

The National Professional Teachers' Organisation of South Africa (NAPTOSA) has rejected calls by the March and March movement to reserve teaching posts exclusively for South African citizens, reports EWN. Executive Director Basil Manuel said teachers employed in public schools would already have met the legal requirements to work in the country. It warned against intimidation or vigilante-style compliance checks at schools. Manuel also dismissed claims that large numbers of foreign nationals are teaching in South African schools. He said improving school safety requires addressing broader community issues, not just conducting searches for weapons and other prohibited items.

MPs Back Summons for Ramaphosa if He Refuses

Members of Parliament serving on Parliament's Impeachment Committee have welcomed legal advice stating that President Cyril Ramaphosa can be summoned to appear if he declines a voluntary invitation, reports SABC News. The committee, whose hearings were stopped by the Western Cape High Court, agreed that a summons should only be issued if Ramaphosa refuses to attend voluntarily. MPs are also considering the standard of proof to apply during the proceedings. Ramaphosa is opposing the committee's urgent direct appeal to the Constitutional Court. He argued that the matter is not urgent and does not warrant direct access.

Social Development Ends Wasteful Communications Outsourcing

The Department of Social Development has admitted that outsourcing nearly all of its communications functions was wasteful and has begun terminating the arrangements, reports EWN. Department officials said millions of rand were spent on 10 communications service providers, including work such as developing communication strategies despite having in-house staff capable of performing those duties. Officials also defended spending nearly R500,000 on hotel accommodation for the acting spokesperson during her seven-month secondment. It argued that it was significantly cheaper than the costs previously incurred through extensive outsourcing.
