World.title: Northern Romania hit by extended drought
World.content:
The northern parts of Romania are experiencing a prolonged lack of precipitation and high temperatures, coupled with historic minimum flows for numerous regional rivers.

The Someș-Tisa Water Basin Administration announced this week that 12 hydrological stations have reached zero flow, while another 15 have recorded historic minimum flows, well below the normal values for this period.

In the Crasna river basin and the tributaries of the Lower Someș and the Someșul Mic, runoff is below 10% of the multiannual norm, while in the Tur, Iza, Lăpuș, Sălăuța and Șieu river basins flows represent 10-25% of the multiannual average values.

Higher values, but still below the average specific to this period, were recorded at hydrometric stations in the mountain basins in the eastern part of the Someș-Tisa hydrographic area, namely the Someșul Mare upstream of the confluence with the Sălăuța (20–40%) and the Vișeu (40–60%).

At 34 stations out of the total of 103 hydrometric monitoring points on the watercourses in the basin, the previous minimum flow record was reached or exceeded. A dozen water sites in the region, or 11.6% of the total, had zero flow. The filling degree of the main reservoirs that constitute raw water sources is between 33% and 93%.

According to the Someș-Tisa Water Basin Administration, cited by Mediafax, the most vulnerable is the Vârșolț reservoir on the Crasna River, in Sălaj County. The water reserve in the lake is currently at the lowest level of the past ten years.

“The only reservoir that currently presents a risk from the perspective of available reserves is Lake Vârșolț, located on the Crasna River, in Sălaj County. The current water stock in this reservoir represents the lowest volume recorded in the past ten years,” the specialists stated, while calling on locals to use water sparingly.

Romania declared a nationwide energy state of alert for August amid reduced electricity generation caused by severe drought and exceptionally low river levels. Unit 1 of the Cernavodă nuclear power plant remains shut down because of low Danube levels, while Unit 2 continues operating under close monitoring.

World.title: Energy demand spikes in Romania despite government's plea to limit consumption
World.content:
Energy demand in Romania approached record levels for this summer on Wednesday, August 5, despite a call from the government for the population, companies, and institutions to voluntarily limit their consumption during evening hours.

Specifically, Romania’s consumption rose during the critical interval 9 pm to 11 pm to almost 7,700 MW, one of the highest levels this summer. To cover the demand, Romania imported nearly a third of its requirement for Wednesday evening, according to Economedia.

At the peak, the largest contribution to domestic production came from hydroelectric power plants, with approximately 1,804 MW. Hydrocarbon-fired power plants produced 1,393 MW, coal-fired plants 972 MW, while nuclear energy provided 679 MW. Wind production was very low, only 55 MW, and photovoltaics were still supplying 121 MW after sunset. Storage installations contributed approximately 232 MW.

The record consumption for this summer was reached on June 29, with a maximum of 7,971 MW. One day later, consumption rose to 7,907 MW. The highest consumption in 2026 was recorded on 21 January, of 9,213 MW.

To keep the national energy system afloat, the government requested that gas and coal-fired power plants operate at maximum capacity. Automakers Dacia and Ford have temporarily halted production at their Romanian plants until August 19 for scheduled maintenance, a move that will also reduce electricity demand.

Romania declared a nationwide energy state of alert for August amid reduced electricity generation caused by severe drought and exceptionally low river levels. Unit 1 of the Cernavodă nuclear power plant remains shut down because of low Danube levels, while Unit 2 continues operating under close monitoring.

The executive rejected the risk of a blackout or any significant issues with household fuel use. However, last week, Romanian prime minister Ilie Bolojan asked public institutions, companies and citizens to voluntarily reduce consumption during peak hours in order to ease pressure on the energy system. The PM specifically pointed to the period between 9 pm and 11 pm, when Romania is seeking to curb demand. Opponents in the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians Party (AUR) criticized the call, pointing to the government’s failure to provide energy.

World.title: Documentary on Romania's 'Ice Man' Tibi Uşeriu to premiere at Toronto International Film Festival
World.content:
The Ultra Runner, Canadian filmmaker Mila Aung-Thwin’s documentary following Romanian ultra-marathoner Tibi Ușeriu, will have its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) in the TIFF Docs 2026 program.

The film follows Tibi Ușeriu, a three-time winner of the 6633 Arctic Ultra race, as he “battles endless terrain and his own demons in search of a better life for his family, his country, and himself.”

Tibi Ușeriu fled the country after the 1989 Revolution. He went from serving time in jail for most of his young years to being “an example of reintegration and found running as his outlet for a sense of liberation.” He has won four Arctic competitions, with more than 3,000 km run.

He shared his story in the autobiographical bestseller 27 Steps. The book helped kick-start the initiation of Via Transilvanica, the long-distance trail crossing Romania. The trail is a project of NGO Tășuleasa Social, established by Tibi’s brother, Alin Uşeriu. Last summer, Tibi Ușeriu embarked on a symbolic journey from Rome to Drobeta-Turnu Severin as part of a campaign to promote Via Transilvanica.

The film follows Tibi “across the dark forests of Transylvania, the Arctic’s frozen emptiness, and the towering brutality of the Italian Alps” as he faces a reckoning between the man he used to be and the one he is trying to become.

Multiple award-winning (Sundance, Emmys, CSAs) director Mila Aung-Thwin describes the film as not really about sport but “about an internal struggle with survival, guilt, willpower, family, and the strange human capacity to reshape a life without ever fully escaping it.”

"From the outside, an ultramarathon can look strangely simple: one body crossing a hostile landscape. Pushing forward through snow, darkness, exhaustion, and silence. What drew me to the subject was the motivation to push beyond the limits of the human body. But when I met Tibi Uşeriu, I realized this was not really a physical test, but a mental one. When he started running, he would simply disappear into himself,” director Mila Aung-Thwin explains.

“Tibi’s life contains several lives that seem impossible to reconcile: a childhood marked by violence and deprivation, escape from communist Romania, years in the criminal underworld, armed robberies, prison, and then, improbably, endurance running. He has described running as the force that helped him rebuild himself. The challenge was how to film an interior landscape. In the Arctic, the white emptiness became more than a setting; it became a mirror. The silence, repetition, cold, and isolation allowed Tibi’s past to surface not as explanation, but as sensation. The film moves between physical endurance and memory, between the visible body and the invisible burden it carries,” he added.

Tiberiu Ușeriu, Alin Uhlmann Ușeriu, Maria Mihaela Ștefănuț, David Ușeriu, Eftina Moeșan, and Ana Szekely are featured in the film.

The Ultra Runner is produced by Montreal's EYESTEELFILM and Ontario-based production house winterhouse pictures. Bob Moore and Mike MacMillan are the producers. Mila Aung-Thwin, Daniel Cross, Valerie Shamash, Mandy Chang, Mark Reynolds, and Ada Solomon are executive producers. Van Royko is director of photography; Ryan Mullins is the editor.

The film is then set to be released in theatres across Canada in the spring of next year.

World.title: ISB Celebrates Another Outstanding Year of IB Diploma Results
World.content:
Partner Content

For every IB Diploma student, results day is more than a collection of numbers. It is the culmination of two years of curiosity, perseverance, late nights, ambitious goals, and personal growth. At the International School of Bucharest (ISB), the May 2026 IB Diploma Programme results once again tell a story of excellence, one that reflects not only academic success but also the strength of a community committed to helping every student thrive.

This year, ISB's top score reached an outstanding 44 out of 45 points, with four students achieving 40+ points, 18 students scoring 35+, and 29 students earning 30 or more points. The school average of 33.0 points stands well above the global IB Diploma average of approximately 30.6 points for the May 2026 examination session, continuing ISB's tradition of academic excellence and consistently strong performance.



These achievements are not isolated successes, they are part of a sustained record of outstanding results. Over the past three years, ISB students have earned two perfect IB scores of 45/45, while 17 students have achieved exceptional results of 40 points or higher.



This remarkable consistency reflects the dedication of our students, the expertise of our teachers, and a learning environment that encourages every learner to reach their full potential.



The results also open doors to some of the world's most prestigious universities. In recent years, ISB graduates have gone on to study at institutions including the University of Oxford, Sorbonne University, Cornell University, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), University College London (UCL), King's College London and many other leading universities across Europe, North America, Asia and beyond.



Among this year's graduates is Giorgio S., who scored 44/45p and will continue his academic journey at the University of Oxford. Reflecting on his 13 years at ISB, he shared:

"After spending 13 years at this school, it's hard to put into words how much it has meant to me. Looking back, I realise that what made my experience so special wasn't just the academics, but the people and the environment around me. My teachers always went above and beyond, giving their time, energy and support whenever I needed it and I'm incredibly grateful for everything they've done.



Football was also a huge part of my school life. Some of my best memories came from representing the school, training with friends and creating memories I'll always look back on.



As I move on to Oxford, I'll carry with me the values, friendships and lessons this school has given me. I'll always be proud to have been part of this community and I'm excited to see what the future holds." said Giorgio S.

Reflecting on this year's achievements, IB Diploma Programme Coordinator, Mr. Yusuf Suha Orhan, said:

"These results are a testament to the dedication, resilience, and growth our students have demonstrated throughout their IB journey. The Diploma Programme is designed to challenge students academically while helping them develop into compassionate, reflective, and internationally minded individuals. We are incredibly proud of what the Class of 2026 has accomplished, not only in their examination results but in the character, confidence, and lifelong learning skills they have developed along the way. I would also like to thank our exceptional teachers and supportive families, whose commitment has been instrumental in our students' success." said Mr. Yusuf Suha Orhan, IB Diploma Programme Coordinator.

Yet, as every IB graduate knows, the Diploma Programme is about far more than examination scores. It is a journey that shapes confident learners, thoughtful leaders, and compassionate global citizens.



Reflecting on her experience, Evelin I., one of ISB's top scorers, who will study Biochemistry at King's College London, shared:

"Looking back, choosing the IB Diploma Programme was one of the best decisions I could have made. The IB encouraged me to continue pursuing my love for sports while also strengthening my leadership and volunteering skills." said Evelin I.

She also credits her success to the people around her, explaining that her results reflect not only her own hard work but also "the constant support of my teachers" and the collaborative spirit of the ISB community.



For top scorer Gabriel L., who will study Mathematics at Sorbonne University Paris, the greatest achievement was not the number on his results sheet.

"Looking back, though, my final grade is not my most defining achievement... We've become critical thinkers and driven writers, shaped by curiosity." said Gabriel L.

His words perfectly capture the essence of the IB Diploma Programme: resilience through challenges, intellectual curiosity, meaningful friendships, and personal growth that extends far beyond the classroom.



These reflections remind us that an IB education is measured not only by points, but by the people students become. The programme encourages learners to think independently, embrace complexity, communicate with confidence, and develop the knowledge and character to make a positive difference in the world.



As ISB celebrates another successful graduating class, these results stand as a testament to the school's core values of Honesty, Empathy, Responsibility, and Open-mindedness. They also reinforce ISB's reputation as a school where students are challenged to excel academically while being empowered to discover their passions and prepare for life beyond school.



Congratulations to the IB Diploma Programme Class of 2026, their families, and the dedicated teachers who supported them every step of the way. Your achievements inspire the entire ISB community, and we look forward to seeing the impact you will make at the world's leading universities, and in the world beyond.

World.title: More than one in four Romanian localities risk losing funding over failure to join state e-payments platform
World.content:
More than one in four local authorities in Romania risk losing access to parts of their public funding after failing to enrol in Ghiseul.ro, the government's online platform for the payment of local taxes and fees, interim Deputy Prime Minister Oana Gheorghiu announced.

Under the law, all municipalities and local administrations must be connected to the platform by August 25.

According to Gheorghiu, 919 of Romania's 3,187 administrative units have yet to comply with the requirement.

"Over 2.5 million Romanians cannot benefit from the advantages of digitalisation today and are forced to physically go to city hall," Gheorghiu said, arguing that universal participation in Ghiseul.ro is essential to ensure citizens can access public services online regardless of where they live.

The deputy prime minister said she had sent reminder letters to the 919 mayors concerned, warning them that they have 20 days to complete the enrolment process.

"In case of non-compliance with the deadline, the law provides for the cessation of funding of local budgets, both with quotas deducted from income tax and with amounts deducted from certain state budget revenues intended to balance local budgets, with a few exceptions," she said, quoted by Profit.ro.

The measure could affect transfers from the state budget that are used to finance local government operations, although statutory exceptions remain in place.

Gheorghiu added that the situation highlights the need for broader administrative reform.

"Romania urgently needs administrative reform and a reduction in the number of mayors," she said.

Ghiseul.ro platform is Romania's official online payment portal for public services, allowing citizens to pay local taxes, fines and other public charges electronically. In 2023, the Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digitalisation and the Authority for the Digitalisation of Romania also launched a mobile application for the platform, through which more than 400 types of payments can be made.

(Photo: Gov.ro)

World.title: Romanian Parliament approves Integrity Law with controversial PSD and AUR amendments
World.content:
Romania's Senate on August 5 approved the Integrity Law, a key milestone under the country's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), sending the legislation to President Nicușor Dan for promulgation, according to Curs de Guvernare.

The bill includes two controversial amendments backed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), which critics argue risk being struck down by the Constitutional Court.

The law was adopted by 104 votes to eight, with seven abstentions and two senators not voting. One AUR senator, six Save Romania Union (USR) senators and one unaffiliated senator voted against the bill.

According to Curs de Guvernare, the legislation could jeopardize a EUR 790 million grant under the European Union's Recovery and Resilience Facility if it is declared unconstitutional. The president may return the law to Parliament for reconsideration once before deciding whether to promulgate it.

One of the disputed amendments, promoted primarily by PSD, would bar from holding public office dignitaries who had previously been found to be in a conflict of interest. The provision is widely seen as targeting Timișoara Mayor Dominic Fritz, who also serves as president of the opposition USR.

A second amendment, proposed by AUR, extends asset declaration requirements to spouses and "spouse-like partners" of public officials. Legal experts, including former Constitutional Court judges cited by Curs de Guvernare, have criticized the wording as too vague to meet constitutional standards. President Dan's partner, Mirabela Grădinaru, published her declarations of assets and interests on August 5.

On August 3, USR accused PSD and AUR of negotiating amendments designed to target political opponents.

"At the behest of Sorin Grindeanu, PSD and AUR insist on creating retroactive punishments to eliminate their opponents from office, even if this means democratic vandalism and pushing Romania towards illiberalism," USR said in a statement.

The party warned that Romania could lose "almost EUR 800 million" in European funding if the legislation is ultimately found to breach constitutional principles.

(Photo: Gov.ro)

World.title: ‘Our Parents Carried us to Safety’: Disabled Kosovo Children Recall Escape in 1999
World.content:
Her father recalls: “They took my car because they liked it. It was a [Volkswagen] Golf Mk2,” he says. His disabled children were “left in the mud” by the side of the road, he adds.

“We had no wheelchairs,” Ganimete notes. “My mother and father carried us everywhere.”

One by one, Sali carried each of the children onto a village bus that was already crowded with other displaced Kosovo Albanians. “We spent the whole night in there,” he recalls.

“There must have been more than 100 people in that bus,” says Ganimete. “My father held my two brothers on his lap, and my mother held me.”

As the bus waited to leave, she watched Serbian forces separate young men from the crowd. “They took them to a garage and beat them. We could see it from the bus.”

She also remembers police demanding money and gold jewelry from refugees.

After spending the night on the bus, they were ordered to head towards Malisheva the next morning.

“When we arrived, Serbian police and paramilitaries had set up a checkpoint. I saw people being killed there. I thought: ‘This is where our lives will end,’” says Sali.

As they travelled through Kosovo, scenes of destruction unfolded around them. “We saw houses burning the entire way. We saw bodies lying by the roadside,” he adds.

A shocking memory that has stayed with him is of a young man trapped beneath his overturned tractor trailer in Rahovec: “I could hear him screaming, but nobody could help him. Today, there is a memorial to him there.”

At the border with Albania, the Serbian police became suspicious of one of Morina’s sons.

“They told me: ‘This one is wounded. Where are you taking him? He’s a KLA soldier.’ I explained that he had a disability and couldn’t walk. I pulled up his legs so they could see,, he says.

That moment remains among Ganimete’s worst memories: “I’ll never forget how my father lifted my brother to show his legs. The policeman narrowed his eyes, lowered his head, and walked away.”

“My older brother walked until he was four,” Ganimete recalls. “Then he developed a fever and was diagnosed with muscular dystrophy. My younger brother was born with the condition. I also walked until I was three or four before developing symptoms. Our other brother and sister do not have the disease.”

After being displaced from their home, their parents had to carry all three children around. “For our family, carrying us was an extra burden compared to everyone else,” she says.

Holding back tears, she says that as a child, “I often thought that maybe it would have been easier if one of us three had died, just to make things easier for our parents.

“What would life have meant for us if our father had been killed?” she asks.

Without their parents, she says, the three children could not have catered to their own most basic needs. “Our parents are irreplaceable,” she observes.

Finding refuge in Albania

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Accused of “Vote-Buying” With Cash Pledges
World.content:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has announced a set of financial payments for all adult citizens in Serbia, alongside subsidies for various groups – leaving critics wondering whether the measures are an attempt at vote-buying.

In early July, Vucic announced during an appearance on RTS that the state would likely provide financial assistance to all citizens aged 18 or older, emphasising that the funds would not come from the state budget. Two weeks later Vucic gave more detail during a Morning programme on TV Prva, announcing two payments for adults scheduled for September.

“Payments will be made to pensioners and to those entitled to benefits under the pensioners’ welfare system. Separate payments will be made to those receiving social benefits. On top of all that, we are also proceeding with this payment from the Share Fund for all adult citizens, which we would not be able to do without adding around 150 million euros from the budget,” Vucic said.

World.title: IVF for Single Women Raises New Conflict of Interest Questions for Czech PM
World.content:
Bringing IVF to single women

The ethics committee’s inconclusive discussions did not prevent Health Minister Vojtech – a member of the ruling ANO party and close ally of Prime Minister Andrej Babis – from continuing to push his draft bill and taking it to the next step for discussion.

Compared with most of Europe, Czechia’s reproductive policies remain relatively strict to this day. It is also one of the few EU member states where women without a male partner cannot access artificial insemination techniques – along with the likes of Slovakia, Poland, Lithuania and Italy – thus making them only available, on paper, to heterosexual couples.

“There is a large group of single women who are secure and would like to have a child, but they cannot legally have one in the Czech Republic,” said Nicole Mardesicova, vice-chairwoman of the assisted reproduction department at the Czech Gynaecological and Obstetrics Society.

The draft amendment, submitted on June 24 for interdepartmental consultation by Health Minister Vojtech together with the government’s human rights commissioner, Tatana Mala, would update the Act on Special Health Services, which many have long criticised as outdated. It states, for example, that “artificial insemination may be performed on a woman of childbearing age… upon a written request from the woman and man who intend to undergo this heath service together.”

In its current form, the reform would merely abolish the requirement for a man’s written permission, opening up assisted reproduction to single women and, implicitly, to lesbian couples.

It would, however, keep other regulations in their current format: only women up to 49 years old can access those services, and public health insurance only covers their reimbursement for women under 40 and for a limited number of attempts.

Based on the Health Ministry’s proposal, women making the request alone would, however, not be covered by health insurance and should cover the costs on a self-pay basis regardless of age or number of attempts. This, in turn, raises another question on whether the access will be de-facto reserved for wealthier women who can afford it.

“There are women who, for various reasons, do not have a partner. What is important to me is that they are here, they are interested, and I do not think that the state should prevent them from having a child if they are able to take care of it,” reasoned Vojtech.

“Moreover, the need to have a partner is already being circumvented: they can come with any acquaintance or friend who declares themselves as their partner, and the centre providing artificial insemination has no way of verifying this,” he added.

World.title: Falling Water Levels on Danube Threaten Serbia’s Electricity Supply
World.content:
The low level of the Danube is especially affecting electricity generation.

However, Dusan Zivkovic, director of the Electric Power Industry of Serbia, EPS, told RTS on Wednesday that the electricity supply was stable – and would remain so.

“This is a period of major challenges, but I would again emphasise that citizens and businesses should not be concerned about the regular supply of electricity,” Zivkovic said.

According to him, electricity generation at the Djerdap hydropower plants has been reduced by the exceptionally low water level, but EPS had prepared the system for such circumstances.

He expects the period of low inflows to continue, partly because of limited snowfall in the Alps during the last winter as well as more recent weather.

World.title: Turkey Submits Long-waited PKK Disarmament Law to Parliament
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament received a long-awaited framework law on Wednesday aimed at providing the legal basis for disarming the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party, PKK, and regulating the judicial procedures for people linked to it, marking the most comprehensive legislative step yet to end the four-decade-long conflict.

Ruling AKP Group Chairman Abdullah Guler said the proposal should not be seen as an amnesty but as a legal framework for managing the post-disarmament process.

“The legislation is intended to place the process on a clear legal footing, while preserving Turkey’s fight against terrorism and ensuring that all measures are implemented under the rule of law,” Guler said.

The “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration” was submitted to the Grand National Assembly with the signatures of 360 lawmakers.

Support came from the ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, its nationalist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party, MHP, the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the pro-Kurdish and Islamist HUDA PAR, some MPs from the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, members of the New Path parliamentary group and several independents.

The draft law lays out the legal framework for the post-disarmament process, including temporary judicial provisions for eligible people convicted of, or investigated over, PKK-related offences.

It includes mechanisms such as supervised release, sentence postponement and judicial supervision under specified conditions following the organisation’s dissolution and disarmament.

The draft stipulates that its provisions would take effect only after Turkey’s National Security Council, MGK, determines that the PKK and its affiliated structures have fully disbanded and surrendered all weapons

Under Turkey’s constitution, 400 votes in parliament are required for the law to be adopted directly, while support from 360 lawmakers would be sufficient to send the proposal to a nationwide referendum.

The government has made clear it wants the legislation enacted by parliament rather than through a public vote.

But not all the parties support the initiative. The Good Party and Victory Party have declared opposition to the legislation.

The New Welfare Party has called for the proposal to be put to a referendum, while the New Party, recently established as Turkey’s new main opposition party, has yet to announce its position. With parliament seeking broader support, its stance is being closely watched.

The legislation follows political developments that began earlier. In February 2025, jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to lay down its arms. His appeal followed an unexpected peace initiative by Devlet Bahceli, leader of the MHP, a key ally of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s AKP.

The initiative led to the establishment of a parliamentary commission and regular visits to Ocalan by a delegation from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party. The new framework law is regarded as the closest Turkey has come to establishing a comprehensive legal basis for ending the decades-long conflict.

More than 40,000 people have been killed since fighting between the PKK and Turkish security forces began after Ocalan founded the group in 1984.

The vote on the bill is expected to take place after the summer recess, in autumn.

World.title: Kosovo’s Kurti Urged to Share Power, to Avoid New Polls
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku (first left) and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti meet in Pristina, July 10, 2026. Photo: Albin Kurti/Facebook

Kosovo opposition parties urged incumbent Prime Minister Albin Kurti to give them a greater share in upcoming institutions – if he wants to avoid new snap elections.

Ramush Haradinaj, an MP for the Alliance, formerly the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, AAK, told the media on Wednesday that in order to solve the current impasse over the next President, Kurti has to reach a political compromise.

“The [election] result demands joint decision making,” Haradinaj said one day before the new parliament, elected in June snap polls, holds its inaugural session.

“One of main posts, Prime Minister or President, belongs to the opposition parties. The election winner should read the election result this way,” he added.

In the June 7 elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje Movement won 53 of the 120 seats, down four from the last December 2025 election, but well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22 seats. The Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, which is Kurti’s most likely coalition partner, won 18 seats.

A repeat of the parliamentary deadlock that paralysed the country for much of 2025, when no party had enough seats to elect parliamentary officials and form a government, has likely been avoided – but only when it comes to the election of a speaker and a government, for which the winning party needs only a bare minimum of 61 votes.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority to form the next government by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serbs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 snap elections has not been solved; the parties still need to come to an agreement to elect a new President. Failure to do this within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament would trigger another election.

“Kurti is seeking all the main posts and decision-making institutions for himself and is aiming to humiliate the opposition by offering them only participation in the government. This is not what voters have decided, this is the logic of a regime. Leaders of totalitarian regimes are afraid of shared decision making. I think the opposition can help in forming the institutions, but there should be joint decision making,” Haradinaj said.

His comments came a day after Kurti met LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku in an attempt to find an agreement on forming new institutions. The meeting ended without a deal – but both sides sounded cautiously optimistic.

“We are ready to avoid the new elections at any price … Kosovo needs institutional stability, more work and not political drama,” Abdixhiku said, referring to the political deadlock that brought the country three elections in 16 months.

However, Abdixhiku sounded reluctant to take the post of parliamentary speaker for his party in return for supporting Vetevendosje’s candidate for President.

“The LDK has no appetite for [the post of] speaker, which is more of a ceremonial figure and should be proposed by the biggest party [Vetevendosje],” he said.

On the other hand, Kurti said there was still a will “to work together” with the LDK in future. “No one wants new elections but if we don’t have an agreement, if we don’t move ahead, they can unfortunately happen despite the lack of a wish [for them],” Kurti said

“We need a political agreement which respects the elections result – and is not a substitute for it,” Kurti added.

World.title: Croatia’s Operation Storm in Pictures, 31 Years On: Homes Restored, Fewer People
World.content:
Storm was not only a legitimate liberation operation led by Croatia’s first president, Franjo Tudjman, Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said at the central ceremony marking the anniversary of Operation Storm.

It was also, he added, an action that saved Bihac in northwest Bosnia and Herzegovina from a looming humanitarian catastrophe, changed the balance of power in Bosnia and paved the way for peace and the Dayton Agreement, which ended the 1992-5 war in Bosnia.

Croatia is neither engaged in an arms race nor threatening anyone, Plenkovic continued. However, “We are not afraid of anyone” and “will know how to respond to any threat” he warned.

He stressed that Croatia would never again be unprepared or unprotected, guided by the principle: “If we want peace, we must be able to defend it.”

Plenkovic said Croatia was not alone in this effort as it is a member of NATO. He stressed that investing in defence is not preparation for war but an investment in the security of the country, its homes, schools and factories. Such investments, he said, also strengthen investor confidence and make Croatia a more attractive place to live and work.

To compare the wartime landscape with the present day, BIRN set out to recreate photographs taken on August 5 and 6, 1995, with the help of two photographers.

One of them, artistic and documentary photographer Zeljko Gasparovic, 72, from Novska, volunteered during Croatia’s War of Independence and never parted with his camera. As a result, he built one of the largest private photographic archives documenting the war.

All photos can be slid left and right to compare the past and present.

World.title: EU Caught Between Child Protection and Privacy With Encryption Rules
World.content:
Sasa Mrdovic, Professor of Computer Networks at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering of the University of Sarajevo, said from a technical perspective it is difficult to clearly determine which communications should be exempted from encryption protection – i.e. to enable their decryption for the purpose of detecting criminal offences, including the most serious forms, such as child sexual abuse.

He explained that the fundamental characteristic of end-to-end encryption is precisely that the content of a communication can only be read by the end users participating in the conversation.

He added that removing encryption, or enabling access to communications, would raise additional questions regarding jurisdiction and security.

He recalled that such an approach was simpler in traditional communication systems. In order to intercept communications, postal services or telecommunications providers could grant access, and law enforcement agencies, with court orders, could obtain access to telephone conversations.

Modern digital communications operate differently.

“Here, because the infrastructure through which communications are transmitted is not under the control of a state, institution, or a single organisation, it is much more complicated to find a way to enable lawful access to communications while at the same time not compromising the privacy and security of all users,” Mrdovic concluded.

Agovic Djozo said a more effective approach to detecting and combating online material depicting child sexual abuse requires action at multiple points in the system before such content reaches private encrypted communications.

In her view, technology companies must apply the principle of “safety by design”, meaning they should assess risks and build protective measures before products are launched on the market.

Instead of focusing solely on private messages, efforts should also target the services, platforms, and infrastructure that enable the production and distribution of illegal content.

As an example, she cites the Internet Watch Foundation, IWF, which identified AI-generated child sexual abuse material on a hidden version of a chatbot site where users could select sexualized personas and generate additional images.

She noted that financial investigations can play an important role in combating commercial networks that distribute child sexual abuse material.

According to her, data from the company Chainalysis shows that commercial CSAM networks use subscription models and cryptocurrencies, but the public and permanent nature of blockchain transactions can enable the tracking of payments, the linking of addresses, and the identification of infrastructure.

In one case, according to those findings, a network was identified involving more than 5,800 crypto addresses and over $530,000 in received payments.

Additional measures include simpler content reporting, more effective removal of known CSAM, digital forensics, international data sharing, specialized investigative teams, victim support, and preventive education for children and parents.

BIRN also requested a comment from Meta, but no response was received by the time of publication.

World.title: Danube Recedes, Shipping Stopped: “Water Level Has Never Been This Low”
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – The Danube has receded so much that shipping has had to be stopped, with experts claiming that the river’s water level has never been this low.

An extremely low water level on the Danube has seriously hindered navigation near Vukovar in recent days. Some ships can no longer continue their journey, cargo vessels are stranded, and Croatia’s largest river port has had almost no traffic for ten days. Index reports that the water level of the Danube near Vukovar has dropped to minus 60 centimetres. In some sections of the fairway the river is only about 1.2 metres deep, forcing ships to reduce their cargo or stop sailing altogether.

The low water has exposed sandbanks, rocks and other underwater obstacles that are normally hidden at usual river levels. “We’ve now got to watch out for all the sandbanks, for the rocks – for all the underwater obstacles that until now were under water and inaccessible. Now, unfortunately, we keep having problems with them,” said Saša Piljaš, president of the Dunav Vukovar Sport Fishing Association, as reported by HRT.

two cargo vessels are stranded not far from erdut

The problems first affected smaller boats and are now making navigation difficult even for the largest vessels. “The fairway should be at least two metres deep for it to be worthwhile for shippers to transport cargo. Anything below that means sailing at reduced capacity, so profitability becomes questionable,” said Borna Čerina, head of the Navigation Safety Service at the Vukovar Port Authority. A cruise ship has been moored in Vukovar for a week, while two cargo ships are stranded near Erdut.

“In the fairway near the village of Erdut we have two cargo ships that ran aground a few days ago and are still sitting there. They will either have to lighten their load or wait for the water level to rise,” Čerina said.

no navigation at the port of vukovar for ten days

The consequences of the low water level are also being felt by the Port of Vukovar. In recent weeks shippers were still arriving with almost half the usual cargo, but even that traffic has now stopped.

“Over the last ten days we’ve had no navigability at all. All the barges are anchored either in their ports or in certain areas, waiting for a better draught,” said Marijan Kuprešak, director of the Port of Vukovar. If the water level does not rise soon, the port could lose a large part of its contracted traffic. “Partners who signed contracts with us were supposed to move around 200,000 tonnes of goods through the Port of Vukovar over the next three months – a significant tonnage for the port and significant revenue. It is now questionable whether the partners will organise some other form of transport, by cargo or by truck,” Kuprešak emphasised.

“I’ve never seen anything like this”

Retired port captain Ivan Barović, who worked on the Danube for more than 20 years, said he had never experienced a situation like this before. “There have been ice blockages around Dalj, and there have been high water levels when we had flooding at this spot. But the water level has never been this low,” Barović said.

The Danube is navigable almost all year round, and interruptions until now have mostly been caused by ice or floods. Such a prolonged suspension of navigation near Vukovar, according to Barović, has not been recorded before. “Captains have to use all their knowledge to bring ships safely into port. It’s another matter how profitable it is to load a ship to only 50 percent of its draught so it can pass certain sections,” he said. He warned that conditions like these may not remain an isolated case.

“I’m afraid we can’t be too optimistic, but we have to take certain steps. This is a situation where we have drought here and floods in some other area,” he stressed. The lowest water level ever measured on the Danube closr to Vukovar was recorded about a hundred years ago and stood at minus 110 centimetres.

World.title: Will Croatia Have Enough Electricity and Water?
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Prolonged drought, the absence of heavier rainfall and high temperatures have seriously affected Croatian rivers, springs and pumping stations. Will Croatia actually have enough electricity and water?

As Domagoj Puljizovic reports for Poslovni, the Danube and Drava have dropped to record low levels, inflows on the coast and islands have decreased significantly, and electricity production in hydropower plants has weakened.

Despite the challenges, the director-general of Croatian Waters (Hrvatske vode), Zoran Đuroković, says that the water supply for the population is not currently under threat. The water level of the Sava has fallen to –298 cm, while historical minima have been broken on the Danube and Drava. Due to unfavourable hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK) will gradually reduce reactor power to 80 percent during the night of 6 August.

This is a planned measure to ensure that the average daily temperature of the Sava does not exceed 28 °C and that the average daily temperature rise remains within three degrees. NEK has been operating continuously for 280 days since its overhaul in November 2025; if conditions worsen, power will be reduced further. The last time NEK operated at reduced power because of Sava temperature and flow was in 2003.

recovery won’t happen quickly

“There is no doubt that Croatia will have enough electricity,” Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said on Tuesday, adding that there is “no threat whatsoever” regarding NEK. Turning back to water supply:

“The situation is quite serious. This is already a prolonged low-water period,” Đuroković told HRT, warning that a rapid recovery cannot be expected. The Danube at Batina has fallen to –144 cm, surpassing the minimum recorded as far back as 1909. A historically low level has also been measured on the Drava, where the previous record of –172 cm has been exceeded with a drop to –192 cm. High water temperatures are also a problem.

The situation is even more sensitive on the coast, islands and karst areas. The long period without rain has reduced the yield of springs and pumping stations, prompting many water utilities to call on citizens and businesses to use water rationally.

“Inflows there are already greatly reduced, so capacities are being cut,” Đuroković said. In some areas pressure drops in the network are being recorded, but water supply remains stable. Conservation measures are being introduced and the use of water for irrigation, filling swimming pools and other non-essential purposes is being restricted, but the basic needs of the population are not currently threatened.

In Lika the situation is relatively stable, although the yield of some springs has decreased, particularly in the Brinje area. Đuroković warned that the disappearance of the snow cover has eliminated an important natural water-storage source for Lika watercourses.

Continental Croatia is currently in a more favourable position thanks to groundwater and large river systems. “There will be no shortages on the continent. The situation is quite good,” he said. Zagreb’s Water Supply and Sewerage company (ViO) also says there is no cause for concern, stating that water extraction in the city area is proceeding without difficulty.

“In the City of Zagreb, water extraction is taking place smoothly and there are currently no indications of possible disruptions in water supply,” ViO emphasised. The city company stresses that it continuously invests in the new network and maintenance of existing infrastructure and is implementing an action plan to reduce water losses, which last year amounted to 55 percent. They add that their water inspection service checks cases of illegal connections, and citizens can report suspicions of unauthorised water use to vodno.redarstvo@zgh.hr.

Croatian Waters has intensified monitoring and sent water-warden services into the field. Special attention is focused on smaller watercourses, which become sensitive to pollution due to low flow and high temperatures.

“Any inflow of pollution into these small rivers can cause ecological incidents,” Đuroković warned, calling on cities, municipal companies and economic entities to carefully treat wastewater. Recovery of water levels is not expected in the next five to seven days. The drought is already affecting hydropower plants, especially those on the Drava, where production has been reduced due to weaker inflows.

Croatian Waters and HEP are coordinating the use of available water so as not to endanger the biological minimum in the rivers. In Istria the key role is played by the Butoniga reservoir, which is currently sufficiently full. Larger restrictions are not expected there, but citizens are still being urged to use water rationally.

no reductions… for now, anyway

Istrian Water Supply and Sewerage Buzet has warned users in the areas of Vižinada, Kaštelir-Labinci, Višnjan, Tinjan and parts of Poreč and Kanfanar to immediately limit irrigation of green areas and washing of yards, and that if consumption is not reduced the first degree of restriction could be introduced. Vodovod Pula-Labin, which supplies the Pula and Labin areas and part of central Istria, says that water supply is regular and that reductions are not currently planned.

HEP: We’ll secure electricity from our own sources and by purchasing

In the event of a halt in production from the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK), Hrvatska elektroprivreda (HEP) would secure the necessary quantities of electricity through production from its own available generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities on the wholesale market, HEP told Hina on Wednesday.

“In the event of a halt in production from NE Krško, HEP would secure the necessary quantities of electricity by engaging production from other available own generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities of electricity on the wholesale market,” HEP stated.

The Ministry of Economy, responsible for energy, says that the Croatian and Slovenian governments are taking all necessary activities to ensure that the Krško Nuclear Power Plant continues to operate stably and safely even under conditions of high Sava River temperatures.

“We are in constant communication with the Slovenian side and jointly monitoring the development of the situation, with the aim of preserving the security of electricity production and supply,” the ministry told Hina. NEK reported on Wednesday that due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, it will begin operating at 80 percent reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026, and will announce a return to full power when conditions allow.

“Due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava River, NEK will, as announced, begin a gradual reduction of reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026. In the first step, power will be reduced to 80 percent,” NEK reported on Wednesday.

This is a planned and controlled temporary measure necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Environmental Consent (OVS), according to which the daily average temperature of the Sava River at the point of complete mixing downstream of the Brežice Hydropower Plant must not exceed 28 degrees Celsius, and the average daily temperature rise must not be greater than three degrees.

World.title: Đurđenovac: The Small Croatian Town That Was Once a European Industrial Giant
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Đurđenovac is a small, overlooked Croatian town that not only used to have almost 600 kilometres of railway tracks, but was once a European industrial giant.

Situated far from anywhere that often ever gets a mention, Đurđenovac isn’t somewhere splashed across the glossy pages of travel mags. Turning the pages of the history book back, however, we’ll see that it was once booming. It actually grew alongside a sawmill and a tannin factory, gained workers’ colonies, schools and a kindergarten, and became the first electrified place in all of Slavonia.

If you walk through Đurđenovac today, Putni kofer reveals that you’ll mostly hear little else other than birdsong and the occasional passing car. About a hundred years ago, however, the sounds there were completely different. Through the dense old forests around the town, locomotives rumbled day and night, hauling logs to a factory that was one of the strongest industrial hearts of this part of Europe. According to publicly available data from the Croatian Technical Encyclopaedia, in 1929 the factory in Đurđenovac operated a narrow-gauge forest railway an astonishing 582 kilometres long. To put that in perspective, it is roughly the same as the straight-line distance from Zagreb to Sarajevo and back. Along that network ran a whole small army of trains, and the local company’s rolling stock numbered 61 locomotives and as many as 2,800 wagons.

it all began with a businessman from austria…

To understand all this better, we have to go back to the distant year of 1866, when the Viennese entrepreneur Josip Pfeiffer, after reaching an agreement with the landowner Ladislav Pejačević on the exploitation of the forests, built a steam sawmill in Đurđenovac. Over several decades and several changes of ownership, a tannin factory (a substance essential for leather processing) was added to the sawmill in 1889. From 1895 the company operated as Neuschloß’s Našice Tannin Factory and Steam Sawmill, later known simply as Našička.

As the factory eventually grew, so did the town around it. Đurđenovac developed into a purpose-built industrial town with workers’ colonies, schools, a post office, a kindergarten and a workers’ club. It was so far ahead of its time that it became the first electrified place in Slavonia. In as early as 1891, the factory received electric lighting, and by 1917, electricity had reached every apartment in the town.

Hundreds of kilometres of track led deep into Papuk and Krndija

All of this needed to be fed with wood, almost constantly, and in enormous quantities. That’s why, in parallel with the factory, a narrow-gauge railway developed that pushed out from Đurđenovac deep into the surrounding forests of Papuk, Krndija and beyond. The little trains climbed the slopes, hauled logs to the sawmill and tannin works, and then returned empty for a new load. Year after year the network was extended until by 1929 it had grown to the aforementioned 582 kilometres.

At that time the company was part of a holding with its headquarters in Geneva, with branches in Romania, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Austria, and offices in Belgrade, Sombor, Rijeka, Zurich and Milan. In its best days, up to the Second World War, more than 10,000 people worked for the firm as a whole, of whom around 1,400 were in Đurđenovac itself. For a Slavonia town, those numbers sound almost unreal today.

an entire railway system simply vanished…

“Everything that grows must one day stop,” says an old folk saying. In the middle of the twentieth century, trucks increasingly took over the transport of wood from the forests; they were faster and cheaper than tracks that needed constant maintenance. Forest railways thus gradually lost their purpose, and those in and around Đurđenovac were dismantled during the 1960s. Rails and sleepers were pulled out of the ground, and many of the old alignments were turned into the roads we drive on today, often without realising that a locomotive once ran there.

After the Second World War the company operated under various names, first as the Tannin Factory and Steam Sawmill, then as DIP, and finally as DIK Đurđenovac. It ran into business difficulties at the beginning of the 1990s, and bankruptcy was declared back in 1994. DIK ceased operations in 2007, although some successors continued wood processing in parts of the former facilities. The cultural-historical complex of Đurđenovac is today protected and entered in the Register of Cultural Goods of the Republic of Croatia.

World.title: Veteran Recalls the Moment Operation Storm Began
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – On the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, Croatian veteran Ivan Mikulić recalls the moments when he and his fellow soldiers realised that a major operation was about to begin – even before they knew its name.

Mikulić, a member of the 3rd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, spoke about the days that changed the course of the war and the emotions surrounding Croatia’s advance toward Knin. At the time, soldiers on the ground had not been officially told that Operation Storm was beginning, but many sensed that something extremely significant was approaching.

“Our unit was in Donji Kazanci, on the Livno–Grahovo route. On August the 3rd, we were moved to Pržine, near Grahovo, to a peat factory. At that point, we concluded that an operation could begin in the morning, even though we knew nothing about Storm. But as soon as we were moved there, we knew we were going forward in the morning,” Mikulić recalled.

When artillery fire began around 05:00 on August the 4th, the uncertainty entirely disappeared. “There was a sense of anxiety and excitement among the soldiers. People had already heard that the operation was definitely starting. When the artillery barrage began, there was an explosion of sheer joy. Some even raised a toast,” he said.

The long Road to Knin

Mikulić also remembers the moment his unit entered Knin and moved toward the city’s famous fortress. The soldiers did not immediately enter the fortress area, as security positions had already been established ahead of them and some units encountered delays along the way. “We reached the fortress and stopped there. We sat down on the wall,” he recalled.

Soon, local residents began approaching the soldiers and offering them refreshments.

“The beer had already arrived, Karlovačko had already reached the fortress. However, it was no longer possible to actually enter the fortress,” Mikulić said. At that moment, the Croatian flag had not yet been raised on the fortress, but the approach had already been secured.

A Victory Marked by Sacrifice

Despite the intense heat and the expectation of heavy fighting, the battle in Knin did not unfold as many soldiers had anticipated.

“We expected a fight, but there wasn’t one because they had all fled. It was complete and utter chaos. There were civilians hanging around in the city itself as well, but overall everything went well,” Mikulić said. However, victory came with a heavy price. He noted that the 4th Guards Brigade lost four soldiers in Knin itself.

memories that will remain forever

Over three decades later, Mikulić says the memories of those days remain vivid and clear.

During the war, he served on many fronts, from Kruševo and Zadar to Dubrovnik and Mostar. “I lost many friends, and that cannot be forgotten. It really wasn’t that long ago,” he said. As Croatia remembers Operation Storm, stories from veterans like Mikulić serve as a reminder that behind the historic images of victory were the experiences, sacrifices, and personal memories of the people who lived through those defining moments.

World.title: Remembering Three Young Croatian Soldiers Who Fell in the Final Battle of Operation Storm
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – As we mark the 31st anniversary of one of the most important events in modern Croatian history, we remember the thousands of defenders who fought for freedom. That includes three young Croatian soldiers of the 4th Guards Brigade who tragically lost their lives in the very final hours of Operation Storm.

Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera all lost their lives killed on the 5th of August, 1995, in a small hamlet not far from Golubić, as Croatian forces advanced toward Knin and the final victory of Operation Storm. Their deaths came on the very day when the operation was reaching its historic conclusion, a reminder that even in the final moments of victory, Croatian soldiers continued to face fierce fighting and sacrifice.

The Final Battle Near Knin

Ante Brekalo, commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, led the advance across Dinara toward Knin. When his unit reached Golubić, they encountered very strong resistance.

“I was honoured to have such men in my company, men I could lead,” Brekalo later recalled. He said the three young soldiers lost their lives during intense close combat. Miroslav Vođera, who had previously served in the Yugoslav Army before joining the Croatian Army, was killed near a house during the fighting. His fellow soldier Ivica Bošnjak remembered him as a true example of what a soldier should be.

“His life ended only a few hours before it was announced that everything was free,” Bošnjak said. He also recalled the intensity of the battle, describing how fighting continued with gunfire and grenades exchanged between the two sides. Vođera, he said, attempted to call for surrender but was killed while trying to enter the building.

Remembering Young Comrades

Miro Moro was among those who discovered the bodies of Stipan Dundović and Ivan Svalina. These three soldiers were only 20, 22, and 23 years old. Moro, who had witnessed many difficult moments during the war, said that this particular memory remained especially painful. He especially remembered Svalina, a young man from his own village.

“That was a child from my village. That morning I saw him with a smile on his face,” Moro recalled. Svalina had joined the unit as a teenager, and his commanders remembered him as a cheerful, friendly and very dependable soldier. Brekalo described him as someone who always helped others and inspired confidence among his fellow soldiers. “He was a true fighter who never, ever left anyone behind,” he said.

A Tradition of Remembrance

Every year on the anniversary of Operation Storm, veterans gather at the site where the three soldiers fell, where a memorial has been built in their honour. Veterans from across the region, including Zadar, Split, Sinj, Imotski, Šibenik, and parts of neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, come together to remember them.

They also honour other fallen defenders from those final days, including Dražen Kuduz, who died in an accident on the approach to Knin on the same day. “They will never be forgotten for as long as we’re alive,” said Josip Bebek, president of the Association of Veterans of the 4th Guards Brigade in Šibenik-Knin County.

A Legacy That Lives On

In Crivac, the hometown of Ivan Svalina, the memory of their youngest fallen soldier remains especially strong.

Around 150 residents of the small village joined the Homeland War, almost half of the local population at the time. Svalina was the youngest from the village to lose his life. His sister Marija Vučić said losing him left a permanent emptiness. She and her other sister also served during the war, spending four years on front lines across Croatia, from Zadar to Dubrovnik. A monument dedicated to Ivan Svalina was unveiled in the centre of the village last year, created by sculptor Petar Melvan. His fellow soldiers plan to visit it every year in remembrance.

For those who knew them, Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera represent more than names from history, they are remembered as young men whose courage and sacrifice became part of Croatia’s story of independence. The Municipality of Muć also plans to open a memorial room this autumn dedicated to all those from the area who lost their lives during the Homeland War and Croatia’s fierce struggle for independence.

World.title: 31 Years Since Operation Storm: Veterans Recall the Battle for Knin and the Moment History Changed
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – 31 years have passed since Operation Storm (Oluja) altered the course of the Croatian War of Independence, and veterans have recalled the fierce battle for Knin.

Today, Croatia marks Victory and Homeland Thanksgiving Day, the Day of Croatian Defenders, and the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, the military and police operation that became a turning point in the country’s modern history. Launched on August the 4th, 1995, Operation Storm saw Croatian forces manage to regain control of areas that had been held by rebel Serb forces, opening the path toward the final stages of the Homeland War.

Over three decades later, those who took part in the operation continue to remember the days that changed the course of Croatia’s modern history. Among them is Perica Prpić, president of the Association of Special Police Units from the Homeland War “Sharks”, who recalled the moments before the operation began while stationed with fellow soldiers on Velebit Mountain.

He remembers hearing the announcement from Croatia’s first president, Franjo Tuđman, before the operation began, while artillery fire could already be heard in the distance. “The moment I remember the call from President Tuđman, I still get goosebumps. We heard the artillery preparation in the distance. It had begun. You cross yourself, hug your fellow soldier, and start moving down Velebit. It’s just a unique feeling when you know there’s no turning back now,” Prpić said in an earlier interview.

The Battle for the “Igla” Position

Josip Bebek, a member of the 4th Guards Brigade who participated in Operation Storm, also recalled the beginning of the operation.

His unit advanced toward Knin from the direction of Bosansko Grahovo in the early hours of August 4, but encountered heavy resistance along the way. The obstacle was a strategically important hill known as “Igla” (“Needle”), which was held by rebel Serb forces. “We got about halfway there and then we stopped. We faced strong resistance. They held a position called Igla. It was extremely difficult to capture. Once we took Igla, everything moved forward more smoothly,” Bebek recalled. Taking control of that position became a key moment in the advance toward Knin.

Entering Knin

The following morning, after artillery preparation, Croatian forces entered Knin. “We literally walked into Knin,” Bebek said, describing the city at the time. He recalled that the city was largely empty and that his unit encountered no significant resistance after entering. “The 7th and 4th Guards Brigades never killed anyone, there was no resistance, and thankfully there was no need for it,” he said.

Bebek also remembers a personal encounter that stayed with him. He helped an elderly man and brought him to the military barracks, where he was later able to choose whether to remain in Knin or leave for Serbia. “I don’t know what he eventually decided, but later I met his brother, who actually told me their life story,” he said.

From Adrenaline to unbelievable levels of Pride

Although 31 years have passed since Operation Storm, Bebek says the emotions connected to those days remain strong and the memories vivid. “The dream of every Croatian soldier was to reach Knin. After every liberation operation we were happy, but we knew entering Knin would mean the end. That was the finish line,” he said.

At the time, he remembers the feeling of adrenaline and youthful determination. Today, those memories are replaced by pride and gratitude. “When I think about it today, I feel happiness and tears still fill my eyes with pride. We have our own country; we achieved that dream. May God ensure this never, ever happens to anyone again,” Bebek said.

After the war, Bebek remained a professional soldier. In 2003, he moved from Split to Knin, where he still lives today. For him, life in Knin is now simply everyday life.

As Croatia marks 31 years since Operation Storm, veterans continue to remember not only the military victory, but also the experiences, sacrifices, and personal stories behind one of the most significant events in the country’s history.

World.title: Croatia to Experience Peak Heat on Thursday With Temperatures Up to 42 Degrees
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – Croatia is currently under a particularly strong heat dome, with the peak of that heat set to beat down on the country on Thursday. In some areas, the temperatures could reach a dizzying 42 degrees.

Index reports that a very powerful “heat dome” traps extremely hot air over southern and southeastern parts of the continent. According to meteorologists from Severe Weather Europe, the hottest conditions are expected over the Balkans, Italy, Greece, and parts of the western Mediterranean, with some locations forecast to reach or exceed 42 degrees.

For Croatia, the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue climbing through the week, with Thursday expected to be the peak of the heatwave. Inland parts of the country face the highest temperatures, potentially approaching 42 degrees, while the Adriatic coast will also experience very hot weather, although sea breezes should keep coastal temperatures somewhat lower than inland areas.

a high pressure system from north africa

The extreme heat is being driven by a strong high-pressure system stretching from North Africa into southern and central Europe. This atmospheric pattern allows very warm air from the Sahara to spread northward while preventing cooler Atlantic air from moving into the region. As a result, the hot weather is expected to persist for several days.

Meteorologists warn that the prolonged high temperatures significantly increase health risks, especially for older adults, young children, and people with chronic medical conditions. Authorities advise people to stay hydrated, avoid all kinds of more strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, seek shade or air-conditioned spaces whenever and wherever possible, and check on vulnerable family members and neighbours.

The article also highlights an increased wildfire risk all across southern Europe. The combination of extreme heat, dry vegetation, and periods of gusty winds creates conditions where fires can ignite easily and spread rapidly. Fire services across several Mediterranean countries remain on heightened alert.

a colder front is coming!

Looking beyond the peak heat, the forecast suggests that a cold front will begin moving into central Europe later in the week, bringing thunderstorms to some regions and a noticeable drop in temperatures. Croatia is expected to see this change after Thursday, although forecasters caution that any storms accompanying the front could be locally severe, with heavy rain, strong wind gusts, hail, and frequent lightning possible.

Overall, the article’s main message is that Thursday is expected to be the most dangerous day of the current heatwave in Croatia, with temperatures possibly reaching 42 degrees in some inland areas before a cooler, more unstable weather pattern arrives later in the week.

World.title: Bizarre Medieval “Vampire” Found in Pakrac Cemetery
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – An extremely bizarre Medieval “vampire” has been found in a Pakrac cemetery, with archaeologists believing that the particular method of burial was to “prevent the vampire returning among the living”.

Index reports that a very mysterious medieval burial discovered at the Stari Grad Pakrac archaeological site has once again brought attention to ancient beliefs about vampires and the fear of the dead returning among the living. Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a person buried face down, an unusual burial position that experts believe may have been an intentional ritual. According to archaeologist Krešimir Vacek, the way the body was placed suggests that people of the time wanted to prevent the deceased from returning after death.

The “vampire” burial likely dates back to the late 13th century and was found at a medieval cemetery connected with the former settlement around Stari Grad Pakrac. Archaeologists have been researching the site for years, uncovering numerous graves and important historical remains.

This is not the first unusual discovery of its kind at the location. Earlier excavations revealed another so-called “vampire” burial, a skeleton inside a valuable sarcophagus that was missing its human head. Instead, researchers found animal remains believed to be part of a horse skull. Such practices were linked to medieval beliefs that certain people could return from the grave and harm the living.

In medieval Europe, fears of supernatural forces were widespread, and communities sometimes carried out unusual burial practices when they believed someone could become a threat after death. The latest discovery in Pakrac offers another rare insight into the beliefs, fears, and rituals of people who lived more than 800 years ago.

World.title: Estonian sprinter break and re-breaks national U20 100m record in Oregon
World.content:
Petrogradov in fact broke and then rebroke the record on day one at the ongoing World U20 Athletics Championships in Eugene, Oregon.

He clocked 10.37 seconds in the heats, securing a place in the semifinals and breaking his own PB and the domestic record of 10.43, set just two weeks earlier at the national Championships in Pärnu.

In the semifinal a few hours later, the Estonian continued his strong form and ran 10.31 seconds in the semifinal, placing him 10th overall and bringing a new national record again.

Of the other over a dozen Estonians taking part in Oregon, Miia Ott clocked a season-best 11.64 seconds, which placed her 30th in the girls' 100 meters, Allika Inkeri Moser advanced to the final after clearing 4.10 meters in the pole vault, Katarina Versti came 24th in the girls' discus with a throw of 46.47 meters, and Mia Uusorg, competing in the girls' heptathlon, set a personal best of 13.71 seconds in the 100-meter hurdles and in the shot put with 11.33 meters. and was in ninth place by the end of the day one, while Annika Põlluaas finished 21st in the heptathlon's first day.

The championships run to Sunday.

World.title: Minister drops plans for up to €100m in state child healthcare funding
World.content:
Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller (Reform) has dropped plans to seek tens of millions of euros from the state budget to cover free child healthcare, leaving the issue to the next administration.

A previous plan had been to obtain €50–100 million a year from the state budget to go towards child healthcare at a time when the state Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa) is facing budgeting pressure.

At the end of April this year, Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller presented the government with her own ideas on how to rescue the Health Insurance Fund from its long-term financial difficulties.

Joller's main proposal was that in the first year — 2029 — the state would pay an additional €51 million to the Health Insurance Fund on behalf of children. The contribution would then increase each year, reaching €109 million annually by 2032 to cover children's healthcare costs.

Workforce covers healthcare costs for as many people again

Estonia's healthcare system is, as things stand, financed almost entirely through the social tax paid on the wages of working people by the employer. However, working people only make up around half the total number of people entitled to free health cover.

Children and young people under the age of 19 are, of course, entitled to free healthcare, including expensive dental treatment, despite no social tax contributions being paid on their behalf.

Minister Joller proposed in spring that the workforce should no longer have to finance the country's entire healthcare bill — especially children's treatment — through social tax contributions alone. Under this plan, from 2029 the state would start making additional payments from the state budget to the Health Insurance Fund to cover child healthcare.

The Health Insurance Fund continues to face a major financial shortfall. According to its original forecast, this year's budget is expected to end more than €100 million in the red, while in the coming years the fund will also have to draw on reserves accumulated in previous years.

In April this year, the Ministry of Social Affairs gave its assessment that, thanks to the worsening economic outlook, it is no longer certain that the reserves will last to 2029 as initially forecast. It noted that if the situation develops in line with the Ministry of Finance's spring economic forecast, the 2029 deficit will also be almost 50 percent larger than previously expected.

Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) headquarters in Central Tallinn. Source: Madis Mumma/ERR

The material Joller presented to the government acknowledged that, given the current state of the budget and the focus on security spending, finding additional money for healthcare would be difficult, but argued that investing in people's health is also an investment in the economy and national security.

Minister leaves decision to next administration

Joller has now abandoned the proposal. At this fall's state budget strategy negotiations she will not be requesting state funds for that purpose, and has effectively left the decision to the next administration.

"The decision on this allocation will have to be made sooner or later. [...] Let the next government decide," the minister said.

While the government's website still contains the agenda for the April 30 cabinet meeting where the proposal was discussed, the description focuses primarily on funding children's healthcare from the state budget. Joller now says it was one of several proposals submitted to the government.

"It wasn't my main proposal this spring—it just may have caught your eye," she told ERR.

Joller did not answer ERR's question about the response her proposal received from the cabinet, noting only that each minister was allowed to present three priorities during the state budget strategy talks.

Funding on tech innovation still sought

One of the priorities for which the minister says she will be seeking funding this autumn is expanding the training capacity for doctors and nurses, as well as increasing the number of medical residents. According to the minister, this would cost the state between €5 million and €8 million per year.

"If we don't deal with this, we won't get anywhere. The second issue I'll be pursuing is focusing on digital innovation—whether we can, for example, introduce artificial intelligence into healthcare," the minister said.

A waiting room at North Estonia Medical Center (PERH). Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Joller said she still wants €20 million a year from the state budget strategy from the year after next for healthcare digital innovation, saying the money should maintain the health information system instead of relying on the Health Insurance Fund until 2028. Her proposal is based on think tank the Foresight Center's "digital hope" scenario, which found that while upfront costs would initially exceed the benefits, the investment could deliver significant long-term efficiency gains.

Other input from Joller in April included criticism of significantly increasing the role of private healthcare insurance, and her ministry has also highlighted studies which show healthcare systems based on universal health insurance and solidarity in risk-bearing generally provide better access to healthcare services and greater health equality across population groups. Strongly promoting private insurance could create a parallel healthcare system which would divide society into those who could get top-notch services and those who would see a decline in service quality.

Also, private health insurance is often purchased by professionals, often younger people, and so does not correlate to those with the greatest healthcare needs, the ministry said. Increasing patients' out-of-pocket payments is not seen as the way forward either.

The ministry's conclusion was that private funding could be directed in a way that better supports prevention and health promotion.

As employers can currently provide up to €400 per year in tax-free health promotion benefits, a figure unchanged in almost a decade, the ministry noted that three-quarters of the money is spent on private insurance and medical services rather than prevention. Joller had also proposed reviewing the tax incentive to encourage genuine investment in employee health, and also considering indexing those tax-free health promotion benefits to inflation.

More detailed proposals on involving private funding should be completed by the end of the year, Joller told ERR.

Joller is not the first person to suggest a shakeup of child health coverage. Three years ago, one of Joller's predecessors as social affairs minister, Riina Sikkut (SDE), had already put forward the idea of applying to children the same logic which already applies to pensioners, with the state itself regularly paying a fixed amount to the Health Insurance Fund on their behalf. That system has been in place since 2018.

A table from the Ministry of Social Affairs shows that by allocating additional funding to the fund to cover children's healthcare costs, revenues and expenditures could be balanced by 2032.

Riigikogu elections take place in March, meaning another administration will enter office after that. Any decision on whether the state should begin directly financing children's healthcare will now fall to the next government.
