World.title: Why Georgia’s prime minister is talking about ‘Russophobia’ ahead of anniversary of August war
World.content:
Just days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement on what he described as “Russophobia”.

In the statement, Kobakhidze draws connections between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic politics and the rhetoric of the Georgian opposition. He argues that the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine to “fuel Russophobia among its agents worldwide, including in Georgia.”

The prime minister accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current hardline stance as “Russophobia”.

The statement has reignited debate over the 2008 war. This time, however, the focus extends beyond how the war began and Russia’s responsibility for it. Instead, the prime minister shifts attention away from Russia’s actions and towards the position of his political opponents in Georgia.

The opposition has questioned not only the substance of Kobakhidze’s remarks, but also the timing of their publication. Why did the prime minister choose to speak about “Russophobia” on the eve of the war’s anniversary? Why does his statement focus on anything other than Russia’s responsibility? And what is the government doing to address the continuing occupation and the possibility of further annexation?

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

One of the central arguments in Kobakhidze’s statement is that Georgia’s opposition groups did not adopt a hardline stance towards Russia after the 2008 war. According to the prime minister, their position changed only in 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Kobakhidze notes that after the August 2008 war, Mikheil Saakashvili’s government chose to maintain economic, tourism and cultural ties with Russia. He also points out that the government unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

“After Russia occupied parts of Georgia in 2008 and recognised the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the United National Movement not only refrained from pursuing a hardline policy towards Russia, but shortly after the war its leader personally welcomed Russian citizens at the border and encouraged them to visit Georgia as tourists and invest in the country.”

According to Kobakhidze, neither members of the then government nor figures who are now in opposition objected to that policy. He specifically named opposition politicians Elene Khoshtaria, Zurab Japaridze and Misha Mshvildadze.

“We all remember how today’s leading ‘Russophobes’ — Elene Khoshtaria, Zurab Japaridze, Misha Mshvildadze and others — welcomed Russian tourists, Russian money, which apparently ‘didn’t smell’ at the time, and closer trade, economic and cultural ties with Russia.”

Based on this, Kobakhidze argues that the opposition’s current anti-Russian rhetoric and what he calls “Russophobia” are not the result of a consistent political position but of instructions received from abroad. In his statement, he describes his opponents as “foreign agents” and links their actions to the “deep state” and the “Global War Party.”

“The foreign agents declared Russia their sworn enemy only after it launched its second invasion of Ukraine.”

Kobakhidze asks why the same attitude did not emerge in 2008, when Georgia itself became the victim of Russian aggression.

“A logical question arises: why did they become Russophobes now, rather than when Georgia was under attack? Do they not even formally regard Georgia as their homeland? Is Ukraine their homeland instead?”

Another of his arguments concerns Elene Khoshtaria, who receives inherited royalties from Russia for the work of her late father, Soviet-era theatre director Goga Khoshtaria. Kobakhidze presents this as an example of what he describes as the opposition’s inconsistency.

“We all know that Russophobic politicians, NGO representatives, journalists and activists have remained silent about the millions of Russian roubles transferred to Elene Khoshtaria from the Russian state budget.”

Timing of the statement

Kobakhidze published his statement just a few days before the 18th anniversary of the August 2008 war.

At this time of year, Georgians traditionally commemorate those killed in the conflict, internally displaced people and the territories occupied by Russia. Critics have therefore questioned why the prime minister shifted the focus away from Russia’s responsibility and towards what he describes as the opposition’s “Russophobia”.

Irakli Pavlenishvili of the United National Movement views the statement in that context. In his opinion, raising the issue of “Russophobia” in an occupied country on the eve of the war’s anniversary is no coincidence.

“Promoting this narrative just before the anniversary of the August war is exactly what the Kremlin would want and encourage. It is impossible to believe that complaining about Russophobia in occupied Georgia at such a moment is a coincidence.”

Pavlenishvili argues that this rhetoric pushes Russia’s responsibility into the background while turning Georgia’s former government and the opposition into the main targets of political debate.

“This is another deliberate psychological and propaganda operation against the Georgian people. But they will have to accept that they will not be able to weaken or destroy anti-occupation sentiment among the Georgian public.”

Grigol Gegelia of the Lelo – Strong Georgia movement also emphasised the timing of the statement. He argues that, in the days leading up to the anniversary of the August war, Kobakhidze chose to confront fellow Georgian citizens instead of Russia.

According to Gegelia, the prime minister’s main focus at this time should have been Russia’s aggression and Georgia’s security.

“First and foremost, he should have been talking about Russian aggression and about the fact that Georgia was the first link in the chain of events that later continued elsewhere.”

What do Kobakhidze’s critics say?

Kobakhidze’s critics do not deny that Saakashvili’s government welcomed Russian tourists and maintained some economic ties with Russia after the war. The disagreement lies in how that policy should be interpreted.

Opposition figures distinguish between the Russian government and ordinary Russian citizens. In their view, welcoming tourists did not amount to supporting the Kremlin’s policies.

Gigi Tsereteli, leader of the European Georgia party, says the government sought to avoid creating the image of a xenophobic state. At the same time, he notes, Tbilisi continued to demand that Russia comply with the 12 August 2008 ceasefire agreement.

“Georgia was not a xenophobic country. The idea was to show that many Russians themselves opposed Putin’s expansionist policies. We had nothing against ordinary people. If peaceful tourists wanted to come, they were welcome. If someone was doing business without supporting the war, there was no problem.”

According to Tsereteli, maintaining economic and humanitarian ties was part of Georgia’s diplomatic strategy. At the time, there was still hope that international pressure would persuade Russia to honour its commitments.

“There was an attempt to reverse the process after 2008 and encourage Russia, through diplomacy, to fulfil its obligations. That was the rationale behind this policy.”

He adds that Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 fundamentally changed that approach. It demonstrated that the prospects for reaching diplomatic agreements with Moscow had diminished even further.

“The war in Ukraine convinced everyone that there is no longer any real basis for dialogue with Russia.”

Irakli Pavlenishvili makes a similar argument. He says it was important for Georgia after 2008 to show that its conflict was not with the Russian people.

“Because of people like Kobakhidze, who promoted these narratives, we constantly had to explain that we were not fighting Russians, that we were not xenophobic and were not looking for conflict. We could still welcome them as ordinary tourists.”

Pavlenishvili also notes that the previous government faced the opposite criticism at the time. Its opponents accused it of adopting an excessively harsh and xenophobic tone towards Russia.

“The contexts of 2008 and 2022 are different”

Philosopher Levan Gambashidze argues that the biggest flaw in Kobakhidze’s comparison is that it ignores how much the political context has changed. In his view, comparing the post-2008 period with the present day is misleading. Russia’s behaviour has changed, and so has the policy of the Georgian government.

According to Gambashidze, under the previous government there was no widespread perception that the state was pursuing a pro-Russian course.

“There was no sense that we were subordinated to Russia.”

He says the key question is not Kobakhidze’s individual arguments, but his motives. Gambashidze asks who benefits from portraying “Russophobia” as a problem.

“Which country would be concerned about growing ‘Russophobia’ around the world? Russia. Now ask yourself why the Georgian government would be concerned about it.”

According to Gambashidze, since 2022 the authorities have repeatedly warned the public about the possibility of war with Russia. He argues that this has itself contributed to growing fears of Russia.

“If ‘Russophobia’ means fear or hostility towards Russia, and if Georgian Dream has been warning its own population about the possibility of war with Russia since 2022, then what explains the rise in these ‘Russophobic’ sentiments after 2022?”

The Telavi incident

Some of Kobakhidze’s critics also link his statement to a recent confrontation between Georgian citizens and Russian tourists at a wedding in the town of Telavi.

Gigi Tsereteli suggests the statement may have been prompted by the public reaction to that incident. He also says Russia could use such episodes as a pretext to exert political pressure on Georgia.

Grigol Gegelia goes further, arguing that Russian security services could exploit the growing flow of Russian tourists to stage provocations.

“We have long warned that allowing Russians to enter the country without proper controls would end badly. Now Russian intelligence has fertile ground for provocations. It can use these people to carry them out.”

What arguments does Georgian Dream make?

Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party have echoed the main points of Kobakhidze’s statement almost word for word.

“You clearly remember what Saakashvili, Khoshtaria and Japaridze were saying. They unilaterally introduced visa-free travel for Russian citizens, transferred ownership of our strategic assets to Russian state-owned companies, cast the decisive vote in favour of Russia’s accession to the World Trade Organization, welcomed Russian tourists at the border because that was the task they had been given, and became Russophobes only after Russia invaded Ukraine,” said Levan Machavariani, first deputy chair of the Georgian Dream parliamentary faction.

Machavariani also cites rulings by international courts to support the government’s position. He points out that Georgia won legal cases against Russia in Strasbourg and The Hague.

“For us, Russia has been an occupying power since August 2008. It makes no difference what it did later in another country.”

Parliamentary Vice Speaker Nino Tsilosani also argues that the opposition’s attitude changed in line with the international political agenda.

“For years after the August 2008 war, we watched today’s radicals applaud the promotion of Russian tourism and Russian capital instead of protesting against it.”

Tsilosani likewise argues that the opposition’s current rhetoric stems not from Georgia’s own experience but from “instructions from abroad” received after 2022.

“Remaining silent about the suffering of your own people while shouting slogans dictated from abroad is neither patriotism nor genuine solidarity. It is simply unquestioning service to someone else’s interests.”

The opposition’s main question

Some opposition parties do not engage with Kobakhidze’s historical comparisons at all. Instead, they focus on the government’s current policies.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the Gakharia – For Georgia party argues that debating the policies of 2008–2012 cannot replace answers about the ongoing occupation and the risk of annexation.

“Does Irakli Kobakhidze mean that today he should continue the same policy that the United National Movement pursued after 2008? Is he using the United National Movement to justify his own collaboration with Georgia’s main enemy — Russia?”

According to Sharashidze, the current government should be responding to Russia’s actions in the Tskhinvali region and assessing the threat of further integration of the occupied territory.

“What matters is not what happened in 2008. What matters is what is happening today.”

Georgia’s Western course

Kobakhidze’s critics also link his statement to Georgia’s foreign policy. In their view, the prime minister’s text portrays the West, the opposition and civil society — rather than Russia — as the country’s main threats.

According to Gigi Tsereteli, although the previous government made many mistakes, it never abandoned Georgia’s Western course.

Tsereteli argues that Kobakhidze’s statement repeats familiar Russian propaganda narratives, particularly by portraying civil society and Western partners as part of a system of external control.

“I believe the text was, at the very least, edited by people affiliated with the Kremlin.”

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Ahali party, offered an even harsher assessment. In his view, the statement confuses historical facts with political concepts.

“I cannot recall even Bidzina Ivanishvili’s texts containing such a mess, so much slander and falsehood, such confusion of facts, dates and concepts, and, above all, Russophilia on this scale.”

World.title: Opinion: ‘The prime minister’s statement is demagoguery and part of election preparations”
World.content:
Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s recent statement serves the interests of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, so effectively that it has virtually guaranteed Kobakhidze’s position until the next parliamentary elections.

According to Zakareishvili, the prime minister understands Ivanishvili’s political objectives even better than Ivanishvili himself.



According to Zakareishvili, the claim about “Russophobia” is consistent with Kobakhidze’s political style. He also argues that Georgian Dream’s main objective is to distance the country from the European Union.

Just days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement on what he described as “Russophobia”. In it, he drew connections between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic politics and the rhetoric of the Georgian opposition. Kobakhidze argued that the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine to “fuel Russophobia among its agents worldwide, including in Georgia.”

Paata Zakareishvili said: “This is a very important, albeit disturbing, text. I am struck by Kobakhidze’s cynicism, audacity and well-crafted demagoguery.

This is clearly a carefully prepared statement that was likely drafted by several people. It operates on multiple levels, but its central message is that Georgia’s problems are purely domestic. Russia has been pushed almost entirely out of the picture. The same is true of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.

They are very cleverly trying not to deny that Russia occupied part of Georgia in 2008. Instead, they portray the occupation as the result of the short-sighted and provocative policies of the then ruling United National Movement.

Georgian Dream is preparing for the elections. It fears the opposition may abandon its boycott and decide to take part. Support for Georgian Dream is not growing — it is declining. If the opposition changes course and mobilises voters, more dissatisfied people may go to the polls and vote against Georgian Dream. The ruling party wants to secure more votes, so it is presenting itself as the guarantor of peace.

It is obvious that Georgian Dream cannot ban opposition parties because that would trigger severe sanctions from the West. For Europe, arresting opposition politicians is not as serious as banning political parties. So instead of outlawing them, Georgian Dream will push the Russian factor to the forefront.”

“Europe and the European Union have changed significantly since 2022. Instead of getting into the European boat and saying, ‘Yes, Europe made mistakes in the past, but now it is doing the right thing, and we remain committed to the European path,’ Georgian Dream has done the opposite. It has taken an absurd position. On the one hand, it criticises Europe for failing to respond properly during the 2008 war. On the other, now that Europe has adopted what they themselves describe as a more appropriate approach, they attack it.

It is clear that Georgian Dream does not really want Europe, regardless of the context of the 2008 war. Its main objective is to distance Georgia from the European Union.”

Expert on Kobakhidze’s “Russophobia” remarks

World.title: Azerbaijan’s TikTok arrests: limits of ‘public morality’ and freedom of expression
World.content:
TikTok arrests in Azerbaijan

In late July and early August, Azerbaijani authorities detained a number of popular TikTok users one after another under administrative procedures. Courts later sentenced them to short-term administrative detention.

Officials said the arrests were prompted by “clear disrespect for society”, “offending public morality” and behaviour deemed contrary to “national and moral values”. However, the sequence of the arrests and the broad interpretation of the legal provisions involved have once again raised questions about the balance between freedom of expression and the state’s efforts to protect what it defines as “public morality”.

According to publicly available information, the following individuals have been detained:

Magsad Bagirov, known online as “Chevik”, was detained on 27 July. The TikToker, known for his anti-religious statements, received a 10-day administrative detention sentence under Article 510.2 of Azerbaijan’s Code of Administrative Offences for actions publicly displayed online that were deemed offensive to public morality.

Uzeyir Abbas was detained on 28 July over posts which authorities said had insulted religious beliefs.

Mujgan Mammadzade was detained on 30 July in Baku’s Sabunchu district. A court sentenced her to 10 days of administrative detention under the same Article 510.2.

Murad Gasymov, known as “Murad Sade”, was detained on 30 July and sentenced to 30 days of administrative detention.

Sanur Azizov was detained on 1 August in Baku’s Sabail district. A court sentenced him to eight days of administrative detention under Article 510.1, which covers petty hooliganism, defined as actions showing clear disrespect for society.

Alikram Heydarov was detained on 2 August and received an eight-day administrative detention sentence under the same Article 510.1.

Legal background

The legal basis for these arrests stems from amendments to the Law on Information, Informatization and Information Protection, which came into force in early 2026.

The amendments introduced liability for publishing online content deemed to “offend public morality”, show “clear disrespect for society”, contain “obscene language or gestures”, or involve “the display of body parts in a manner contrary to national and moral values”. Articles 510.1 and 510.2 of Azerbaijan’s Code of Administrative Offences have become the main legal mechanisms for enforcing these provisions.

The problem is that terms such as “public morality” and “national and moral values” are not clearly defined in Azerbaijani legislation. As a result, the same act may be treated in one case as an exercise of the right to freedom of expression and, in another, as an administrative offence amounting to hooliganism.

Lawyer’s opinion

“The way Articles 510.1 and 510.2 of Azerbaijan’s Code of Administrative Offences are being enforced, together with the amendments introduced in 2026 to the Law on Information, Informatization and Information Protection, raises serious legal concerns.

Terms such as ‘public morality’, ‘clear disrespect for society’, ‘national and moral values’, and ‘obscene language or gestures’ are not defined through clear, objective or predictable criteria. As a result, one official or judge may view the same act as a legitimate exercise of freedom of expression, while another may classify it as an administrative offence.

Article 47 of Azerbaijan’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression, while Article 71 guarantees the protection of human and civil rights and freedoms. Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects freedom of expression and allows restrictions only when they are prescribed by law, necessary in a democratic society and proportionate. According to the established case law of the European Court of Human Rights, any restriction must also be foreseeable. People must be able to understand in advance which actions could expose them to legal sanctions.

The current provisions do not meet that standard. Their wording is so broad and open to subjective interpretation that they can apply to almost any critical, satirical, anti-religious or otherwise unconventional content. This creates a risk of selective enforcement, encourages self-censorship and effectively restricts freedom of expression.

Short-term administrative detention may formally appear to be a relatively mild sanction. However, its systematic use can have much broader consequences. People begin avoiding sensitive topics, while the range of acceptable content on online platforms gradually shrinks to what is considered the safest. Rather than strengthening public morality or public order, this approach increases legal uncertainty.”

Human rights and legal uncertainty

The core concern underlying this assessment is legal uncertainty. In legal theory and international practice, it is regarded as one of the most serious threats to fundamental rights and freedoms because it affects not only those who face prosecution, but also encourages society as a whole to act more cautiously for fear of punishment.

Selective enforcement: Vaguely worded legal provisions create conditions for selective enforcement. The same platform may host other forms of offensive, hateful or obscene content, yet authorities may choose to prosecute only particular types of posts, such as anti-religious content or material they consider “disrespectful”. Such practices raise questions about compliance with the principle of equality before the law, guaranteed by Article 25 of Azerbaijan’s Constitution, as well as the prohibition of discrimination.

The same platform may host other forms of offensive, hateful or obscene content, yet authorities may choose to prosecute only particular types of posts, such as anti-religious content or material they consider “disrespectful”. Such practices raise questions about compliance with the principle of equality before the law, guaranteed by Article 25 of Azerbaijan’s Constitution, as well as the prohibition of discrimination. The chilling effect: The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly warned that vague and overly broad legal provisions pose risks to freedom of expression. Fear of punishment may encourage people to censor themselves. This effect is particularly visible on platforms such as TikTok, where younger users may begin avoiding sensitive topics and refrain from expressing critical or unconventional views. As a result, the space for public debate narrows and the diversity of opinions declines.

This effect is particularly visible on platforms such as TikTok, where younger users may begin avoiding sensitive topics and refrain from expressing critical or unconventional views. As a result, the space for public debate narrows and the diversity of opinions declines. The principles of necessity and proportionality: Even if protecting public morality is accepted as a legitimate aim, any restrictions must be necessary and proportionate to that objective. Administrative detention ranging from eight to 30 days may appear relatively short. However, its systematic and frequent use can turn punishment into a tool of control. Given the availability of alternative measures, such as warnings, platform moderation policies and media literacy programmes, the necessity of depriving people of their liberty raises important legal questions.

World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Israel accused of targeting journalists in deadly series of strikes
World.content:
Human rights organisations have accused Israel of committing a war crime in southern Lebanon, alleging the Israel Defense Forces deliberately targeted two Lebanese journalists earlier this year.

Amal Khalil, a 42-year-old journalist working for the Al-Akhbar newspaper, was killed in the attack in the village of Al-Tiri on April 22. Her colleague Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old freelance photographer and camera operator, was seriously wounded.

Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch investigated the incident, piecing together firsthand accounts from Faraj, emergency crews who tried to save the pair and examining photos and videos of the attack.

There were three strikes by the IDF on Al-Tiri that day. The military said it had been targeting Hezbollah fighters.

The first strike hit a vehicle in front of the car Khalil and Faraj were in, forcing the journalists to take shelter.

An hour later, a second strike hit their vehicle and the pair were wounded in the explosion. The third strike followed an hour after that.

During that time, Israeli surveillance drones were hovering overhead.

"The drones got extremely close, coming through the broken roof. Less than a meter away," Faraj told investigators.

"I was covering my face, thinking of a video I had seen where a drone killed someone like that. I thought it would explode in my face.

"The drones didn't carry visible explosives, but they were hovering and provoking fear constantly."

At the time, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam accused Israel of a war crime.

The chain of events led the two human rights organisations to demand an investigation.

"After the first strike had eliminated the military-stated target, and with two drones flying low overhead, the Israeli military knew or should have known that two civilian women were sheltering in that building," Amnesty International's Heba Morayef said.

"Despite this, they proceeded with what we have reasonable grounds to believe amounted to a direct attack on civilians, demonstrating a shocking disregard for international humanitarian law."

Human Rights Watch said the investigation shattered the IDF's insistence that it did not target journalists.

"The facts and evidence show that it has repeatedly done so," the organisation's Ramzi Kaiss said.

"Amal Khalil and Zainab Faraj are the latest victims in a long series of such attacks.

"The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew or should have known that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours."

Investigations outline timeline of the incident

The investigations laid out a timeline of events leading up to the first, second and third strikes.

They found Khalil and Faraj had driven towards Al-Tiri, close to the town of Bint Jbeil, on April 22.

The purpose of their journey was to verify reports Israeli soldiers had withdrawn from the area, as part of their reporting on the war in Lebanon.

The pair were following another vehicle driven by Ali Nabil Bazzi, the local mayor, and his friend Mohammed Hourani.

The IDF has claimed the two men were Hezbollah operatives.

Moments after arriving in Al-Tiri, before 2:30pm, the vehicle the two men were in was attacked.

Calls we made to the Lebanese Civil Defence and the Lebanese Red Cross a little more than 10 minutes later.

One of the Civil Defence officials said the crews were held at a Lebanese military checkpoint and told by officers they were waiting for approval from the IDF to enter the site.

This was a process implemented as part of the November 2024 ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, involving officials from the UN peacekeeping force stationed along the border to monitor the situation.

Still stuck at the checkpoint, Civil Defense called the journalists and told them to rush to leave the area immediately as there was no guarantee Israel would not attack again.

Screenshots of a video call between Faraj and her sister show the car travelling in front of Khalil and Faraj burning after the Israeli strike. (Supplied: Human Rights Watch)

The pair had been seeking shelter near their car and surveillance drones were circling.

"There was a crack in the roof, and we could see the quadcopter right above peering in," Faraj told Human Rights Watch.

"For one hour, we waited under the tiled roof and the entire time there were two quadcopters above us.

"The quadcopter would go up and come down. It kept doing this."

At about 3:40pm, the second strike hit the journalists' car. Khalil and Faraj were injured in the attack but managed to get word back to the Civil Defense that they could not get out.

"Glass and debris flew toward us. My ear felt like it burst," Faraj told Amnesty International.

"She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn't move her leg."

The women managed to seek shelter inside a nearby building while waiting for help. Civil Defense crews remained waiting at the checkpoint.

Red Cross abandoned scene due to threat

The third Israeli strike, according to the investigations, came at about 4:25pm.

It hit the building the women were hiding inside, causing it to collapse and trapping them under the rubble.

The Lebanese Red Cross was given permission to enter the area after 5pm, without Civil Defense support, and the crews managed to rescue Faraj.

She had suffered a fractured skull, injuries to her right eye and leg, and a crushed hand. Khalil remained trapped under the rubble.

The Red Cross crews were forced to leave at about 6pm after threats of further attacks.

It was not until about 7:20pm that authorisation was received for crews to return to the site — and only after a flurry of phone calls, including from the offices of the Lebanese president and prime minister.

This time, Red Cross crews arrived with an ambulance and a small bulldozer to try to pick through the rubble of the building.

Islamic Risala Scout Association paramedics waiting for approval to access al-Tiri at a Lebanese Army checkpoint 2.6 kilometres north of the strike site. (Supplied: Human Rights Watch)

That work began at 9pm and Khalil's body was recovered. Her time of death, as recorded on her death certificate, was 7pm. The cause was recorded as "cardiac arrest due to a head trauma and severe bleeding".

Amnesty International said the Lebanese government should join the International Criminal Court and demand an investigation for war crimes.

"The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful air strikes, including direct attacks on civilians," Ms Morayef said.

"Amal Khalil's killing must be independently and impartially investigated. It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel."

Israel claims two Hezbollah military operatives killed

In response to the investigation by the human rights groups, the IDF told the ABC that Khalil was killed "during a sequence of events in which two military operatives in Hezbollah's military wing, Ali Nabil Bazi and Mohammad Al-Khourani, were eliminated".

"The incident has been referred to the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism to conduct a comprehensive factual assessment," it said in a statement.

"Upon its completion, the findings will be submitted to the Military Advocate General for review, who will determine whether any additional measures are required.

"The IDF regrets any harm caused to journalists. The IDF does not target journalists and respects freedom of the press and the important role journalists play."

World.title: Live: Legend's first try in four years puts Cowboys on top
World.content:
Round 23 of the NRL season will kick off on Thursday night with Gold Coast hosting North Queensland.

The Cowboys will be out to make amends after last week's humiliating loss to the Roosters where they conceded the third-most points in a single game of any team in history.

The Titans will be playing for pride but have made progress in recent weeks and will fancy their chances of adding another win to their tally.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

Live updates Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 13 Key Events 4 Tries 4 Halftime: North Queensland 18 lead Gold Coast 4 N By Nick Campton Some pretty good footy in patches through that first half, Titans will be very disappointed with some of their defence. 38' Luki powers over for Cowboys N By Nick Campton Kini throws an awful pass to Haas' ankles and the big fella knocks it on. Cowboys will get the last say before halftime. Purdue goes short to Luki, he absolutely tramples De Groot and smashes his way over the line! So long as he's got this down clean it'll be a try....and he has! Great strength from the backrower. Drinkwater from out wide, he swings the kick through and it's 18-4 Cowboys. 33' Gold Coast error N By Nick Campton A Brimson pass on the last is knocked on and the Titans will get more ball inside the attacking half...only for Campbell to throw a pass over the sideline! It was intended for Sami and he couldn't quite hit the pedal to reel it in, he's been carrying a knee injury since he scored the try. 30' Titans get their first N By Nick Campton Laybutt's pass goes to ground and Fifita picks it up. A try here would be huge, the Titans have had the better of the last few minutes. Brimson slides through and can see the line but Drinkwater just manages to drag him down. Campbell's bomb on the last is knocked on by Burns and the Titans have some more good ball. Campbell goes short to De Groot and he slings a nice one-handed pass to Sami who dives over in the corner! Nicely worked by Gold Coast. Campbell can't convert and it's 12-4 Cowboys. 22' Close shave for Titans N By Nick Campton Clifford takes a bomb and slings a pass out the back to Cotter who puts it over the line! But referee Adam Gee rules the pass was forward and then, to compound things, Cotter is ruled to be offside. Lucky escape for the Titans, they're just keeping touch right now. 19' Titans can't strike N By Nick Campton Taulagi gets a hand to a pass and knocks it on, Titans have a fresh set on the attacking 40. A high tackle helps them build some pressure. Brimson dinks a kick through on the last, Ieremia has a shot at the ball but it's a very difficult chance and he can't get it down. Cowboys restart from the 20. 13' Cowboys get another N By Nick Campton A set restart puts the Cowboys back in the red zone, Purdue jumps out of dummy half and he's got Clifford running a good, hard line to score an easy try. That was soft and that was ominous. Drinkwater converts and it's 12-0 in quick time. 9' Titans can't reply N By Nick Campton Taumalolo loses it as he brings the ball back from the kick off to put the Titans right on the attack. It's not much of a set and they knock it on late in the count. Cowboys hang on. 7' Taumalolo breaks four-year tryscoring drought N By Nick Campton Drinkwater nails a 40/20 to put the Cowboys on the attack. Just a few plays later Luke drops Taumalolo over and he powers his way in for a try! I can't believe it! That's his first try in four years! Drinkwater converts and it's 6-0 Cowboys. And away we go! N By Nick Campton Cowboys kick us off, running right to left. Tips N By Nick Campton I'm going the Cowboys for this one but given the week they've had, who knows what could happen? They're trying to rebound from the kind of loss that happens once a century. Let's say Cowboys by ten with Jason Taumalolo to score first, just because. Final teams: Titans vs Cowboys N By Nick Campton A couple of changes for Gold Coast - Lachlan Ilias has been benched with AJ Brimson moving from centre to halfback and Jaylen de Groot lining up out wide. Sam Verrills will start at hooker with Oliver Pascoe moving to the bench and Josh Patson will start at second row with Arama Hau riding the pine. Only change for the Cowboys is John Bateman joining the bench and Kaiden Lahrs dropping off. Hello and welcome to the ABC's live blog for Titans-Cowboys. N By Nick Campton Yes, we're back at it again - another Thursday night, another live blog for your footballing pleasure. It's an all-Queensland affair tonight with Gold Coast hosting North Queensland. Should be an interesting one given the Cowboys are trying to come back after conceding 82 - yes, 82 - points last week against the Roosters. Intriguing stuff! Let's see what happens next.
