World.title: Citizenship granted to Iranian soccer players who sought asylum
World.content:
Two Iranian women's soccer team players who sought asylum in Australia after competing in the Asian Cup have been granted citizenship.

Iran competed in Australia in March as war broke out in the Middle East after a US-Israel attack on the Islamic Republic.

Concerns were raised about the national team's safety after the players refused to sing the Iranian national anthem ahead of their game against South Korea and were criticised on Iranian state television.

Seven team members, including a handler, were granted humanitarian visas to remain in Australia, but five withdrew their claims and returned to Iran.

Concerns were raised over the potential for the players to face retribution from the Iranian government when returning home. (AAP: Russell Freeman)

'Deeply grateful'

The two remaining players, Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, were granted citizenship on Wednesday.

Ms Pasandideh and Ms Ramezanisadeh were sworn in as citizens by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at a ceremony in Brisbane.

The women were sworn in by Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke. (Supplied)

They were accompanied by members of the local Iranian community, with friends and supporters celebrating the occasion.

Ms Pasandideh said it was "one of the happiest days of my life".

"After everything we've been through and all the challenges we faced, this moment means more than words can express," she said.

"Thank you, Australia, for giving me this opportunity. I'm honoured to be part of this nation."

The two women said the ceremony and their citizenship "meant a great deal to us". (Supplied)

Ms Ramezanisadeh said she was "deeply proud to become an Australian citizen".

"Australia has given me the opportunity to build my life and my future, and I feel, more than ever, that I belong here," she said.

" At the same time, my roots and my memories of Iran will always remain a part of who I am. "

More Iranians living 'in limbo'

Associate legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre (HRLC) Laura John urged the government to extend the same pathway to citizenship to Iranians formerly in offshore detention who have been living in Australia for years.

She said the HRLC understood that about 700 refugees have lived in the Australian community for more than a decade on "short-term, insecure bridging visas".

How community united to help Iran's footballers The remaining members of Iran's women's football team might have left Australia, but the journey is far from over, as members of the Iranian-Australian community share what really went into the fight to protect their countrywomen.

"Almost most half are from Iran and cannot return there," Ms John said.

"Many have close family members, including children and spouses, who are Australian citizens or permanent residents."

She said HRLC clients Fatemeh Lahmidi and Mahsa Mazaheri have been in Australia for more than 13 years and have not yet been granted citizenship.

Ms Lahmidi, who is a mother, aged care worker and refugee from Iran, said she was happy for the soccer players but felt "heartbroken" she was unable to obtain citizenship.

"My family has been waiting for so many years, and it's hard to understand why we are still living with so much uncertainty while others receive citizenship so quickly," she said.

"Australia is the only home my children really know.

" We have done our best to build our lives here, and all we want is the chance to stop living in limbo and finally have the safety and security every family hopes for. "

Small business owner Ms Mazaheri said her daughters and husband were Australian citizens and that the country had been her home for more than 10 years.

"It is painful to see the difference in how some people are treated while many others, like us, remain in uncertainty for so many years," she said.

World.title: Police settle lawsuit with Gippsland man left with brain damage
World.content:
A young father who suffered permanent brain damage after a Victorian police officer fell on him during a bungled arrest has quietly settled a lawsuit with the force, in a deal believed to be worth millions.

Brodie Holt last month reached a confidential settlement with Victoria Police in the Supreme Court over the incident outside a pub in his home town of Traralgon, which left him with injuries so severe that he was forced to move back home with his parents.

Mr Holt, now 27, still has no memory of what happened and only remembered waking up in The Alfred hospital after being roused from an induced coma. His family was told he had post-traumatic amnesia.

He watched security footage of the alleged incident on Wednesday for the first time, four years after the incident.

Brodie Holt still has no memory of his 2022 arrest. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"It was pretty brutal," he told the ABC after watching the video.

" They just treated me like I was some piece of meat. "

"[They were] just throwing me around, pushing me into walls and shit and then I supposedly fell over, which is not what happened at all."

His mother, Kellie Holt, who launched the lawsuit as his guardian, said the incident forever changed the way she saw police.

Brodie Holt has been heavily reliant on his parents since the incident. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

She had to quit her job at the local supermarket to care for her son, who is completely reliant on her.

"No-one is taking accountability for it, they're just throwing money at it to go away," she said.

Her husband, Joe Holt, said it had shattered his trust in police.

"Now I wouldn't trust them at all. I would never contact them even if someone was trying to break into my house," he said.

Kellie Holt says her family would never trust the police again. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Arrest happened on Mother's Day

A Victoria Police spokesman said allegations against an officer were "found to be unsubstantiated".

"Victoria Police resolved a subsequent civil claim based on independent legal advice," the spokesman said.

Court documents reveal that the special damages claimed by the young father — including medical treatment, loss of earnings and ongoing care — come in at $13.7 million.

On Mother's Day in 2022, Mr Holt was out drinking with friends at the Hotel Traralgon when he was arrested by three police officers in the early hours of the morning.

The details of what happened before, during and after the incident are still hotly contested by both sides in court documents seen by the ABC.

Brodie Holt's lawyers say he broke no laws when arrested at the Hotel Traralgon in 2022. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Lawyers for Mr Holt said he had broken no laws when he was arrested and escorted outside where he was handcuffed.

They told the Supreme Court he was shoved into a brick doorway on the way out and that after he spat on the ground he was threatened, grabbed by the throat, thrown against a brick wall and then tackled to the ground where his head struck the concrete.

Victoria Police said it arrested Mr Holt because he was drunk and a potential danger to himself and others.

They conceded he "struck" a brick doorway on the way out of the pub, but said he spat at police, resisted them after being handcuffed and had to be restrained so he would not headbutt them.

Brodie Holt was put into an induced coma at The Alfred hospital after his arrest. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Victoria Police told the Supreme Court the officer who tackled Mr Holt to the ground "lost his footing and his balance", which caused the young father's head to strike the concrete.

"This was not intended by any police member," it said.

Incident was 'entirely avoidable' says lawyer

Mr Holt was taken to Latrobe Regional Hospital before being flown to Melbourne.

His lawyer, Jeremy King from Robinson Gill, said what happened to Mr Holt was "entirely avoidable".

"At its worst, all you could really say was that Brodie might be guilty of mouthing off to police and as a result of that he suffered a lifetime brain injury," Mr King said.

"He requires care, he won't be able to work and he's very reliant on his parents and family for a lot of support.

His parents say it feels like they're raising their son all over again. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"I think what's important to understand in this case is that this happened in a regional area and that if you live in a regional area, it's almost impossible to complain about police because you're complaining about someone who is effectively in your local community.

" You're effectively trying to complain about your neighbour and it's a huge disincentive for people to make complaints. "

'Forgetful' Brodie now struggles to be a parent

Since his injuries, Mr Holt has moved back into the family home with his parents and remains entirely reliant on them.

"It's like I have to look out for him all over again," Joe Holt said.

His injuries have affected Brodie's parental relationship with his five-year-old daughter. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The couple said it was like living with a forgetful teenager again and that his injuries had affected the relationship he had with his own five-year-old daughter.

"He was always the doting dad running after her, doing everything for her, looking after her," said his father.

"It's just kids growing up, you just put up with it, whereas nowadays he just gets irritated by it all," he said.

" I wanted a normal life with my son, take him out to the footy … that type of shit. "

"And now I can't … he's a different person."

World.title: Bangladesh's ousted 'Iron Lady' plans to return to politics. Can she do it?
World.content:
Politics has defined almost every chapter of Sheikh Hasina's life.

Widely known as Bangladesh's "Iron Lady" during her 15 years in power, the former prime minister and daughter of the country's founding leader lived a life shaped by the nation's most powerful political dynasty.



She was last seen in her home country fleeing on a military helicopter while thousands of protesters stormed her official residence, the culmination of weeks of mass demonstrations against her leadership.



Now, two years later, a rare appearance from the 78-year-old suggests she is unwilling to accept that her political career is over.

Despite being sentenced to death by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal, she used her first public address since fleeing the country in 2024 to publicly declare she would return home in December.

Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina vows to return to Bangladesh The 78-year-old fled to India in August 2024 by helicopter at the height of the student-led uprising that toppled her government.

In a tightly packed room at New Delhi's Foreign Correspondents' Club, journalists strained to hear the former prime minister via a dodgy audio link on a large screen.

But rather than confront the crimes she has been convicted of, and sentenced to death over, in Bangladesh, the press conference instead resembled a carefully choreographed relaunch of her now-banned Awami League.

Rather than reflecting on the allegations against her, Hasina spoke of returning to Bangladesh and reclaiming her political future.

Will Sheikh Hasina really return?

Sheikh Hasina's family were assassinated in the 70s, forcing her into exile. (AP: Pavel Rahman)

The prospect of returning to Bangladesh is hardly an attractive one.

Beyond the death sentence, Hasina faces multiple criminal cases, including allegations of murder, attempted murder and abduction. Bangladesh's BNP government has repeatedly said she would be arrested immediately upon arrival.

But whether she ultimately boards a flight to Dhaka may be beside the point.

Simply declaring that she will return allows Hasina to project defiance, reassure loyal supporters she has not abandoned them, and place herself back at the centre of Bangladesh's political conversation.

Her return would also create a dilemma for Bangladesh's government.

Tarique Rahman became Bangladesh's prime minister earlier this year. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Although the BNP has repeatedly demanded Hasina's extradition, bringing her back into Bangladesh also risks reigniting the political tensions that have only recently begun to settle after years of upheaval.

Sreeradha Datta, an international affairs professor at Om Prakash Jindal Global University, said that despite the Awami League being banned from politics, Hasina's public statement would likely "uplift the lagging spirit" of loyalists.

"There is very little leadership; most of the senior Awami leaders have fled. I think this is Hasina's way to motivate them," she said.

Professor Datta said the BNP government likely feared Hasina's return would spark a mass mobilisation of Awami League supporters.

"There's the possibility of violence," she said.

Bangladesh court issues death sentence against ex-PM who fled country A Bangladesh court has sentenced ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to death after finding her guilty of crimes against humanity.

Hasina's political influence is not lost on the BNP.

In the lead-up to the event, Bangladesh's government warned local media against publicising her speech and criticised New Delhi for allowing it to proceed.

Professor Datta also believes the death sentence itself could eventually become negotiable.

"I think they would rethink it. She was the prime minister, and I think the government will say, 'We're a different Bangladesh; we're not vindictive like we used to be' to convey a sense that they are much more evolved."

A calculated move by India

In the days leading up to the event, Bangladesh criticised India for allowing the address to proceed, calling it another setback in already strained bilateral relations.

New Delhi responded by describing it as a private event beyond the government's control.

In practice, however, it is difficult to imagine a politician as controversial and strategically significant as Sheikh Hasina staging a high-profile public appearance in India's capital without approval.

"If the Indian government didn't want this to happen, it would not have happened," Professor Datta said.

The protest movement was met with a violent police crackdown. (Reuters: Mohammad Ponir Hossain)

India's continued decision to shelter Hasina remains deeply contentious. For the families of the estimated 1,400 people killed during the 2024 protests, her exile in New Delhi represents denied justice.

But politically, exile may suit both governments better than extradition.

Bangladesh's BNP government can continue portraying India as the protector of a convicted former leader while avoiding the domestic instability her return could trigger.

India, meanwhile, retains a politician who has been loyal to India's interests for decades and may still command loyalty among sections of Bangladesh's political elite.

World.title: Phone tap reveals fugitive developer’s $100k offer to Perrottet brother
World.content:
Phone taps played to a NSW corruption inquiry have revealed fugitive property developer Jean Nassif offered to support the Liberal preselection of one of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet's brothers.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is investigating whether people linked to the NSW Liberal Party solicited funds from prohibited donors and other sources to advance the interests of the right-wing NSW Reformers faction.

It is examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were also exchanged for political favours, including damaging former minister David Elliott's career and removing building commissioner David Chandler.

The inquiry heard the offer during a recorded phone call from June 2021 between Mr Nassif and Reformers member Jean-Claude Perrottet, who told the commission Mr Nassif became his client while he was working at Medallion Finance.

A number of phone taps featuring Jean-Claude Perrottet were played at the inquiry. (AAP: George Chan)

In the recording, Mr Perrottet discussed possible investment opportunities before Mr Nassif turned the conversation to politics, suggesting $100,000 could go to one of the Perrottet brothers seeking preselection, or alternatively be channelled through Liberal figures Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Asked which brother Mr Nassif was referring to, Mr Perrottet said: "I don't know what he's talking about, to be honest. It's clear it makes no sense."

Counsel assisting the commission, Juliet Curtin, argued the call showed members of the Reformers faction were seeking financial backing for factional activities, and that Mr Nassif was offering to contribute.

"I just don't agree with that characterisation. This is obviously just nonsense," Mr Perrottet replied.

"You can hear from my tone on the phone."

Dominic Perrottet, who referred the allegations to ICAC in 2022, is not accused of any wrongdoing.

'An evil man'

In another phone tap, Jean-Claude Perrottet was heard approaching Mr Nassif to discuss potential investment opportunities before the conversation again turned to politics.

In the recording, Mr Nassif claimed he was being targeted by Mr Chandler and alleged then-Hornsby MP Matt Kean was working with former minister David Elliott in a bid to replace Dominic Perrottet as premier.

Mr Nassif: "They're leading the fight now against your brother. They want to destroy his image. He's a Christian. He's an evil man." Mr Perrottet: "Yeah, I know. I didn't know it was a crime to be Christian these days." Mr Nassif: "You know, I've got all my community behind him." Mr Perrottet: "I appreciate that, Jean."

When the discussion turned to factional issues in Castle Hill and Baulkham Hills, Mr Perrottet told Mr Nassif, "Help in that area would be awesome."

He was also heard thanking Mr Nassif for his support of the family, saying, "It's making a difference, the work you're doing."

While giving evidence to the commission, Mr Perrottet described it as a throwaway comment.

Regular $5k payments for Perrottet brother

Ms Curtin suggested Mr O'Hara (above) paid money to Beckington, which then made its way to Mr Perrottet. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The commission was also shown text messages between Jean-Claude Perrottet and Mr Ellis discussing the first of what became regular $5,000 payments to Mr Perrottet.

The inquiry heard Mr Perrottet received the monthly payments from Beckington, a company with contracts involving Catholic Schools NSW and hotelier Michael O'Hara, for work he told the commission he could not remember doing.

In the messages, Mr Perrottet asked Mr Ellis to send him money, with Mr Ellis replying: "It's $5k, not five-and-a-half, you sneaky man."

Mr Ellis also explained that Mr O'Hara paid Beckington $5,000 a month, including GST, and advised Mr Perrottet to include GST within a $5,000 invoice rather than adding it on top.

Text messages show Mr Perrottet asked Mr Ellis (above) to send him money. (Supplied)

Ms Curtin suggested to Mr Perrottet that the messages showed he was receiving money paid by Mr O'Hara to Beckington.

"I honestly don't recall whether that's the case," Mr Perrottet responded.

"Maybe, I'm not sure … I honestly don't recall whether an agreement was made with Christian."

Fiji trip questioned

Last week, the inquiry heard Jean-Claude Perrottet travelled to Fiji during the 2023 parliamentary inquiry into allegations of illegal donations involving Liberal Party operatives and developers.

The commission heard Mr Perrottet travelled "with financial assistance from others named in allegations".

When asked on Thursday if he went there deliberately to avoid giving evidence at the parliamentary inquiry, Mr Perrottet maintained he believed it was a "sham inquiry".

"I went to Fiji because I had I was not in a good place and I didn't want to partake in what I believed is a sham inquiry," Mr Perrottet said.

World.title: High Court finds secret recording can be used as evidence in DV case
World.content:
Victim-survivors of domestic violence may now be able to use secret recordings of admissions of abuse to seek safety after a major High Court decision.

Yesterday, Australia's highest court dismissed an appeal from a man convicted of raping his wife while she slept on two occasions.

He had argued a recording of him admitting to the first rape was obtained illegally.

While most recordings of private conversations are illegal, the High Court found the recording was allowed and able to be used as evidence because it was necessary to protect the victim's "bodily autonomy and integrity".

"The covert recording was the reminder to the complainant, by replaying it to herself, to avoid being exposed to the real risk of being raped," the court said in its unanimous judgement.

" The interest of a person in not being raped is an interest deserving of the very strongest protection. "

The man, known by the pseudonym Potter, was found guilty in South Australia of raping his sleeping wife on two occasions while the jury could not reach a verdict on two further counts.

The South Australian man's appeal was knocked down in the landmark judgment. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A month before the last rape, his wife recorded a conversation on her phone where she confronted Potter about the attacks and he admitted to doing them.

The woman gave evidence that she made the recording to "convince myself never to go back to him no matter what happened".

Protecting the rights of victim-survivors to record — and use as evidence — confessions of abuse inflicted on them is a major milestone for domestic violence law in Australia, legal expert Melbourne Law School's Heather Douglas said.

"The decision is important as it explicitly recognises that a lawful interest includes a right of bodily autonomy and integrity in the context of recordings," Professor Douglas said.

"Domestic and family violence is a violation of bodily autonomy and integrity."

How perpetrators use the court system to inflict harm Jessica Seage fought for six years for the man who raped her to be convicted. Experts say her experience is a stark example of how perpetrators abuse the system to inflict more pain on their victims.

The influence of the High Court's decision could extend beyond criminal cases, potentially allowing for similar recordings to be used in protection applications, Professor Douglas said.

However, it remains to be seen how far courts will allow secret recordings to be used to as evidence against less obvious forms of abuse.

"Much of the most damaging domestic and family violence is non-physical, such as coercive control, and this form of abuse impacts autonomy," Professor Douglas said.

"I would hope the understanding extends to that."

The husband is serving a nine-and-a-half-year prison term.

AAP

World.title: ‘Marshall should go’: Top corruption buster says fire union boss unfit to lead
World.content:
The workplace regulator should try to oust United Firefighters Union leader Peter Marshall from office over findings by Victoria’s corruption commission of backroom misconduct, according to prominent anti-corruption barrister Geoffrey Watson, SC. Victoria’s Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission released its Operation Richmond report on Wednesday, following a long-running legal battle by Marshall to prevent its release. United Firefighters Union secretary Peter Marshall in 2018. Eddie Jim It detailed events from 2014 to 2019 as the state Labor government and the UFU battled over enterprise bargaining agreements applying to fire agencies. And a decade after the political firestorm described in the report engulfed the Andrews government, many of the issues continue to loom large in Victoria’s fire services, with Fire Rescue Victoria recently accusing the union of bullying in an open letter posted to its website.



The Operation Richmond report, released this week, found senior public officers engaged in serious and concerning conduct, but on Thursday, Marshall rejected all accusations made against him in the document. “The IBAC report is very creative writing,” Marshall told this masthead. “That could have been done with a crayon. The only thing that’s missing is the pictures.” Related Article IBAC Champagne toasts, text boasts and treachery aplenty: Unpacking IBAC’s bombshell report The investigation exposed how former premier Daniel Andrews, ministers and senior bureaucrats ran secret backroom operations, misled cabinet, purged public boards, and repeatedly capitulated to pressure from Marshall and his union. The watchdog detailed secret hotel negotiations, middle-of-the-night text messages to ministers, undisclosed conciliation back channels, and the dismissal of boards that resisted union-backed workplace agreements.



Watson, who advised the administrator during the federal intervention into the CFMEU producing the landmark Rotting from the Top report, said the Fair Work Commission must examine whether Marshall remains fit to hold office under federal workplace laws. “There is no way that a person who’s identified as having conducted himself in such a manner – which involved threatening conduct and was the subject of complaints, and who avoided following procedures in a very careful, practised manner – there’s no way in the world that person should be heading up this union,” he said. Jane Hume, opposition industrial relations spokeswoman, said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese should remove the UFU’s affiliation with the Labor Party in the wake of IBAC’s Operation Richmond report. “The UFU isn’t interested in integrity in the union movement,” she said. Peter Marshall (centre, with microphone) leads a rally of firefighters in 2016 at Parliament House. Justin McManus Federal Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth was approached for comment, but her office did not respond by deadline.



Marshall, 64, has operated as the central powerbroker of Victorian emergency services for more than three decades, transforming his 4300-strong union into one of the state’s most formidable political forces. Related Article Updated

IBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Raised in a working-class family in West Brunswick, Marshall joined the Metropolitan Fire Brigade as a firefighter and responded to major industrial disasters, including the 1991 Coode Island chemical storage fire. He became state secretary of the firefighters’ union in 1995 and has held the post ever since. Disclosures filed with the Fair Work Commission show the union paid him a wage of $447,839 last financial year. Watson said there was mounting evidence that problematic union leadership in Australia led “to massive downstream problems. Marshall should go as the leader of the UFU, and I would urge the people at the Fair Work Commission to look at Operation Richmond with a view to seeing whether they can take steps to remove him.”



He said the Fair Work Act gave the Federal Court “ample power to have certain people declared” as inappropriate to lead a union. Defending his record and approach, Marshall rejected suggestions that his advocacy crossed boundaries or that his access to government figures was improper. “I’m privileged to represent very decent people who do a very important job, and that is they put their life on the line, protecting life and property,” he said. “I only have one audience to answer to, and that’s my members.” Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own Marshall defended his frequent communication, including calling Andrews at 4am, with senior politicians and public officials detailed in the Operation Richmond report, arguing this was standard across politics. “You tell me which union doesn’t speak to the government of the day. You tell me which business person doesn’t speak to conservative governments. Are we really saying that we want to put parliament into a glass bubble?” Marshall also attacked the corruption watchdog’s methods, questioning its use of phone intercepts and raids.



“Phone intercepts in relation to criminality or corruption have a place,” he said. “My house was raided by eight IBAC officers. They took my private papers, my family papers, my medical records. They listened to phone calls between my [partner], my family. There’s a total intrusion in your privacy. There’s an abolition of any civil rights you may have.” Watson countered that standing integrity bodies needed strong powers to investigate public sector misconduct and unpick complex arrangements. “You need extraordinary investigating powers which enable you to unpick [corruption]. The point with the public sector is that you do need these powers,” Watson said. “Of course [anti-corruption agencies like IBAC] should have them; it’s a critical component of the investigative powers of an organisation like this.” Watson also criticised the legal challenges that had delayed publication of Operation Richmond for several years. “This thing has been delayed for years by court processes,” he said, comparing Victoria’s processes with NSW, where “procedural fairness is afforded in a particular fashion”. Related Article Country Fire Authority The CFA wrote 33 pages about what went wrong last summer. Then its assessment was cut in half



Many of the issues at the heart of IBAC’s findings on Wednesday continue to plague Victoria’s fire services today. In July, Fire Rescue Victoria Commissioner Gavin Freeman wrote an open letter to the UFU urging it to put away “disgraceful” tactics to influence his organisation. He said that this “clearly amounts to bullying and creates a serious risk to the health and safety of FRV employees”. Freeman also noted the union had “unique” access to FRV workplaces, employees and systems, and urged them not to abuse this access. On Thursday, Victorian government minister Vicki Ward said it was taking IBAC’s recommendations “very seriously”. World.title: GenAI war continues as Alexa+ upgrades Amazon’s smart home
World.content:
Analysis TechnologyAI GenAI war continues as Alexa+ upgrades Amazon’s smart home Tim Biggs August 6, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a time of transition for big tech’s original voice assistants. Google has already rolled out its Gemini for Home to existing smart speakers and displays, while Apple is planning a new generative AI Siri for later this year. This week it’s Amazon’s turn, with the e-commerce giant announcing Alexa+ is launching in Australia. However, with a new breed of AI assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic and others already on all our devices, is it too late for the previous generation of chatty helpers? Alexa+ will work on most of Amazon’s Echo devices, but its latest models are designed with generative AI in mind. What is Alexa+? Supplanting the original Alexa that has been active in Australia for eight years, the new generative AI version is being promoted as more conversational, deeply personalised, and capable of completing real-world tasks. Built on Amazon’s own Bedrock cloud infrastructure, the new Alexa can choose between dozens of AI models including from Anthropic, Meta and others depending on the query, meaning it should adapt to give fast, efficient answers or complete longer tasks.



As with the new Google and Apple assistants, Alexa+ promises to go beyond the precisely worded, transactional interactions we’ve generally had with smart speakers to hear the weather or set kitchen timers. Amazon says the new system can intuit your meaning, parse rambling language and use context to help understand what you want. It remembers things you tell it about your preferences and your family, and you can even connect your calendar or upload documents to it. It will get to know the different members of your household by their voice or face. Alexa+ is initially rolling out to Australia as a preview. It works on most existing Echo devices, and users who want to test it out can sign up at the website and may be invited in the coming weeks. Anybody who buys one of the most recent devices (Echo Show 8, Echo Show 11, Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio), which have been custom-built for AI, will be invited automatically. Users will be able to decline the upgrade and stick with classic Alexa, at least for now. Alexa+ will be free during the preview, but afterwards it will be available via a $30-per-month standalone subscription, or included with Amazon Prime. And given Prime is $10 per month, it’s clear Amazon sees more value in using Alexa+ to pull people into the ecosystem than charging for it separately. Alexa in the time of ChatGPT So why choose a dedicated home assistant when Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT already live on our phones and laptops? Amazon’s Michele Butti, vice president of Alexa international, argues the advantage comes down to ambient, hands-free availability and shared household context.



“The ability to manage your smart home, the ability to play your entertainment, with great devices that have really phenomenal sound, or basically a TV on your Echo Show, no one else has offered those capabilities. It is the best ambient experience,” he said. If you don’t want to rely on your phone or computer, or you can’t because you’re cooking or doing something else, “then nothing like Alexa and now Alexa+ [will] allow you to use your voice to control your entertainment, your smart home, to have simple questions or simple tasks”. Alexa will soon be available via text chat on phones and web browsers, so you can access the same personal assistant outside of home. Some examples Butti gave of specific features enabled by Alexa+ involved the system using its new contextual capabilities. You could ask it to remind your son to do his homework the next time it saw him, and the message would trigger when he walked into range of your device’s camera. Or you could describe what you wanted your lights or air-conditioning to do, even if you didn’t know the names and settings of each device. “You can explicitly tell Alexa what you want her to remember about you and your family – ‘I don’t like mushrooms, and my friends Daniela and Ricardo that always come over for dinner, they are vegetarians’ – so that Alexa knows what to recommend. She learns through the interactions to get to know you and your family so that she becomes a better assistant,” he said.



“And [for smart home control] she can understand your intention, so you don’t need to remember the exact name. You can say, ‘take down all the blinds, but not the one in the office because I still want to see the sun there’. Something like that could have never happened before.” How the home genAI battle is shaping up Related Article Analysis

AI AI-powered Siri is on the way – but is it worth using? Generative AI models and smart home ecosystems are on an inevitable collision course. As Google, Apple, and Amazon revamp their assistants, they are racing against OpenAI and Anthropic to control the central interface between consumers and their purchases, appliances and communications. But while chatbots focus on information retrieval, with Google and OpenAI building infrastructure to go shopping on your behalf, Amazon’s retail dominance and hardware presence give it a distinct advantage in turning conversational AI into actual real-world commerce. For consumers, this tug-of-war marks the end of the simple smart speaker that plays your music and sets kitchen timers, and the rise of the paid digital concierge. The promise is a home that finally understands natural language and handles chores on your behalf without rigid commands.



The catch is that convenience now comes with tighter ecosystem lock-in, encouraging you to choose whether your daily life is run by Amazon, Apple, or Google, and meaning that even controlling your blinds becomes part of another monthly subscription. Meanwhile, as Amazon, Google and Apple move their assistants closer to the chatty, all-knowing design of a ChatGPT, the native generative AI companies will begin moving further into homes. Either way, the bot that offers to reword your emails and plan your trip itineraries will eventually be the same one that watches over your home, if for no other reason because you don’t want to pay for two ecosystems. World.title: Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player
World.content:
Geelong have backflipped on a written agreement with a senior player, who has a history of concussion, that waived his legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma. The Cats were forced to scrap the waiver on Thursday after the AFL revealed it had not approved the arrangement. However, the agreement was ratified by the Geelong board, chaired at the time by current AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond. The AFL is facing mounting legal actions over its liability for head trauma sustained on-field. AFL Photos The deal was also condemned by the AFL Players Association. The Geelong player, who has asked not to be named, signed the agreement acknowledging his elevated risk of concussion in 2024.



“The AFL and AFLPA are aware of a complex and unique case in which a Geelong player was cleared as fit to play following an assessment by an AFL concussion panel,” the league said in a statement. “The player then signed a letter acknowledging the potential risk and sought to waive some potential future legal rights, which was not lodged with or approved by the AFL or the AFLPA. “Geelong has advised the AFL today that the waiver in the letter will be removed, noting that the player continues to acknowledge potential risks. “The AFL is satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play.” Geelong CEO Steve Hocking confirmed the Cats had removed the waiver and said the player had not been directed to medically retire.



“Geelong Football Club acknowledges that the letter signed with one of its players went further than was intended and recognises the absence of the AFLPA in the process,” Hocking said in a club statement. “At the time, the club was involved in extensive discussions with a player, their family and representative in relation to that player’s concussion history. AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui “Those discussions, including medical advice from the club’s chief medical officer and the AFL concussion panel, were documented in the letter, signed by the player.” Hocking said the Cats were not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, nor attempting to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws.



“The club’s focus throughout the process was providing care and support to the player, with the intention to give the player agency in the decision-making process around their own playing career. “The club always aims to ensure that players are provided with information to enable them to make informed decisions about their careers.” The letter was approved by the Geelong board under then president Drummond, who made a statement to this masthead on Thursday night. “This matter was complex, sensitive and very carefully considered by the Geelong board at the time,” Drummond said. “The club has today addressed the reasons for decisions in relation to the player and the appropriate changes it will make going forward.” A source with knowledge of the deal but who was unable to speak on behalf of the club said the letter had given the Cats a level of comfort that the player had given informed consent and was aware of the risks.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL injury ward ‘Vague and embarrassing’: Cats’ doctors hit back at Rooke class action concussion claim Drummond left the Cats at the end of the 2024 season and is now the AFL chairman. The source said the player was happy with the support, care and treatment he had been given and wanted to continue his career. The player has played without issue since and, according to the source, continues to be supportive of the club. Two former Geelong doctors are caught up in a legal class action case with former Cats star Max Rooke as the lead plaintiff.



Rooke and a raft of players have alleged their lives were impacted by serious head knocks. The class action, brought by Margalit Injury Lawyers, is set to be heard in the Supreme Court of Victoria from May next year. Former Geelong doctors Chris Bradshaw and Geoff Allen are two of the listed third parties mentioned in Rooke’s statement of claim. AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher was critical of the Cats earlier on Thursday. “The game has a duty to provide a workplace that protects the health, safety, and wellbeing of players and all clubs hold this duty as employers,” Gallagher said.



“Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and standard playing contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws. Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.” Melbourne coach Steven King responded to the report at his media conference. Concussion is a growing issue for the AFL. Marija Ercegovac “All I’ll say about that is, as a club, or me personally, I would never do anything or ask my players to put themselves at risk,” King said. “I think what we are doing, and the things we have implemented in the game to help look after players’ safety and wellbeing has been really positive.



“As a coach, my opinion is, I would never ask a player to put himself at risk to play. Those decisions are with our doctors and medical team and that’s where, as a coach, I leave them to be honest.” Former Geelong defender Max Rooke is the lead plaintiff in a class action against the AFL. Paul Rovere WorkSafe is also investigating the AFL’s concussion management protocols. Sports law expert Leon Harris, who is doing his PhD in head trauma and concussion liability, said he was not surprised to hear such a contract had been drawn up. He said whether it was enforceable was another matter. “You can’t contract your way out of a statutory liability. If you have breached workplace health and safety requirements, you can’t say, ‘oh no we got them to sign a waiver for any injury they suffer at any point, we’re in the clear’,” Harris said.



Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist “So under the civil liability legislation in theory you would have rights still even if you were encouraged to contract your way out of those rights, but it just becomes a fight you don’t really want. “If the player as an adult knows the risk that they’re running by continuing to play and is willing to voluntarily assume that risk then, in a way, that’s up to the player. But the question then becomes, is it OK for a professional sporting organisation to allow somebody in that situation to assume that risk of harm, and that potentially is more of a moral question than a legal question.” Harris said part of the problem was that there was still a grey area around the issue as it was yet to be fully decided in court. There remained limited research around the prolonged effects of repeated sub-concussive head trauma, he added. While numerous legal actions have been brought in Australia and overseas, most have resulted in settlements.



“I think eventually it will end up going to a court to make a decision, whether it’s here, whether it’s in England … and they will make a ruling and a variety of sports will have decisions to make, unless those sports start putting rules in place now to deal with sub-concussive events, not just concussion.” - with Sam McClure Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: I’m alive today thanks to strangers who don’t even know my name
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessReal life Opinion I’m alive today thanks to strangers who don’t even know my name Ruby Atkinson Student August 6, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Why me? Why you? Why anyone? The question of “why” circled endlessly in my mind. When my life changed forever, I wondered why I was chosen from just 0.03 per cent of Australians. Ruby Atkinson today, aged 15. My life was simple, perfect, and sometimes even boring. I lived my life day by day, never imagining that my “normal” was about to be lost. After school on Friday, my parents saw the exhaustion written over my face. The paleness of my skin appeared cold and the darkness took over my eyes. It was dinner and straight to bed, they told me. The next morning they took me for a blood test, fearing that it might be low iron at worst. But deep down I wished it was nothing at all. As redness was drawn out of me, the sting from the prick remained so vividly in my mind, the first of many hundreds to come. Just four hours later, we were shocked to see our GP at the front door. She looked pensive and spoke calmly, “I’ve been trying to call you. You need to go to Sydney Children’s Hospital immediately. They are waiting for you”.



Ruby and her family, during her treatment for leukemia. We quickly gathered our things and flew out the door to be met by a team of professionals. Within what seemed like moments, we were delivered the news by a tall man in a suit, “I hope I am wrong, but I know I am right. Your daughter has leukaemia”. My heart dropped. I could hear the rapid beats. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. It was like a truck had run over my heart. I stood there frozen in time, confused and disengaged. Although my parents didn’t admit it, I knew that this was harder for them. I watched a singular tear flow down my mum’s cheek, before others joined the race. Ruby Atkinson during her treatment: I never imagined that my “normal” was about to be lost. Cancer is a word that is scarier than it sounds. Only six letters, yet a word that everyone fears as it creeps uninvited into people’s lives. It does not ask permission, it does not care who you are, it simply walks right into your life and changes it forever. I didn’t know it yet, but the intense years that followed, with endless blood tests, transfusions, medicines, overnight hospital stays, and surgeries, would all be endurable because of cancer research.



For me, cancer wasn’t just a disease. It was infinite time; time waiting in silence, time hearing nothing but my heartbeat, time under bright white hospital lights, time breathing tangy, antiseptic wafts. A pause in time. Related Article Brain cancer Clinical trial based on Richard Scolyer’s treatment offers new hope for brain cancer patients I entered this netherworld in these moments, mastering the art of waiting and noticing the little things that slowly became my new normal. The way my mum never let go of my hand, the steady beeping of machines, my dad’s continual “dad jokes” and the sad eyes of visitors walking by. Cancer has a way of bringing you firmly into the present. But all the while I could not help but wonder... …why me? I slowly realised that the question was never “Why me?” but “Why them?” Why would people I haven’t even met choose to help someone like me? A cancer diagnosis isn’t cured by just one doctor; it takes a whole research team, scientists far and wide in laboratories, people dedicating years to finding answers, all too rarely seeing their work in person. The people who I never met had the biggest impact on my life, not because they had to, but because they chose to. Every sunset I see and every “normal” day I live in is thanks to a stranger in a white coat who doesn’t even know my name. Ruby Atkinson is a Year 9 student.

World.title: Turning HSC band 5s into 6s: How this Sydney school raised the bar for every student
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC Turning HSC band 5s into 6s: How this Sydney school raised the bar for every student Christopher Harris and Nigel Gladstone August 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At Crestwood High in Sydney’s north-west, the start of the school year begins with the top student from the previous year addressing the next crop of HSC graduates. “When the dux comes back and talks honestly about how they studied, managed their time and balanced their lives, it’s very authentic,” says principal Tania Wright. If it’s meant to motivate them, it appears to be working. A Herald analysis of Higher School Certificate results using the metric of the average scores in each subject reveals Crestwood High is among the most-improved schools of recent years. On the annual HSC results rankings based on band 6s, released in December, the school placed 23rd among public non-selective schools, but on average scores across the full cohort it makes the top 10.



Crestwood has lifted its average HSC score across subjects to 80 last year, outperforming its average score over the past three years. Last year music 1 was the school’s top subject, followed by English advanced, with students recording an average score in each subject above 85. It was followed by visual arts, mathematics advanced and investigating science. Students from last year’s Crestwood High HSC class, which had an average score of more than 79 across all subjects. Sam Mooy The dux of the school is not the only one doing a presentation on success. Staff address other teachers in their faculties if the NSW Education Standards Authority results analysis shows they have excelled in a certain topic.



“Teachers who have achieved success, in terms of their HSC results within their subject, present to the rest of the staff about the particular aspects of teaching that they deliver, what their focus is on, and how they’ve been able to get the best out of the students,” Wright said. She said teacher expertise is also critical to results. There has been a concerted effort to shift students performing at a band 5 (a mark between 80 and 89), so the teachers workshopped what to do to push students up to band 6, and also band 4 into band 5. “We backward map from year 12 back into year 7. So, incrementally from year 7, each aspect of their writing becomes more and more sophisticated with their particular year groups.” Lake Macquarie High, south of Newcastle, recorded a 10 percentage point increase to its average score between 2023 and 2025. The school has also been recognised by the Department of Education as one of the state’s most-improved schools.



Principal Brendan Maher began leading the school more than a decade ago. “When I got there I had the difficulty of facing having the school closed because it was so underperforming and losing students so quickly,” he said. His first job was building connections in a bid to lift his school’s enrolments. The staff were talented teachers, he said, but benefited from professional learning. “I spent a motza on professional learning, to build staff confidence to learn and try new things,” he said.



Maher himself became a teacher after being made redundant when the BHP steelworks in Newcastle closed in September 1999. Related Article HSC The best public schools for HSC English, ranked Speaking as their school marked public education week, he said having staff work to mark HSC exams also boosted results. “I have a very highly committed executive team and staff, a lot of staff are encouraged to do HSC marking, which is the best level of professional development.” The school is a gifted and talented partner school, and recent upgrades to help teach the curriculum include a marine ecology lab, indoor gym, recording studio and commercial kitchen upgrade.



“Our focus isn’t on the band 6 results, it is the students who don’t think they can get the HSC, and they walk away with band 2s and 3s.” Related Article HSC We re-ranked schools by HSC averages. This is what the most precise data reveals But HSC results might be helping to lift enrolments, which have jumped from just under 250 students to more than 500 students next year. This analysis of HSC data uses precise average subject marks, contained in public high schools’ annual reports, across all subjects, released in July. This analysis stands in contrast to the Herald’s end-of-year HSC league tables, which use limited performance data provided by the NSW Education Standards Authority.



Other schools that had big improvement in average scores between 2023 and last year include Monaro High School, Casino High School and Kurri Kurri High School. Related Article HSC The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone An analysis of public schools released last year found top-performing schools “almost always” focused on high expectations, explicit teaching, effective feedback, using data to inform practice, assessment, classroom management, wellbeing and collaboration. Dr Jennifer Buckingham, the NSW Department of Education’s executive director of the Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation, said in the HSC a school’s strong learning culture often played a part. “It is not being competitive; they share resources, they’re a crew, students are sharing their knowledge with each other and seeing it as a group effort,” she said. World.title: Two sides of the coin on government priorities
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Two sides of the coin on government priorities August 6, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Political life’s a gamble. To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. In contrast to the government’s refusal to prioritise public good over private profit when it comes to gambling and gas, Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen’s insistence that data centres invest in renewable energy and pay the price is a welcome display of political fortitude (″⁣Bowen lays down the law to states on data centres″⁣, 6/8). Just as welcome is the agreement expressed by Belinda Dennett, chief executive of Data Centres Australia.

On the other hand, the refusal of the Queensland and Northern Territory governments to give their consent is as predictable as it is disappointing.

The issue that appears not to have been addressed in the debate is the data centres’ immense thirst for cooling water. The supply of clean renewable energy can be planned for and achieved.

How to provide water at scale in Australia’s arid, drought-prone land is a question that is crying out for an answer.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Now, to examine the ‘whales’ of pollution

Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen describes data centres as energy consumption ″⁣whales” predicted to use 10 per cent of the national grid’s electricity by 2050. It’s timely for Bowen to use federal powers to ensure these “whales” pull their weight: that they offset their electricity use with investments in wind and solar energy and storage.

This is good policy that works towards “Australian households and Australian energy reliability being put first”. Surely, the next step for fairness for Australian households is to ensure the “whales” of pollution – our oil and gas companies – pay for the climate consequences of their pollution. It’s only fair that they should pay for the fire, flood and wild weather damage that oil and gas

pollution create.

Karen Campbell, Geelong Labor, do the right thing on gambling

The government’s timid response to gambling reform (“Coalition, Greens force PM to rethink gambling reforms”, 6/8) is presumably explained by lobbying efforts from the gambling and connected industries, highlighting potential job losses. While many people “gamble responsibly”, many do not. The industry needs to be reined in, with advertising restrictions or banning a “no brainer” first step. If jobs are lost because the growth of this industry is curtailed (there is no guarantee that limiting advertising will achieve this), then so be it.

Big business never hesitates to make employees redundant if they can find more cost-effective options such as offshoring or AI. The government should stare down industry pressure and do what they did with the housing tax change legislation – the right thing.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick



Coming to grips with inflation

Australia’s inflation rate has been much higher in the past than it is now. During the 1970s and ’80s, the annual inflation rate was often above 10 per cent. However, governments at that time did not feel the need to offer cost-of-living support in the form of the ″⁣baubles and charms″⁣ dangled in front of the public in the way the federal government and increasingly state governments do now.

As columnist Peter Hartcher suggests (Comment, 1/8), governments now seem fixated on addressing the symptoms of inflation, the so-called cost-of-living crisis, rather than its cause. They don’t want to think about the cause because that would mean government admitting it is, at least partly, responsible for inflation.

No, it’s far easier for government to dangle another sparkly trinket and hope the public falls for it.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills Cabal is treating Labor as a fool

I’m on board with your correspondent’s conspiracy theory (Letters, 6/8) that a global cabal of fossil-fuel companies is behind the rise of populist parties like One Nation. However, after reading columnist Caitlin Fitzsimmons’ excellent analysis, “Fuel tax rebates undermining climate action goals” (6/8), I can only conclude that same cabal is also supporting the Labor government.

Peter Cook, Essendon THE FORUM Has to be cut-off point

Any ode to the beauty and health benefits of trees always generates correspondence advocating for governments and councils to enforce tree preservation at all costs (″⁣Not too late to provide statewide tree measures″⁣, 4/8).

My perspective urges more consideration for the private home owners’ situation. I have more than 20 trees on my suburban block, most planted by us. However, it has been a pre-existing planting of a Himalayan cedar dominating the front garden close to the house that has proved problematic. Its massive size towers over our heritage home, many limbs have dropped, bringing down power lines on numerous occasions, and risks of further falls prevent any activity under canopy stretching the width of property. Regular reduction via pruning is very costly.

State and local governments need to introduce the criteria enabling removal in exceptional circumstances where the species of trees has outgrown its position in an urban residential garden.

Diana Yallop, Surrey Hills Channelled message

Your correspondent (Letters, 5/8) offers three good and pragmatic reasons not to ignore One Nation in political reporting.

But it is his final sentence that is the most cogent – the proposition that One Nation voters are unlikely to access the nominated media sources. The One Nation organisation seems to have hitched its wagon to the Murdoch organisation’s media – and its supporters’ views and outlook are likely to be influenced by the latter’s content.

Admirable as the letters are in The Age (concerning One Nation), they are messages to similar-minded Australians and not likely to reach those people who currently indicate a voter preference for One Nation.

Brian Kidd, Mt. Waverley



The easy option

It is quite right for One Nation to bar certain media outlets from its media conferences for their continuous asking about the party’s policies and candidates’ controversial views.

In her earlier years, such questions would draw from Pauline Hanson the response of “Please Explain”.

Much easier not to be embarrassed or have to explain at all.

Harry Kowalski, Ivanhoe Premise broken

It’s terrific to see opposition to the premise that all perpetrators of sexual offences need their identity protected for the good of their mental health (″⁣Psychiatrists cast doubt on court orders″⁣, 6/8).

Protecting the identity of perpetrators is often framed as concern for their partners and children, and of course, the victim. Learning that a partner, father or family member has raped someone must be horrifying, complicated and confusing, working through feelings of disbelief, betrayal and grief. But protecting perpetrators is about just that: protecting them, their reputation and their social capital. Their ″⁣concern″⁣ for their family (or the victim) was not front of mind when they committed the crime. They were thinking only about their immediate wants and how they could get away with it.

Protecting perpetrators is about upholding the status quo, and this just leads to more of the same.

Christine Craik, Darraweit Guim Drop in the ocean

Caitlin Fitzsimmons captures Australia’s climate policy dilemma perfectly: we’re bailing out a boat with a teaspoon while pouring water in by the bucket (“Fuel tax rebates undermining climate action goals”, 6/8). The $8.8 billion in diesel subsidies paid to big polluters not only encourages more use of dirty fuel, but it far exceeds what is spent on cutting climate emissions via the Safeguard Mechanism.

And the sheer volume of coal and gas Australia exports easily outweighs the gains we make from installing solar panels and batteries at home. Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen often highlights Australia’s impressive uptake of solar, batteries and EVs, but until the Albanese government begins winding down coal and gas production, these improvements will remain a drop in the ocean.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Mystery deliveries

My Bolivian partner was surprised to read about her country’s lack of a functioning postal service in her city, La Paz (“Think the census is annoying? Try a 24-hour lockdown”, 6/8). She is now wondering how all the letters she wrote and received to and from family and friends were magically sent and delivered.

James O’Keefe, Prahran Sign of the times

I applaud the state government’s strategy for saving taxpayers’ dollars in the way it has addressed the “pothole” issue. Instead of wasting money on actually fixing the potholes, it now erects a sign that says, “Rough Surface Ahead.“But the state government has also come up with a new cost-cutting measure. Instead of wasting money on the sign, it simply spray-paints an orange arrow on the road where the pothole is. Marvellous. What will they think of next?

Robert Langworthy, Bayswater North



Take us home . . .

Your correspondent (Letters, 6/8) suggested bringing the Country Roads Board back. Yes, but ensure the board is composed entirely of engineers and ensure that its workload can be organised in the most efficient way, not one that prima facie requires work done by contractors.

Only engineers can ensure we get value for our money.

Laurie Comerford, Chelsea Catastrophes, then, now

Many think the world is in dire straits.

With the senseless Iran war and the Middle East erupting, the man-made climate catastrophes unfolding in Europe and the United States with record temperatures, droughts and fires, people enduring cost-of-living crises, political instability in many countries and populist demagogues on the rise, toxic social media’s extraordinary reach and the uncertain future the consequences of AI pose, the list is endless.

But do we catastrophise the present? Think of the world of the 1940s with Hitler jack-booting his way across Europe, murdering Jews, homosexuals, Jehovah Witnesses, the mad, disabled children and political prisoners and the whole world at war.

We have always lived with world conflict and uncertainty, but is it different in 2026? It is easy to think of the present as dire, but history teaches us that we have lived through many other catastrophes before and survived.

Sandy Jeffs, Christmas Hills Think it through

My dad used to remind me to ″⁣think things through″⁣ whenever I was about to make a momentous decision. The same advice needs to be given to those voters who believe One Nation is the answer to our country’s woes. Nothing could be further from the truth.

At this time of great volatility and uncertainty in the world, the last thing we need is a parliament containing new One Nation members pushing their own far-right barrows of political populism and division with not a positive, constructive idea among them.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris A nation of migrants

It was a brave thing for Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, to defer his speech due yesterday on immigration to allow further internal consultation to more deeply consider flow-on effects (“Opponents circle Labor over delay to migration cut”, 6/8).

Labor intends to reduce migration by 75,000 over the next two years. They are sensible in getting the appropriate and workable numbers of migrants, and Chris Bowen says we need to consider demand for workers.

Migrants have traditionally been small business owners as well as providing labour. They have built infrastructure and enhanced our cultural diversity.

Humanitarian considerations also must play a part in our migrant intake.

Labor must avoid being pushed into actions by the attitude of One Nation and the baying of Liberal politicians for speed in this matter. Government must consider the rights of all constituents, not just the vocal ones.

We are a nation of migrants and multiculturalism, and we should remember and celebrate this.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Need for more rooms

The latest figures from the Coroners Court of Victoria show fatal overdoses in Geelong have increased by 25 per cent compared with the previous year, renewing calls for a medically supervised injecting room.

The evidence from North Richmond is compelling. This service has prevented overdose deaths, reduced public injecting and enabled immediate medical care during overdoses.

Beyond crisis intervention, it provides access to mental health care, housing support and pathways into drug treatment for people who might otherwise never engage with these services.

If we accept the evidence that medically supervised injecting rooms save lives and improve public amenity, why are they confined to so few locations?

Surely, a proven, life-saving health service should be available wherever the need exists, not just in one suburb.

When the evidence is this strong, expanding access to a safe injecting room should be a matter of public health, not politics.

Sue McNamara, Rye



The bankruptcy move

US President Donald Trump has built his commercial empire on never backing down or, when he had to, declaring business bankruptcy to clear the books.

Pity he can’t just pull the whole Iran thing and declare bankruptcy again.

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

If anyone has doubts about One Nation and its policies, the article, ″⁣Victorian pick a self-described conspiracy theorist″⁣ (5/8), about Warren Pickering should relegate the party to political oblivion .

Greg Bardin, Altona North What a thrill to have a conspiracy theorist as leader of the Victorian One Nation party. Just what we need. Jennifer Gerrand, Carlton North



Shaun Carney (Comment, 6/8) lauds the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, for his leadership. I confess that I am disappointed the PM is being so timid. I wish he would go further on taxation reform, gambling reform and other issues. I had hoped for so much more.

Juliet Flesch, Kew Furthermore

I can handle ″⁣learning″⁣ as a noun, as in ″⁣learning is fun″⁣. But ″⁣learnings″⁣, ″⁣understandings″⁣? No thanks. Lindsay Zoch, Mildura I mustn’t have been betting enough. I was only offered a blow-up doll and a packet of aspirin (″⁣Regulators struggle to curb surge of influencers advocating betting″⁣, 6/8).

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West If all airlines enforced a strict and reasonable carry-on baggage rule, it would expedite the boarding process for everyone.

Tony Jackson, Fitzroy It is great that Jetstar is to charge up to $52 for passengers to put bags in overhead lockers. For too long, sensible passengers have suffered from those who bring suitcase-size bags on board, clutter the aisles and hog all the lockers.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris



If wholesale electricity prices are falling, Chris Bowen, why aren’t retail?

Ian Anderson, Surrey Hills President Donald Trump has said, again, that Iran and the United States are close to an agreement on the re-opening of the Strait

of Hormuz. Sure. I can’t understand why anyone listens to Trump any more or takes what he says seriously. Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights Finally

Where do I vote for my favourite pothole?

Luise Mock, Tawonga South

World.title: ‘Marshall should go’: Top corruption buster says fire union boss unfit to lead
World.content:
The workplace regulator should try to oust United Firefighters Union leader Peter Marshall from office over findings by Victoria’s corruption commission of backroom misconduct, according to prominent anti-corruption barrister Geoffrey Watson, SC. Victoria’s Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission released its Operation Richmond report on Wednesday, following a long-running legal battle by Marshall to prevent its release. United Firefighters Union secretary Peter Marshall in 2018. Eddie Jim It detailed events from 2014 to 2019 as the state Labor government and the UFU battled over enterprise bargaining agreements applying to fire agencies. And a decade after the political firestorm described in the report engulfed the Andrews government, many of the issues continue to loom large in Victoria’s fire services, with Fire Rescue Victoria recently accusing the union of bullying in an open letter posted to its website.



The Operation Richmond report, released this week, found senior public officers engaged in serious and concerning conduct, but on Thursday, Marshall rejected all accusations made against him in the document. “The IBAC report is very creative writing,” Marshall told this masthead. “That could have been done with a crayon. The only thing that’s missing is the pictures.” Related Article IBAC Champagne toasts, text boasts and treachery aplenty: Unpacking IBAC’s bombshell report The investigation exposed how former premier Daniel Andrews, ministers and senior bureaucrats ran secret backroom operations, misled cabinet, purged public boards, and repeatedly capitulated to pressure from Marshall and his union. The watchdog detailed secret hotel negotiations, middle-of-the-night text messages to ministers, undisclosed conciliation back channels, and the dismissal of boards that resisted union-backed workplace agreements.



Watson, who advised the administrator during the federal intervention into the CFMEU producing the landmark Rotting from the Top report, said the Fair Work Commission must examine whether Marshall remains fit to hold office under federal workplace laws. “There is no way that a person who’s identified as having conducted himself in such a manner – which involved threatening conduct and was the subject of complaints, and who avoided following procedures in a very careful, practised manner – there’s no way in the world that person should be heading up this union,” he said. Jane Hume, opposition industrial relations spokeswoman, said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese should remove the UFU’s affiliation with the Labor Party in the wake of IBAC’s Operation Richmond report. “The UFU isn’t interested in integrity in the union movement,” she said. Peter Marshall (centre, with microphone) leads a rally of firefighters in 2016 at Parliament House. Justin McManus Federal Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth was approached for comment, but her office did not respond by deadline.



Marshall, 64, has operated as the central powerbroker of Victorian emergency services for more than three decades, transforming his 4300-strong union into one of the state’s most formidable political forces. Related Article Updated

IBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Raised in a working-class family in West Brunswick, Marshall joined the Metropolitan Fire Brigade as a firefighter and responded to major industrial disasters, including the 1991 Coode Island chemical storage fire. He became state secretary of the firefighters’ union in 1995 and has held the post ever since. Disclosures filed with the Fair Work Commission show the union paid him a wage of $447,839 last financial year. Watson said there was mounting evidence that problematic union leadership in Australia led “to massive downstream problems. Marshall should go as the leader of the UFU, and I would urge the people at the Fair Work Commission to look at Operation Richmond with a view to seeing whether they can take steps to remove him.”



He said the Fair Work Act gave the Federal Court “ample power to have certain people declared” as inappropriate to lead a union. Defending his record and approach, Marshall rejected suggestions that his advocacy crossed boundaries or that his access to government figures was improper. “I’m privileged to represent very decent people who do a very important job, and that is they put their life on the line, protecting life and property,” he said. “I only have one audience to answer to, and that’s my members.” Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Carroll declares integrity a non-negotiable – and defends his own Marshall defended his frequent communication, including calling Andrews at 4am, with senior politicians and public officials detailed in the Operation Richmond report, arguing this was standard across politics. “You tell me which union doesn’t speak to the government of the day. You tell me which business person doesn’t speak to conservative governments. Are we really saying that we want to put parliament into a glass bubble?” Marshall also attacked the corruption watchdog’s methods, questioning its use of phone intercepts and raids.



“Phone intercepts in relation to criminality or corruption have a place,” he said. “My house was raided by eight IBAC officers. They took my private papers, my family papers, my medical records. They listened to phone calls between my [partner], my family. There’s a total intrusion in your privacy. There’s an abolition of any civil rights you may have.” Watson countered that standing integrity bodies needed strong powers to investigate public sector misconduct and unpick complex arrangements. “You need extraordinary investigating powers which enable you to unpick [corruption]. The point with the public sector is that you do need these powers,” Watson said. “Of course [anti-corruption agencies like IBAC] should have them; it’s a critical component of the investigative powers of an organisation like this.” Watson also criticised the legal challenges that had delayed publication of Operation Richmond for several years. “This thing has been delayed for years by court processes,” he said, comparing Victoria’s processes with NSW, where “procedural fairness is afforded in a particular fashion”. Related Article Country Fire Authority The CFA wrote 33 pages about what went wrong last summer. Then its assessment was cut in half



Many of the issues at the heart of IBAC’s findings on Wednesday continue to plague Victoria’s fire services today. In July, Fire Rescue Victoria Commissioner Gavin Freeman wrote an open letter to the UFU urging it to put away “disgraceful” tactics to influence his organisation. He said that this “clearly amounts to bullying and creates a serious risk to the health and safety of FRV employees”. Freeman also noted the union had “unique” access to FRV workplaces, employees and systems, and urged them not to abuse this access. On Thursday, Victorian government minister Vicki Ward said it was taking IBAC’s recommendations “very seriously”.
