World.title: GenAI war continues as Alexa+ upgrades Amazon’s smart home
World.content:
Analysis TechnologyAI GenAI war continues as Alexa+ upgrades Amazon’s smart home Tim Biggs August 6, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a time of transition for big tech’s original voice assistants. Google has already rolled out its Gemini for Home to existing smart speakers and displays, while Apple is planning a new generative AI Siri for later this year. This week it’s Amazon’s turn, with the e-commerce giant announcing Alexa+ is launching in Australia. However, with a new breed of AI assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic and others already on all our devices, is it too late for the previous generation of chatty helpers? Alexa+ will work on most of Amazon’s Echo devices, but its latest models are designed with generative AI in mind. What is Alexa+? Supplanting the original Alexa that has been active in Australia for eight years, the new generative AI version is being promoted as more conversational, deeply personalised, and capable of completing real-world tasks. Built on Amazon’s own Bedrock cloud infrastructure, the new Alexa can choose between dozens of AI models including from Anthropic, Meta and others depending on the query, meaning it should adapt to give fast, efficient answers or complete longer tasks.



As with the new Google and Apple assistants, Alexa+ promises to go beyond the precisely worded, transactional interactions we’ve generally had with smart speakers to hear the weather or set kitchen timers. Amazon says the new system can intuit your meaning, parse rambling language and use context to help understand what you want. It remembers things you tell it about your preferences and your family, and you can even connect your calendar or upload documents to it. It will get to know the different members of your household by their voice or face. Alexa+ is initially rolling out to Australia as a preview. It works on most existing Echo devices, and users who want to test it out can sign up at the website and may be invited in the coming weeks. Anybody who buys one of the most recent devices (Echo Show 8, Echo Show 11, Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio), which have been custom-built for AI, will be invited automatically. Users will be able to decline the upgrade and stick with classic Alexa, at least for now. Alexa+ will be free during the preview, but afterwards it will be available via a $30-per-month standalone subscription, or included with Amazon Prime. And given Prime is $10 per month, it’s clear Amazon sees more value in using Alexa+ to pull people into the ecosystem than charging for it separately. Alexa in the time of ChatGPT So why choose a dedicated home assistant when Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT already live on our phones and laptops? Amazon’s Michele Butti, vice president of Alexa international, argues the advantage comes down to ambient, hands-free availability and shared household context.



“The ability to manage your smart home, the ability to play your entertainment, with great devices that have really phenomenal sound, or basically a TV on your Echo Show, no one else has offered those capabilities. It is the best ambient experience,” he said. If you don’t want to rely on your phone or computer, or you can’t because you’re cooking or doing something else, “then nothing like Alexa and now Alexa+ [will] allow you to use your voice to control your entertainment, your smart home, to have simple questions or simple tasks”. Alexa will soon be available via text chat on phones and web browsers, so you can access the same personal assistant outside of home. Some examples Butti gave of specific features enabled by Alexa+ involved the system using its new contextual capabilities. You could ask it to remind your son to do his homework the next time it saw him, and the message would trigger when he walked into range of your device’s camera. Or you could describe what you wanted your lights or air-conditioning to do, even if you didn’t know the names and settings of each device. “You can explicitly tell Alexa what you want her to remember about you and your family – ‘I don’t like mushrooms, and my friends Daniela and Ricardo that always come over for dinner, they are vegetarians’ – so that Alexa knows what to recommend. She learns through the interactions to get to know you and your family so that she becomes a better assistant,” he said.



“And [for smart home control] she can understand your intention, so you don’t need to remember the exact name. You can say, ‘take down all the blinds, but not the one in the office because I still want to see the sun there’. Something like that could have never happened before.” How the home genAI battle is shaping up Related Article Analysis

AI AI-powered Siri is on the way – but is it worth using? Generative AI models and smart home ecosystems are on an inevitable collision course. As Google, Apple, and Amazon revamp their assistants, they are racing against OpenAI and Anthropic to control the central interface between consumers and their purchases, appliances and communications. But while chatbots focus on information retrieval, with Google and OpenAI building infrastructure to go shopping on your behalf, Amazon’s retail dominance and hardware presence give it a distinct advantage in turning conversational AI into actual real-world commerce. For consumers, this tug-of-war marks the end of the simple smart speaker that plays your music and sets kitchen timers, and the rise of the paid digital concierge. The promise is a home that finally understands natural language and handles chores on your behalf without rigid commands.



The catch is that convenience now comes with tighter ecosystem lock-in, encouraging you to choose whether your daily life is run by Amazon, Apple, or Google, and meaning that even controlling your blinds becomes part of another monthly subscription. Meanwhile, as Amazon, Google and Apple move their assistants closer to the chatty, all-knowing design of a ChatGPT, the native generative AI companies will begin moving further into homes. Either way, the bot that offers to reword your emails and plan your trip itineraries will eventually be the same one that watches over your home, if for no other reason because you don’t want to pay for two ecosystems. World.title: Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player
World.content:
Geelong have backflipped on a written agreement with a senior player, who has a history of concussion, that waived his legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma. The Cats were forced to scrap the waiver on Thursday after the AFL revealed it had not approved the arrangement. However, the agreement was ratified by the Geelong board, chaired at the time by current AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond. The AFL is facing mounting legal actions over its liability for head trauma sustained on-field. AFL Photos The deal was also condemned by the AFL Players Association. The Geelong player, who has asked not to be named, signed the agreement acknowledging his elevated risk of concussion in 2024.



“The AFL and AFLPA are aware of a complex and unique case in which a Geelong player was cleared as fit to play following an assessment by an AFL concussion panel,” the league said in a statement. “The player then signed a letter acknowledging the potential risk and sought to waive some potential future legal rights, which was not lodged with or approved by the AFL or the AFLPA. “Geelong has advised the AFL today that the waiver in the letter will be removed, noting that the player continues to acknowledge potential risks. “The AFL is satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play.” Geelong CEO Steve Hocking confirmed the Cats had removed the waiver and said the player had not been directed to medically retire.



“Geelong Football Club acknowledges that the letter signed with one of its players went further than was intended and recognises the absence of the AFLPA in the process,” Hocking said in a club statement. “At the time, the club was involved in extensive discussions with a player, their family and representative in relation to that player’s concussion history. AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui “Those discussions, including medical advice from the club’s chief medical officer and the AFL concussion panel, were documented in the letter, signed by the player.” Hocking said the Cats were not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, nor attempting to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws.



“The club’s focus throughout the process was providing care and support to the player, with the intention to give the player agency in the decision-making process around their own playing career. “The club always aims to ensure that players are provided with information to enable them to make informed decisions about their careers.” The letter was approved by the Geelong board under then president Drummond, who made a statement to this masthead on Thursday night. “This matter was complex, sensitive and very carefully considered by the Geelong board at the time,” Drummond said. “The club has today addressed the reasons for decisions in relation to the player and the appropriate changes it will make going forward.” A source with knowledge of the deal but who was unable to speak on behalf of the club said the letter had given the Cats a level of comfort that the player had given informed consent and was aware of the risks.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL injury ward ‘Vague and embarrassing’: Cats’ doctors hit back at Rooke class action concussion claim Drummond left the Cats at the end of the 2024 season and is now the AFL chairman. The source said the player was happy with the support, care and treatment he had been given and wanted to continue his career. The player has played without issue since and, according to the source, continues to be supportive of the club. Two former Geelong doctors are caught up in a legal class action case with former Cats star Max Rooke as the lead plaintiff.



Rooke and a raft of players have alleged their lives were impacted by serious head knocks. The class action, brought by Margalit Injury Lawyers, is set to be heard in the Supreme Court of Victoria from May next year. Former Geelong doctors Chris Bradshaw and Geoff Allen are two of the listed third parties mentioned in Rooke’s statement of claim. AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher was critical of the Cats earlier on Thursday. “The game has a duty to provide a workplace that protects the health, safety, and wellbeing of players and all clubs hold this duty as employers,” Gallagher said.



“Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and standard playing contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws. Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.” Melbourne coach Steven King responded to the report at his media conference. Concussion is a growing issue for the AFL. Marija Ercegovac “All I’ll say about that is, as a club, or me personally, I would never do anything or ask my players to put themselves at risk,” King said. “I think what we are doing, and the things we have implemented in the game to help look after players’ safety and wellbeing has been really positive.



“As a coach, my opinion is, I would never ask a player to put himself at risk to play. Those decisions are with our doctors and medical team and that’s where, as a coach, I leave them to be honest.” Former Geelong defender Max Rooke is the lead plaintiff in a class action against the AFL. Paul Rovere WorkSafe is also investigating the AFL’s concussion management protocols. Sports law expert Leon Harris, who is doing his PhD in head trauma and concussion liability, said he was not surprised to hear such a contract had been drawn up. He said whether it was enforceable was another matter. “You can’t contract your way out of a statutory liability. If you have breached workplace health and safety requirements, you can’t say, ‘oh no we got them to sign a waiver for any injury they suffer at any point, we’re in the clear’,” Harris said.



Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist “So under the civil liability legislation in theory you would have rights still even if you were encouraged to contract your way out of those rights, but it just becomes a fight you don’t really want. “If the player as an adult knows the risk that they’re running by continuing to play and is willing to voluntarily assume that risk then, in a way, that’s up to the player. But the question then becomes, is it OK for a professional sporting organisation to allow somebody in that situation to assume that risk of harm, and that potentially is more of a moral question than a legal question.” Harris said part of the problem was that there was still a grey area around the issue as it was yet to be fully decided in court. There remained limited research around the prolonged effects of repeated sub-concussive head trauma, he added. While numerous legal actions have been brought in Australia and overseas, most have resulted in settlements.



“I think eventually it will end up going to a court to make a decision, whether it’s here, whether it’s in England … and they will make a ruling and a variety of sports will have decisions to make, unless those sports start putting rules in place now to deal with sub-concussive events, not just concussion.” - with Sam McClure Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: I’m alive today thanks to strangers who don’t even know my name
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessReal life Opinion I’m alive today thanks to strangers who don’t even know my name Ruby Atkinson Student August 6, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Why me? Why you? Why anyone? The question of “why” circled endlessly in my mind. When my life changed forever, I wondered why I was chosen from just 0.03 per cent of Australians. Ruby Atkinson today, aged 15. My life was simple, perfect, and sometimes even boring. I lived my life day by day, never imagining that my “normal” was about to be lost. After school on Friday, my parents saw the exhaustion written over my face. The paleness of my skin appeared cold and the darkness took over my eyes. It was dinner and straight to bed, they told me. The next morning they took me for a blood test, fearing that it might be low iron at worst. But deep down I wished it was nothing at all. As redness was drawn out of me, the sting from the prick remained so vividly in my mind, the first of many hundreds to come. Just four hours later, we were shocked to see our GP at the front door. She looked pensive and spoke calmly, “I’ve been trying to call you. You need to go to Sydney Children’s Hospital immediately. They are waiting for you”.



Ruby and her family, during her treatment for leukemia. We quickly gathered our things and flew out the door to be met by a team of professionals. Within what seemed like moments, we were delivered the news by a tall man in a suit, “I hope I am wrong, but I know I am right. Your daughter has leukaemia”. My heart dropped. I could hear the rapid beats. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. It was like a truck had run over my heart. I stood there frozen in time, confused and disengaged. Although my parents didn’t admit it, I knew that this was harder for them. I watched a singular tear flow down my mum’s cheek, before others joined the race. Ruby Atkinson during her treatment: I never imagined that my “normal” was about to be lost. Cancer is a word that is scarier than it sounds. Only six letters, yet a word that everyone fears as it creeps uninvited into people’s lives. It does not ask permission, it does not care who you are, it simply walks right into your life and changes it forever. I didn’t know it yet, but the intense years that followed, with endless blood tests, transfusions, medicines, overnight hospital stays, and surgeries, would all be endurable because of cancer research.



For me, cancer wasn’t just a disease. It was infinite time; time waiting in silence, time hearing nothing but my heartbeat, time under bright white hospital lights, time breathing tangy, antiseptic wafts. A pause in time. Related Article Brain cancer Clinical trial based on Richard Scolyer’s treatment offers new hope for brain cancer patients I entered this netherworld in these moments, mastering the art of waiting and noticing the little things that slowly became my new normal. The way my mum never let go of my hand, the steady beeping of machines, my dad’s continual “dad jokes” and the sad eyes of visitors walking by. Cancer has a way of bringing you firmly into the present. But all the while I could not help but wonder... …why me? I slowly realised that the question was never “Why me?” but “Why them?” Why would people I haven’t even met choose to help someone like me? A cancer diagnosis isn’t cured by just one doctor; it takes a whole research team, scientists far and wide in laboratories, people dedicating years to finding answers, all too rarely seeing their work in person. The people who I never met had the biggest impact on my life, not because they had to, but because they chose to. Every sunset I see and every “normal” day I live in is thanks to a stranger in a white coat who doesn’t even know my name. Ruby Atkinson is a Year 9 student.

World.title: NZ Warriors recall Luke Metcalf for crucial NRL clash against Penrith Panthers
World.content:
NRL: NZ Warriors v Penrith Panthers

Kickoff: 8pm Friday, 7 August

Go Media Stadium, Auckland

Live blog updates on RNZ

Departing NZ Warriors half Luke Metcalf has been recalled to the starting line-up for their crucial NRL home clash with Penrith Panthers on Friday.

Incumbent halfback Te Maire Martin, who left last week's win against the Gold Coast Titans early, apparently aggravated a hamstring injury at training this week and has been ruled out 24 hours from kickoff at Auckland's Go Media Stadium.

Metcalf, 27, enjoyed a breakout season in 2025, until he suffered a knee injury that ended his campaign and delayed his 2026 return.

Over the summer, he extended his contract with the club, but in his absence, Tanah Boyd consolidated his grip on the No.7 jersey and, uncertain of his future with the Warriors, Metcalf sought an early release and signed with St George-Illawarra Dragons for 2027.

Although Boyd also suffered a season-ending knee injury, Martin was promoted into the halfback position and has held it since Round 11, impressing with his form and also signing a contract extension for 2027.

Metcalf has played just two first-grade games this season - both losses - and tweaked a hamstring against Cronulla Sharks in April. Coach Andrew Webster has resisted calls to bring him back during a mid-season slump that saw four defeats over seven games.

Metcalf has turned out for the club reserves in NSW Cup and occupied a spot on the interchange bench, without being required to take the field.

World.title: Timeline to implement new school subjects 'unrealistic', teachers' union warns
World.content:
Industry leaders are enthusiastic about nine new secondary school subjects announced on Thursday, but the teachers' union warns the timeline to develop and introduce them is extremely tight.

The government says industry skills boards will develop the subjects for introduction in 2029, when a new qualification replaces the NCEA.

The subjects are:

Next-Gen manufacturing

Applied intelligent systems

Construction and built environment

Energy and infrastructure

Engineering technology

Food and fibre systems

Health services and care

Hospitality, food and beverage

Tourism

Education Minister Erica Stanford announced the subjects with Finance Minister Nicola Willis at Meridian Energy's Mākara windfarm, overlooking Cook Strait.

New proposed subjects may sway number of early leavers Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

She said it was critical that industry helped write the new content.

"They are the people on the ground who know what the skills and knowledge are that they will need for the future," she said. "That is being built into the curriculum, so these young people, when they leave school, will have relevant knowledge and skills to be able to.. walk into either jobs, further training, apprenticeships or through to university."

Stanford said the new subjects would vary less than NCEA subjects, and would better equip teens with skills and knowledge that employers wanted.

She said more industry-led subjects may be added.

Stanford said not all schools would be able to offer all nine subjects, and some might work together or with local trades academies to provide them.

Naenae College students Lydia Campbell, Daytona Falwasser, and Reagan Cronje said the subjects provided good opportunities for future generations, but were not sure they would study them. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"There will, of course, always be some in-school provision as well, and that's why we're working with the likes of the PPTA and the Teaching Council to make sure that we can get those people the pay that they require to be able to teach," she said.

Teachers' union vice-president Kieran Gainsford said the PPTA supported industry-led subjects, but there was a lot to work out before 2029.

"In some cases, schools are going to need very technical learning spaces or technical equipment," he said. "They're going to need specialist staff often from industry and those people are going to have to be recruited... and then we have to keep them in schools.

"There's a lot of work to happen between now and then, and unless we get the details pretty pronto, that timeline does start to look a little bit unrealistic."

Gainsford said who would teach the subjects was not clear.

"We're desperately keen to know exactly what the government's plan is for the delivery of these subjects, because until we see that, we can't get started on making it work for the kids," he said.

Gainsford said some of the subjects could be offered by schools and already were, but others, like applied intelligence systems, would require more teachers.

"There's going to have to be some additions to the teaching workforce to make those possible and that needs to happen really now," he said.

"We want those people in schools before we start teaching this stuff."

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge was enthusiastic about the new subjects. RNZ/John Gerritsen

Industry leaders at the launch were enthusiastic and said one of the main effects of the new subjects would be to open students' eyes to potential careers in industries they had never heard of, many of which faced serious workforce shortages in future.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge said the energy and infrastructure subject would bring entirely new courses to schools.

"This is new," he said. "In my sector - energy and infrastructure - there's nothing at school.

"There's a bit of geology, a bit of physics, but really there's nothing about energy and infrastructure."

Aldridge said the board wanted to see the subject offered in all schools.

He said whether the subject would be taught in schools or in trades academies run by polytechnics or other tertiary providers was yet to be determined.

Some of the new subjects, such as tourism and building, already existed in some form in schools.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly said letting industry have a hand in what's taught would have several advantages over the current system.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"One is it raises the status of some trades, so that it gives it equal status within the secondary schools," he said. "Secondly, it does give recognised skills across the country, so when students come out of secondary school, they've got something to show that is a nationally accepted standard that they've achieved.

"It will be more comprehensive and more linked-up, so it's connected to potential employment. At the moment, there are some good courses, but they're not consistent right across the country and really depend on the individual school."

Rotorua Girls High School principal Sarah Davis was seconded to the Education Ministry to work on the subjects.

She said the involvement of industry would ensure the subjects created real pathways to jobs.

Davis said some teachers already had industry qualifications and might be able to teach the new subjects.

World.title: Wellington City councillors vote yes on super-merger proposal
World.content:
Wellington city councillors have unanimously agreed to submit a super-merger proposal to the government this weekend.

Councillors expressed "preference" that Wairarapa be excluded, and for the Hutt Valley, Porirua, and Wellington City to merge. However, they ultimately voted to support a wider regional proposal if mayors agreed on that.

Regional mayors will decide on Friday on the exact model - which could see a Wellington-Wairarapa unitary council - merging 8 councils together.

A layer of community councils could represent the Hutt Valley, Wairarapa, Porirua, Wellington City and Kāpiti.

In an hours-long debate, Councillors discussed whether they should force Upper Hutt into a merged council, whether Wairarapa should be included, or if a referendum should be put to residents.

In the Wellington-Wairarapa region there are currently eight territorial authorities and one regional council. There are 106 elected members, 12 community boards, and 55 community board members in the region.

Councils divided as deadline looms

The backdrop of discussions was fraught before the meeting on Thursday, with councils across the region disagreeing on the model as the deadline for the proposal looms.

Porirua and Lower Hutt city councils, along with South Wairarapa, agreed on a Wellington-Wairarapa council, but Upper Hutt City Council wanted to remain separate.

Masterton and Carterton want to create their own Wairarapa Unitary council, while Kāpiti wanted to remain either its own council or join with Horowhenua.

Mayor Andrew Little said the proposal being considered was "far from perfect", but it was the best the council could do given the rushed timeframe.

The decision was about future generations, he said. Wellington region had been "anemic" economically for some time, and was woefully under-prepared for climate change, he added.

It needed a bigger platform to advocate for itself, he said.

"Put aside Head Start, put aside the dodgy process, can we seriously address those challenges under the status quo?" My view is not."

Councillor Diane Calvert put forward an amendment signalling that councillors wanted four Wellington metro councils to merge, with Wairarapa excluded and forming its own council instead.

She said a survey of Wellington city residents had shown a majority did not want to join with Wairarapa.

Councillor Tony Randle RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Councillor Tony Randle agreed.

He said the Greater Wellington Regional Council was spending $30 million a year more in Wairarapa than it received in revenue from the area - and Wellington city ratepayers were subsidising services.

"What's been missing from this whole thing is the justification, of why Wellington city residents should be funding people who choose to not live in Wellington, but who actually live in far cheaper housing, far far away, and who pay much lower rates."

Little disagreed, arguing that Wairarapa and Wellington were "wholly integrated regions - not just 'rural folks' versus 'urban folks'".

He said excluding Wairarapa would increase transport costs for those residents and have a direct effect on the labour market.

Environmental regulations and management, currently carried out through the regional council, would suffer - to the detriment of the region.

Councillor Jonny Osbourne put forward an amendment - which passed - to seek advice from officials on a possible referendum later on the issue later in the year. It was indicated that central government would not support that.

Porirua and Lower Hutt had already done this, he said.

"If Wellingtonians are not given the same opportunity via a referendum, lingering discord with any significant reform with the way we govern ourselves will exacerbate divisions which naturally occur in communities, but are occurring unfortunately more and more."

That passed, with councillors discussing whether the process had been democratic at all.

What about Upper Hutt?

Councillor Geordie Rogers submitted an amendment that other councils shouldn't be coerced into a merger councillors had voted against.

The comments came after Upper Hutt City Council voted against any amalgamation plans, and mayor Peri Zee said that the city shouldn't be forced into a merger against its will.

Rogers said he was doing this in the interests of Wellington city residents, saying the disagreements between councils could lead to "bad consequences".

The amendment, however, failed.

Upper Hutt mayor urging Wellington councils not to force amalgamation Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Randle conceded four councils didn't want the plan, likening the arrangement to a "shotgun marriage".

"I don't think those marriages really work out," Randle added.

But he ultimately decided not to support the amendment, on the basis that Upper Hutt was part of the region's catchment areas and economy.

What do iwi representatives think?

Kara Puketapu-Dentice presented a letter on behalf of iwi leaders across the region, which urged councillors to think of future generations.

This was not a "restructure of councils", he said, but a chance to build something new.

"The decisions in front of us are mokopuna decisions.

"The people who will live longest inside what we choose are not yet in any of our rooms, and they will not ask which council held which preference in 2026," the letter said.

Kara Puketapu-Dentice RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Councillor Matthew Reweti, representing the Māori Ward, said the Local Government Act and the Head Start process required discussions with iwi.

He said any future model must retain Māori representation.

In Wellington, 68 percent voted to retain the Māori ward, and Porirua, Lower Hutt, Kāpiti, Masterton and South Wairarapa also voted to retain the wards, Reweti said.

"The iwi leaders have come together...and they have asked councils to pursue the Head Start pathway, rather than default to the government's back stop process."

[h] What happens now?

On Friday, mayors will meet to work out the proposal which will go to ministers.

Speaking after the meeting, Little said he was confident an agreement on an amalgamation model could be reached.

World.title: Performance measures linked to reducing emergency housing numbers dropped
World.content:
Highly criticised performance measures linked to reducing the number of people in emergency housing have been dropped by the Ministry of Social Development.

The government had come under intense pressure from the opposition and housing providers in recent months following revelations senior managers at the ministry (MSD) had performance agreements related to reducing emergency housing numbers.

Regional leaders for the ministry have been told, now the emergency housing reduction target was met, the expectation was that they shift their focus to achieving "sustainable housing for people currently in emergency housing and offering other support for those who are not eligible."

But the emergency housing target had already been met before the performance measures were specified last year.

It was revealed in June MSD managers could be pulled into line if they were not contributing to the reduction of people living in emergency housing - something the minister in charge, Tama Potaka, said was a matter for the ministry leadership and not him.

But the MSD boss had defended linking staff performance with cutting emergency housing numbers, saying it's executing the government's policy.

The coalition set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent by the end of 2029 - which was achieved early last year - and introduced rules making emergency housing harder to get into, and harder to stay in.

On Thursday, MSD sent out the latest performance letters for the new financial year to regional leadership.

Group general manager for service delivery Graham Allpress said MSD was asking regional leaders to strengthen their focus on helping people secure stable housing after they leave emergency housing.

Allpress also said he expected the number of households in emergency housing to remain "broadly stable over the coming year."

"There are no goals in the letters for regions to reduce the number of households in emergency housing."

Last year, "housing services effectiveness" was a performance measure, with a number of supporting indicators for the overarching emergency housing reduction focus.

This year, the housing monitors performance measure and supporting indicators were now regarding the overarching "sustainable housing support" focus.

The government's emergency housing target was to be maintained, but there were now measures around achieving a target of initial appointments, early intervention and public housing assessment for those in emergency housing.

Five priority areas were also outlined in the correspondence, including consistency of service, accuracy, employment outcomes, effective management of contracted services, and housing support.

These differ slightly from the previous year's letter: effective and efficient commissioning, leadership of regional teams, consistency and efficiency of service, and driving performance.

As well, regional leaders were told last year that performance targets would be assessed quarterly and "where performance does not meet expectations, you will be required to develop and implement targeted improvement plans to address gaps and restore performance."
